uni-ba-eng-american-lit.title: American Literature
uni-ba-eng-american-lit.description: Puritan beginnings, Transcendentalism, the American Renaissance, Whitman and Dickinson, realism, Modernist poetry and fiction, drama, and African American writing. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. English programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Puritans to the American Renaissance
courses.summary: Puritan writing, the Revolutionary era, Transcendentalism (Emerson, Thoreau), and the fiction of Hawthorne, Melville and Poe.
outcomes: Describe Puritan literature and its worldview
Explain Transcendentalism through Emerson and Thoreau
Analyse The Scarlet Letter's symbolism
Discuss Moby-Dick and Poe's tales

scenes.text: 1630: aboard the Arbella, John Winthrop tells settlers 'we shall be as a city upon a hill'.
1776: Jefferson drafts 'all men are created equal'.

steps.title: Puritan writing
steps.body: Calvinist beliefs: predestination, original sin, the covenant, providence. Forms: sermons, diaries, histories, captivity narratives, plain-style poetry. William Bradford (Of Plymouth Plantation), Anne Bradstreet (The Tenth Muse, 1650; 'To My Dear and Loving Husband'), Edward Taylor (meditations), Mary Rowlandson (captivity narrative, 1682), Jonathan Edwards ('Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God', 1741).

steps.title: Revolutionary and early national
steps.body: Benjamin Franklin (Autobiography; Poor Richard's Almanack), Thomas Paine (Common Sense, 1776), Jefferson (Declaration of Independence). Early fiction: Washington Irving ('Rip Van Winkle', 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow'), James Fenimore Cooper (Leatherstocking Tales; The Last of the Mohicans, 1826).

steps.title: Bradstreet
steps.body: 'If ever two were one, then surely we': domestic love expressed in Puritan terms; ends hoping 'when we live no more, we may live ever' — love tied to eternal life.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' belongs to the Great Awakening (1740s), not the first Puritan generation.

activity.prompt: Puritan era or Revolutionary/early national?

quiz.q: 'A city upon a hill' comes from:
quiz.why: Winthrop's 1630 sermon 'A Model of Christian Charity' uses the phrase.

quiz.q: The Last of the Mohicans is by:
quiz.why: James Fenimore Cooper published it in 1826.
Paine's pamphlet urged independence in plain language.

scenes.text: Emerson in the woods becomes 'a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all'.
1845: Thoreau builds a cabin at Walden Pond 'to live deliberately'.

steps.title: Transcendentalism
steps.body: New England movement (1830s–40s) influenced by Kant, Coleridge, German idealism and Indian scriptures (Gita, Upanishads). Beliefs: intuition over reason, divinity in nature and the individual, the Over-Soul, self-reliance, non-conformity.

steps.title: Ralph Waldo Emerson
steps.body: Nature (1836), 'The American Scholar' (1837, 'America's intellectual Declaration of Independence' — Holmes), 'Self-Reliance' ('Trust thyself'; 'A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds'), 'The Over-Soul', poem 'Brahma'.

steps.title: Henry David Thoreau
steps.body: Walden (1854): two years, two months, two days at Walden Pond; simplicity, economy, nature. 'Civil Disobedience' (1849): refused poll tax opposing slavery and Mexican War; influenced Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

steps.title: Walden
steps.body: 'I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life'; 'The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.' The pond as mirror of the self; seasons structure the book.

activity.prompt: Emerson or Thoreau?

quiz.why: Gandhi read Thoreau's essay and cited it in South Africa.

quiz.q: Emerson's poem 'Brahma' shows the influence of:
quiz.why: It echoes the Katha Upanishad and the Gita on the indestructible self.
Thoreau observes this of the mass of men in the first chapter of Walden.

scenes.text: Hester Prynne stands on the scaffold with baby Pearl and a scarlet A on her breast.
A raven taps at a chamber door: 'Quoth the Raven, Nevermore.'

steps.title: Nathaniel Hawthorne
steps.body: The Scarlet Letter (1850): 17th-century Boston; Hester, Reverend Arthur Dimmesdale (secret father), Roger Chillingworth (vengeful husband), Pearl (living symbol). The A changes meaning from Adultery to 'Able' and perhaps Angel. Themes: sin, guilt, hypocrisy, isolation. Also The House of the Seven Gables, 'Young Goodman Brown'.

steps.title: Edgar Allan Poe
steps.body: Tales: 'The Fall of the House of Usher', 'The Tell-Tale Heart', 'The Cask of Amontillado', 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' (first modern detective story, Dupin, 1841). Poems: 'The Raven' (1845), 'Annabel Lee'. Essays: 'The Philosophy of Composition' (on 'The Raven': death of a beautiful woman is 'the most poetical topic'), 'The Poetic Principle'.

steps.title: 'The Tell-Tale Heart'
steps.body: Unreliable first-person narrator insists on his sanity while describing murder; hears the victim's heart beating under the floor; confesses. Single effect: mounting terror and guilt.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Pearl is Hester and Dimmesdale's daughter, not Chillingworth's.

activity.prompt: Hawthorne or Poe?

items.text: The House of the Seven Gables
The Murders in the Rue Morgue

quiz.why: The minister Arthur Dimmesdale is Pearl's secret father.
C. Auguste Dupin solves crimes by ratiocination in Poe's tales.

quiz.q: 'The Philosophy of Composition' explains how Poe wrote:
quiz.why: Poe claimed to have composed 'The Raven' methodically, working back from the effect.

scenes.text: Captain Ahab nails a gold doubloon to the mast for the first man to sight the white whale.
Only Ishmael survives, floating on Queequeg's coffin.

steps.title: Herman Melville (1819–1891)
steps.body: Typee, Moby-Dick; or, The Whale (1851, dedicated to Hawthorne), 'Bartleby, the Scrivener' (1853: 'I would prefer not to'), Billy Budd (posthumous, 1924). F.O. Matthiessen's American Renaissance (1941) grouped Emerson, Thoreau, Hawthorne, Melville and Whitman.

steps.title: Moby-Dick
steps.body: Ishmael narrates; the Pequod from Nantucket; Ahab lost his leg to the white whale and seeks revenge; crew includes Starbuck, Stubb, Flask, harpooners Queequeg, Tashtego, Daggoo; cetology chapters; 'The Whiteness of the Whale'. Ending: three-day chase, ship sinks.

steps.title: Interpretations
steps.body: The whale as God, nature, evil, the unknowable; Ahab's monomania as Promethean defiance or tyranny; the multinational crew as America; epic, tragedy, encyclopaedia combined.

steps.title: 'Bartleby'
steps.body: A copyist's passive refusal 'I would prefer not to' undoes his lawyer-employer; read as critique of Wall Street work and as existential alienation.

activity.prompt: Moby-Dick character roles.

quiz.why: Melville dedicated it to Hawthorne 'in token of my admiration for his genius'.

quiz.q: 'I would prefer not to' is said by:
quiz.why: Bartleby's polite refusal is the refrain of Melville's 1853 story.
F.O. Matthiessen's 1941 study named the 1850–55 flowering.

questions.q: 'The Fall of the House of Usher' is by:

options: Intuition and the divine in nature

questions.q: Hester's letter later is said to mean:
questions.why: Townspeople reinterpret it through her charity.

questions.q: Rip Van Winkle sleeps for about:

courses.title: Unit 2 · Whitman, Dickinson and Realism
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (American poetry and fiction)
courses.summary: Whitman's Leaves of Grass, Dickinson's lyrics, and the realist and naturalist fiction of Twain, James, Crane and others.
outcomes: Analyse Whitman's free verse and democratic vision
Interpret Dickinson's themes, dashes and slant rhyme
Discuss Huckleberry Finn as realist and moral novel
Describe Henry James's international theme and naturalism

scenes.text: 1855: a thin green book with no author's name on the cover — Leaves of Grass.
1865: 'O Captain! my Captain!' mourns the murdered Lincoln.

steps.title: Leaves of Grass
steps.body: First edition 1855 (12 poems); expanded through the 'deathbed edition' 1891–92. 'Song of Myself' ('I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume'), 'Crossing Brooklyn Ferry', 'Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking', 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd' (Lincoln elegy), 'I Hear America Singing', 'Passage to India'.

steps.title: Style
steps.body: Free verse with long lines; cataloguing; anaphora; parallelism (influenced by the King James Bible); the expansive democratic 'I' who contains multitudes ('Do I contradict myself? / Very well then I contradict myself, / (I am large, I contain multitudes.)').

steps.title: 'I Hear America Singing'
steps.body: Catalogue of workers — mechanic, carpenter, mason, boatman, shoemaker, mother — 'each singing what belongs to him or her and to none else': democratic individuality within a national chorus.

steps.title: Emerson's letter
steps.body: Emerson wrote to Whitman in 1855: 'I greet you at the beginning of a great career.'

activity.prompt: Which Whitman feature is shown?

items.text: Lines of varying length without fixed metre

quiz.q: 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd' mourns:
quiz.why: It is Whitman's elegy for Abraham Lincoln after his assassination in 1865.
Whitman embraces contradiction in section 51 of 'Song of Myself'.

quiz.q: The first Leaves of Grass appeared in:
quiz.why: Whitman self-published it in July 1855.

scenes.text: In Amherst, Emily Dickinson writes nearly 1,800 poems, publishing about ten in her lifetime.
'Because I could not stop for Death – / He kindly stopped for me –'

steps.title: Life and texts
steps.body: Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) lived reclusively in Amherst, Massachusetts. Poems found after her death in hand-sewn fascicles; first edition 1890 (heavily edited); Thomas H. Johnson's complete edition 1955 restored dashes and numbered them.

steps.title: Style
steps.body: Short lyrics in hymn/common metre (alternating 8 and 6 syllables), slant rhyme, dashes, capitalised nouns, compression, startling metaphors. Themes: death, immortality, nature, faith and doubt, the self, love, pain.

steps.title: 'Because I could not stop for Death'
steps.body: Death is a courteous suitor in a carriage with Immortality; they pass the school, 'Fields of Gazing Grain', 'the Setting Sun'; pause at a house that is 'A Swelling of the Ground' (grave); 'Since then – 'tis Centuries'. Calm irony toward mortality.

steps.title: Other poems
steps.body: 'Hope is the thing with feathers', 'I heard a Fly buzz – when I died', 'There's a certain Slant of light', 'Success is counted sweetest', 'I'm Nobody! Who are you?', 'Tell all the truth but tell it slant', 'After great pain, a formal feeling comes'.

activity.prompt: Order the carriage journey in 'Because I could not stop for Death'.
items: They pass the school where children strove
They pass fields of gazing grain
They pause before a house — a swelling of the ground
Centuries feel shorter than the day

quiz.why: She adapted the 8-6-8-6 hymn metre of Protestant hymnals.

quiz.q: The complete 1955 edition was edited by:
quiz.why: Johnson's variorum edition restored her original punctuation.

quiz.q: 'Hope is the thing with feathers' compares hope to:
quiz.why: Hope is an indefatigable bird that sings in the soul and asks nothing.

story.title: All right, then, I'll go to hell

scenes.text: Huck and the escaped slave Jim drift down the Mississippi on a raft.
Huck tears up the letter betraying Jim: 'All right, then, I'll go to hell.'

steps.title: Twain (Samuel Clemens, 1835–1910)
steps.body: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), Life on the Mississippi, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884/85), A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court, Pudd'nhead Wilson. Hemingway: 'All modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called Huckleberry Finn.'

steps.title: Huckleberry Finn
steps.body: First-person vernacular narration; river (freedom) vs shore (corruption: feuding Grangerfords, the Duke and the King's frauds, lynch mob). Huck's moral crisis: society's conscience vs natural sympathy for Jim. Controversial ending with Tom Sawyer's elaborate 'rescue'.

steps.title: Realism
steps.body: Post-Civil War realism (c.1865–1900): ordinary life, middle class, plausible motive, regional dialect (local colour). William Dean Howells (The Rise of Silas Lapham), Kate Chopin (The Awakening, 1899), Sarah Orne Jewett.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Huck's 'go to hell' decision is ironic: by society's standard it is sin; morally it is his finest moment.

activity.prompt: River or shore episode in Huckleberry Finn?

items.text: Huck and Jim on the raft at night
The Duke and King's Royal Nonesuch
Colonel Sherburn faces a lynch mob

quiz.q: Who said modern American literature comes from Huckleberry Finn?
quiz.why: Hemingway said it in Green Hills of Africa (1935).
Kate Chopin's 1899 novel of Edna Pontellier's awakening.
Twain gives Huck a Missouri vernacular voice.

scenes.text: In Rome, innocent Daisy Miller walks with an Italian at night and dies of fever.
In Crane's war, young Henry Fleming runs from battle and longs for a 'red badge'.

steps.title: Henry James (1843–1916)
steps.body: International theme (American innocence vs European experience): Daisy Miller (1878), The Portrait of a Lady (1881, Isabel Archer), The Ambassadors, The Wings of the Dove, The Golden Bowl. 'The Turn of the Screw' (1898, ambiguous ghosts). Point-of-view technique ('central consciousness'); essay 'The Art of Fiction' (1884).

steps.title: Naturalism
steps.body: Influenced by Zola and Darwin: characters shaped by heredity, environment and chance, often in poverty. Stephen Crane (Maggie: A Girl of the Streets; The Red Badge of Courage, 1895; 'The Open Boat'), Frank Norris (McTeague), Theodore Dreiser (Sister Carrie, 1900), Jack London.

steps.title: Portrait of a Lady
steps.body: Isabel Archer, given a fortune, chooses to marry Gilbert Osmond, manipulated by Madame Merle; she returns to Osmond at the end — freedom examined as responsibility.

steps.title: Realism vs naturalism
steps.body: Realism: ordinary life with free moral choice. Naturalism: determinism by forces beyond control.

activity.prompt: Realist or naturalist?

items.text: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets

quiz.q: The Red Badge of Courage is by:
quiz.why: Stephen Crane published it in 1895.
His Americans abroad meet older European manners and corruption.
Naturalists depict characters determined by biological and social forces.

questions.q: 'I heard a Fly buzz – when I died' is by:
'Tell all the truth but tell it slant' expresses:
'The Turn of the Screw' is famous for:

courses.title: Unit 3 · Modern American Poetry and Fiction
courses.summary: Frost, Stevens, Williams, Pound and Plath/Lowell; the Lost Generation: Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Faulkner; Steinbeck and Salinger.
outcomes: Analyse Frost's 'Stopping by Woods' and 'The Road Not Taken'
Explain Imagism and Williams's and Stevens's poetics
Discuss The Great Gatsby and the American Dream
Describe Hemingway's iceberg theory and Faulkner's techniques

scenes.text: A traveller stops his horse by snowy woods on 'the darkest evening of the year'.
After apple-picking, a farmer drowses, unsure if it is ordinary sleep.

steps.title: Frost (1874–1963)
steps.body: New England rural settings, blank verse dramatic narratives and lyrics, colloquial voice in traditional metre ('like playing tennis without a net' — his view of free verse). A Boy's Will (1913), North of Boston (1914: 'Mending Wall', 'Home Burial', 'After Apple-Picking', 'The Death of the Hired Man'), Mountain Interval ('The Road Not Taken', 'Birches'), New Hampshire. Four Pulitzer Prizes.

steps.title: 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening'
steps.body: Iambic tetrameter quatrains rhyming aaba bbcb ccdc dddd (interlocking). 'The woods are lovely, dark and deep, / But I have promises to keep, / And miles to go before I sleep' — repeated last line suggests death and duty.

steps.title: 'Mending Wall'
steps.body: 'Something there is that doesn't love a wall' vs the neighbour's 'Good fences make good neighbors': tradition vs questioning, ironic speaker.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'The Road Not Taken' is often misread as praise of nonconformity; the roads were 'really about the same', and the 'sigh' suggests ironic self-mythologising.

activity.prompt: Which Frost poem?

items.text: Miles to go before I sleep
Two roads diverged in a yellow wood
One could do worse than be a swinger of birches

quiz.why: He valued the tension of metre and called free verse tennis without a net.
It opens North of Boston (1914).

quiz.q: The rhyme scheme of 'Stopping by Woods' is:
quiz.why: Each stanza's third-line rhyme becomes the next stanza's main rhyme.

scenes.text: In a Paris metro station Pound sees faces like 'Petals on a wet, black bough'.
Williams writes of a red wheelbarrow glazed with rain water beside white chickens.

steps.title: Ezra Pound
steps.body: Imagism, 'In a Station of the Metro' (1913, two lines influenced by haiku), Hugh Selwyn Mauberley (1920), The Cantos. Edited Eliot. 'Make it new'.

steps.title: William Carlos Williams
steps.body: Physician-poet from New Jersey; 'No ideas but in things'; American idiom; 'The Red Wheelbarrow', 'This Is Just To Say', Spring and All (1923), Paterson.

steps.title: Wallace Stevens
steps.body: Insurance executive; imagination and reality: 'Anecdote of the Jar', 'The Emperor of Ice-Cream', 'Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird', 'The Snow Man', Harmonium (1923).

steps.title: Mid-century
steps.body: Confessional poets: Robert Lowell (Life Studies, 1959), Sylvia Plath ('Daddy', 'Lady Lazarus', Ariel), Anne Sexton. Beat poets: Allen Ginsberg ('Howl', 1956). Langston Hughes (see Unit 5), Elizabeth Bishop ('One Art').

activity.prompt: Match the poem to the poet.

items.text: In a Station of the Metro

quiz.q: 'No ideas but in things' is the motto of:
quiz.why: William Carlos Williams repeats it in Paterson.
Allen Ginsberg's 1956 Beat poem.

quiz.q: Life Studies (1959) is a landmark of:
quiz.why: Lowell's frank autobiographical poems launched the confessional mode.

scenes.text: Gatsby stretches his arms toward a green light at the end of Daisy's dock.
Old Santiago fights a giant marlin for three days.

steps.title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
steps.body: Jazz Age chronicler. The Great Gatsby (1925): narrator Nick Carraway; Jay Gatsby (born James Gatz), Daisy and Tom Buchanan, Jordan Baker, Myrtle and George Wilson; West Egg vs East Egg; the valley of ashes; eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg; green light. Theme: corruption of the American Dream. 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'

steps.title: Ernest Hemingway
steps.body: The Sun Also Rises (1926; 'Lost Generation' epigraph from Gertrude Stein), A Farewell to Arms (1929), For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940), The Old Man and the Sea (1952, Pulitzer). Nobel 1954. Iceberg theory (omission): seven-eighths below the surface. Code hero: grace under pressure. Short declarative sentences.

steps.title: The Old Man and the Sea
steps.body: Santiago, unlucky for 84 days, hooks a marlin; sharks devour it; he returns with the skeleton: 'A man can be destroyed but not defeated.' Dignity in defeat; Christian imagery.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Nick Carraway, not Gatsby, narrates The Great Gatsby; he is a partly unreliable, involved narrator.

activity.prompt: Gatsby symbol or Hemingway feature?

quiz.q: 'A man can be destroyed but not defeated' is from:
options: The Old Man and the Sea
quiz.why: Santiago says it while fighting the sharks.
He reinvented himself from James Gatz of North Dakota.
Stein's remark appears as the epigraph to The Sun Also Rises.

scenes.text: Quentin Compson breaks his grandfather's watch on his last day at Harvard.
The Joads drive from the Oklahoma Dust Bowl to California.

steps.title: William Faulkner
steps.body: Fictional Yoknapatawpha County, Mississippi. The Sound and the Fury (1929: four sections — Benjy, Quentin, Jason, narrator/Dilsey; stream of consciousness; title from Macbeth), As I Lay Dying (15 narrators), Light in August, Absalom, Absalom!, 'A Rose for Emily'. Nobel 1949. The Southern past and decline.

steps.title: John Steinbeck
steps.body: Of Mice and Men (1937, George and Lennie), The Grapes of Wrath (1939, Pulitzer; Joad family, Dust Bowl migrants, intercalary chapters). Nobel 1962.

steps.title: Post-war fiction
steps.body: J.D. Salinger: The Catcher in the Rye (1951; Holden Caulfield, 'phonies'). Ralph Ellison: Invisible Man (1952). Saul Bellow, Philip Roth, Harper Lee (To Kill a Mockingbird, 1960), Kurt Vonnegut (Slaughterhouse-Five), Thomas Pynchon (postmodernism).

steps.title: 'A Rose for Emily'
steps.body: Non-chronological sections; townspeople as 'we' narrator; the final discovery of Homer Barron's corpse and a strand of grey hair on the pillow — the Old South clinging to the dead past.

activity.prompt: Order the four sections of The Sound and the Fury.

quiz.q: The Sound and the Fury's title comes from:
quiz.why: Macbeth's 'a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury'.
The Joad family flee Oklahoma for California during the Depression.
He constantly condemns adult 'phoniness'.

questions.q: The Great Gatsby was published in:
As I Lay Dying has how many narrators?

courses.title: Unit 4 · American Drama
courses.summary: Eugene O'Neill, Tennessee Williams, Arthur Miller, Edward Albee and later dramatists.
outcomes: Discuss O'Neill's experimental and family tragedies
Analyse Death of a Salesman as tragedy of the common man
Interpret The Glass Menagerie as memory play
Describe Albee and the American absurd

scenes.text: Fog rolls in over a Connecticut summer house; the Tyrone family unravels into night.
Yank, a stoker, is called a 'filthy beast' and goes to the zoo to find where he belongs.

steps.title: O'Neill (1888–1953)
steps.body: Founder of serious American drama; Nobel 1936; four Pulitzers. Provincetown Players. Expressionist: The Emperor Jones (1920), The Hairy Ape (1922). Realist/tragic: Desire Under the Elms, Mourning Becomes Electra (Oresteia in New England), The Iceman Cometh, Long Day's Journey into Night (written 1941–42, staged 1956; autobiographical).

steps.title: Expressionism
steps.body: Distorted settings, symbolic characters, inner states projected on stage. The Hairy Ape: Yank's search for belonging in industrial society; ends crushed by a gorilla.

steps.title: Long Day's Journey into Night
steps.body: One day in August 1912: James Tyrone (miserly actor), Mary (morphine addiction), Jamie (alcoholic), Edmund (consumption; O'Neill himself). Fog symbolises escape and illusion; Mary's final monologue lost in the past.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Long Day's Journey was published and staged posthumously (1956) against O'Neill's wish for a 25-year delay.

activity.prompt: Expressionist or realist family drama?

quiz.q: O'Neill won the Nobel Prize in:
quiz.why: He remains the only American playwright to win the Nobel, in 1936.
It transposes the Oresteia to post-Civil War New England.
Her morphine addiction began after Edmund's birth.

scenes.text: Willy Loman, 63, comes home exhausted, carrying two heavy sample cases.
In Salem, 1692, John Proctor refuses to sign a false confession: 'Because it is my name!'

steps.title: Miller (1915–2005)
steps.body: All My Sons (1947), Death of a Salesman (1949, Pulitzer), The Crucible (1953, Salem witch trials as allegory of McCarthyism), A View from the Bridge. Essay 'Tragedy and the Common Man' (1949): the common man is as apt a subject for tragedy as kings.

steps.title: Death of a Salesman
steps.body: Willy Loman, a failing salesman, believes in being 'well liked'; sons Biff and Happy; wife Linda ('Attention, attention must be finally paid to such a person'); flashbacks to Ben (success) and Biff's discovery of Willy's affair in Boston; Willy's suicide for insurance; Requiem: 'He never knew who he was' (Biff).

steps.title: The Crucible
steps.body: Abigail Williams accuses others of witchcraft; John Proctor's guilt over his affair; Reverend Hale; Judge Danforth; Proctor dies rather than sign a lie.

steps.title: Technique
steps.body: Expressionist memory scenes flow into present without scene breaks; lighting and flute music signal the past — showing Willy's mind.

activity.prompt: Which Miller play?

quiz.why: Miller used the Salem trials to criticise the 1950s anti-communist hearings.

quiz.q: Miller's essay argues tragedy can be about:
quiz.why: 'Tragedy and the Common Man' claims ordinary people can be tragic heroes.

quiz.q: 'Attention must be paid' is said by:
quiz.why: Linda defends Willy's dignity to her sons.

scenes.text: Laura's glass unicorn loses its horn when Jim dances with her.
Blanche DuBois arrives in New Orleans on a streetcar named Desire.

steps.title: Williams (1911–1983)
steps.body: The Glass Menagerie (1944), A Streetcar Named Desire (1947, Pulitzer), Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1955, Pulitzer), Suddenly Last Summer. Southern Gothic, fragile heroines, desire and decay, 'plastic theatre'.

steps.title: The Glass Menagerie
steps.body: A 'memory play' narrated by Tom Wingfield; mother Amanda (faded Southern belle), sister Laura (shy, lame, glass animals), gentleman caller Jim O'Connor (engaged elsewhere). Screen device/legends, music, lighting. Tom: 'Blow out your candles, Laura.'

steps.title: A Streetcar Named Desire
steps.body: Blanche (illusion, the Old South) vs Stanley Kowalski (brutal reality, new urban America); Stella between; Mitch; Belle Reve lost; ends with Blanche taken to an asylum: 'I have always depended on the kindness of strangers.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Tom is both narrator and character in The Glass Menagerie; his opening speech says 'the play is memory'.

activity.prompt: Which play?

quiz.q: The narrator of The Glass Menagerie is:
quiz.why: Tom Wingfield narrates from memory and acts in the scenes.
Blanche and Stella's lost estate symbolises the vanished Old South.

quiz.q: A Streetcar Named Desire won the Pulitzer in:
quiz.why: It received the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1948.

scenes.text: At 2 a.m., George and Martha drag a young couple into their games of 'Get the Guests'.
In Pittsburgh, August Wilson's Troy Maxson builds a fence.

steps.title: Edward Albee
steps.body: The Zoo Story (1959), The American Dream (1961; Esslin included him in the Absurd), Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1962): George and Martha, Nick and Honey; illusions (imaginary son) exposed; 'Exorcism'. A Delicate Balance, Three Tall Women (Pulitzers).

steps.title: Later voices
steps.body: Lorraine Hansberry: A Raisin in the Sun (1959; first Broadway play by a Black woman). August Wilson: Pittsburgh Cycle (Fences 1985, The Piano Lesson). Sam Shepard (True West, Buried Child), David Mamet (Glengarry Glen Ross), Tony Kushner (Angels in America).

steps.title: A Raisin in the Sun
steps.body: The Younger family's $10,000 insurance cheque: Mama buys a house in white Clybourne Park; Walter Lee loses money; refuses Lindner's buyout. Title from Langston Hughes's 'Harlem': 'What happens to a dream deferred?'

steps.title: Linking theme
steps.body: The American Dream recurs: Gatsby, Willy Loman, the Youngers, Albee's satire.

activity.prompt: Match the play to the playwright.

quiz.q: The title A Raisin in the Sun comes from:
quiz.why: It comes from Hughes's poem 'Harlem' about a dream deferred.
Their son is a shared fiction that George finally 'kills'.
August Wilson's ten-play cycle covers each decade of the 20th century.

questions.q: Death of a Salesman premiered in:
Laura's glass animal that breaks is a:
Cat on a Hot Tin Roof is by:
Albee was grouped with the Absurd by:
questions.why: In The Theatre of the Absurd.

courses.title: Unit 5 · African American and Multi-ethnic Writing; Revision
courses.summary: Slave narratives, Du Bois, the Harlem Renaissance, Wright, Ellison, Baldwin, Morrison, Walker, Angelou; Native and Asian American voices; revision.
outcomes: Explain the slave narrative and Du Bois's double consciousness
Discuss the Harlem Renaissance through Hughes and Hurston
Analyse Morrison's Beloved
Revise American literature chronologically

scenes.text: Young Frederick Douglass learns that reading is 'the pathway from slavery to freedom'.
Du Bois writes of 'this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others'.

steps.title: Slave narratives
steps.body: Autobiographical accounts of enslavement and escape: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845), Harriet Jacobs's Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861). Phillis Wheatley: first published African American poet (Poems on Various Subjects, 1773). Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852, white abolitionist novel).

steps.title: W.E.B. Du Bois
steps.body: The Souls of Black Folk (1903): 'The problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line'; the 'veil'; 'double consciousness' — 'two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings'. Debated Booker T. Washington's accommodationism (Up from Slavery).

steps.title: Douglass's turning point
steps.body: His fight with the 'slave-breaker' Covey: 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.' Literacy and resistance as self-making.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Uncle Tom's Cabin is not a slave narrative; it is a novel by a white author.

activity.prompt: Slave narrative or other?

items.text: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl

quiz.why: Du Bois introduced it in The Souls of Black Folk (1903).
Published 1845 with prefaces by Garrison and Phillips.

quiz.q: The first published African American poet was:
quiz.why: Wheatley's Poems on Various Subjects was printed in London in 1773.

scenes.text: 1920s Harlem: jazz clubs, magazines, poetry readings — 'the New Negro'.
'I, too, sing America. / I am the darker brother.'

steps.title: Harlem Renaissance (1920s–30s)
steps.body: Alain Locke's anthology The New Negro (1925). Langston Hughes ('The Negro Speaks of Rivers', 'I, Too', 'Harlem', 'The Weary Blues'; blues and jazz rhythms), Claude McKay ('If We Must Die'), Countee Cullen ('Yet Do I Marvel'), Jean Toomer (Cane), Zora Neale Hurston (Their Eyes Were Watching God, 1937; Janie's quest for voice).

steps.title: 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers'
steps.body: 'I've known rivers ancient as the world': Euphrates, Congo, Nile, Mississippi; 'My soul has grown deep like the rivers' — collective memory and dignity across history.

steps.title: Mid-century
steps.body: Richard Wright: Native Son (1940, Bigger Thomas), Black Boy. Ralph Ellison: Invisible Man (1952; 'I am an invisible man… because people refuse to see me'). James Baldwin: Go Tell It on the Mountain, Notes of a Native Son, The Fire Next Time. Gwendolyn Brooks (first Black Pulitzer, 1950).

steps.title: Contemporary
steps.body: Maya Angelou (I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, 1969; 'Still I Rise'), Alice Walker (The Color Purple, 1982, Pulitzer; 'womanist'), Toni Morrison (next lesson).

quiz.why: Alain Locke's anthology defined the movement.

quiz.q: Their Eyes Were Watching God's heroine:
quiz.why: Janie Crawford narrates her three marriages and search for self.
Ralph Ellison's 1952 novel won the National Book Award.

scenes.text: In Ohio, 1873, a house is haunted by the ghost of a baby girl.
A young woman called Beloved appears, and Sethe's past returns.

steps.title: Toni Morrison (1931–2019)
steps.body: The Bluest Eye (1970, Pecola Breedlove wishes for blue eyes), Sula, Song of Solomon, Beloved (1987, Pulitzer 1988), Jazz, Paradise. Nobel 1993 — first Black woman. Essay Playing in the Dark (1992).

steps.title: Beloved
steps.body: Based on Margaret Garner's case. Sethe escaped slavery from Sweet Home and killed her daughter to save her from recapture; the ghost becomes Beloved; Paul D, Denver, Baby Suggs; 'rememory'; community women exorcise Beloved. Dedication: 'Sixty Million and more'.

steps.title: Other ethnic voices
steps.body: Native American: N. Scott Momaday (House Made of Dawn, Pulitzer 1969), Leslie Marmon Silko (Ceremony), Louise Erdrich. Asian American: Maxine Hong Kingston (The Woman Warrior), Amy Tan (The Joy Luck Club). Latino: Sandra Cisneros (The House on Mango Street).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Beloved is not a straightforward ghost story; it is about memory and the trauma of slavery.

quiz.why: She received the Nobel in 1993.

scenes.text: 1630 Winthrop → 1850 Scarlet Letter → 1855 Leaves of Grass → 1925 Gatsby → 1949 Salesman → 1987 Beloved.
Practise connecting texts by the theme of the American Dream.

steps.title: Key-point sheet
steps.body: Puritans (Bradstreet, Edwards) · Transcendentalism (Emerson 1836, Thoreau 1854) · Renaissance (Hawthorne 1850, Melville 1851, Whitman 1855) · Dickinson · Realism (Twain 1884, James) · Naturalism (Crane, Dreiser) · Modern poetry (Frost, Pound, Williams, Stevens, Eliot) · Lost Generation (Fitzgerald 1925, Hemingway) · Faulkner 1929 · Drama (O'Neill, Williams 1944/47, Miller 1949/53, Albee 1962) · Harlem Renaissance · Morrison 1987.

steps.title: Long answers (original)
steps.body: (1) Transcendentalism in Emerson's 'Self-Reliance'. (2) Symbolism in The Scarlet Letter. (3) Whitman as poet of democracy. (4) Death and immortality in Dickinson. (5) The American Dream in The Great Gatsby and Death of a Salesman. (6) Memory and slavery in Beloved.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.body: Lost Generation; Iceberg theory; Imagism; Memory play; Double consciousness; Harlem Renaissance; Naturalism.

steps.title: Comparison tip
steps.body: Compare across periods: Thoreau's 'Civil Disobedience' with Douglass's resistance; Huck's raft with Gatsby's green light as images of freedom and illusion.

uni-ba-eng-british-lit-1.description: Chaucer, Renaissance poetry and drama, Shakespeare, the Metaphysicals, Milton, Restoration and Augustan literature, and the rise of the novel. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. English programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Chaucer and Medieval Literature
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (British Poetry and Drama 14th–17th c.)
courses.summary: Old and Middle English background, Chaucer's life and works, the General Prologue to The Canterbury Tales, and medieval drama.
outcomes: Outline Old English and Middle English periods and key texts
Describe the frame and design of The Canterbury Tales
Analyse portraits from the General Prologue
Explain Chaucer's realism, irony and humour
Distinguish mystery, miracle and morality plays

lessons.title: From Old English to Middle English

scenes.text: Beowulf fights Grendel in a language modern readers cannot follow without a glossary.
After 1066 Norman French rules the court, and English absorbs thousands of French words.

steps.title: Old English (c.450–1100)
steps.body: Germanic, inflected language of Anglo-Saxons. Alliterative verse with a caesura in each line. Key texts: Beowulf, Caedmon's Hymn, 'The Wanderer', 'The Seafarer'; prose of King Alfred and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

steps.title: Middle English (c.1100–1500)
steps.body: After the Norman Conquest, French became the language of the court and law; English re-emerged in the 14th century, enriched by French vocabulary. Key writers: Chaucer, Langland (Piers Plowman), Gower (Confessio Amantis), the Gawain-poet (Sir Gawain and the Green Knight), Malory (Le Morte d'Arthur, printed by Caxton 1485).

steps.title: Caxton
steps.body: William Caxton set up the first printing press in England at Westminster in 1476; he printed The Canterbury Tales c.1477.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Chaucer wrote in Middle English (London dialect), not Old English. Beowulf is Old English.

activity.prompt: Old English or Middle English text?

items.text: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

quiz.q: Caxton's press was set up in:
quiz.why: Caxton began printing at Westminster in 1476.
William Langland wrote the alliterative dream-vision Piers Plowman.

quiz.q: Old English verse is marked by:
quiz.why: Old English poetry uses stressed alliteration across a line split by a mid-line pause.

scenes.text: In April, twenty-nine pilgrims gather at the Tabard Inn, Southwark.
Harry Bailly, the Host, proposes a story contest: the best tale wins a free supper.

steps.title: Chaucer (c.1343–1400)
steps.body: Courtier, diplomat, controller of customs; called the 'Father of English Poetry' (by Dryden). Periods: French (The Book of the Duchess), Italian (Troilus and Criseyde, The Parliament of Fowls), English (The Canterbury Tales). Buried in Westminster Abbey, origin of Poets' Corner.

steps.title: The frame
steps.body: Pilgrims travel from Southwark to the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury. The Host plans four tales each (two each way); Chaucer completed only 24 tales. Mostly in heroic couplets (iambic pentameter rhymed in pairs).

steps.title: Opening lines
steps.body: 'Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote / The droghte of March hath perced to the roote': spring rains rouse nature and people 'to goon on pilgrimages'. The opening links natural renewal with spiritual longing.

steps.title: Tales and genres
steps.body: Knight's Tale (chivalric romance), Miller's Tale (fabliau, bawdy), Nun's Priest's Tale (beast fable/mock-heroic: Chauntecleer and Pertelote), Pardoner's Tale (exemplum on 'Radix malorum est cupiditas'), Wife of Bath's Prologue and Tale (marriage debate, 'maistrie').

activity.prompt: Match the tale to its genre.

quiz.why: The General Prologue sets the meeting at the Tabard Inn in Southwark.

options: Greed is the root of evil
quiz.why: He preaches 'Radix malorum est cupiditas' while himself greedy, a famous irony.

quiz.q: Who called Chaucer 'the Father of English Poetry'?
quiz.why: Dryden praised Chaucer in the Preface to Fables (1700) as the father of English poetry.

scenes.text: The Knight, 'a verray, parfit gentil knyght', in a rust-stained tunic.
The Prioress feeds her little dogs roast meat and weeps over a trapped mouse.

steps.title: Estates satire
steps.body: The portraits represent the three estates: those who fight (Knight, Squire), those who pray (Prioress, Monk, Friar, Parson), and those who work (Ploughman, Miller, Merchant). Chaucer uses ironic praise: the naive narrator admires what the reader sees through.

steps.title: The Prioress
steps.body: Madame Eglentyne speaks French 'after the scole of Stratford atte Bowe' (not Paris), has dainty table manners and a brooch reading 'Amor vincit omnia'. Irony: worldly courtliness in a nun.

steps.title: The Monk and the Friar
steps.body: The Monk loves hunting and thinks the old rule 'nat worth an oystre'. The Friar Huberd sells easy penance for money. Contrast: the poor Parson who 'first he wroghte, and afterward he taughte'.

steps.title: Wife of Bath
steps.body: Alisoun has had five husbands 'at chirche dore', is gap-toothed and deaf, a cloth-maker, worldly traveller: a lively, independent figure arguing against clerical anti-feminism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not equate Chaucer-the-narrator with Chaucer-the-poet; the 'naive narrator' is a device for irony.

activity.prompt: Ideal figure or satirised figure?

quiz.why: 'Love conquers all' ambiguously suggests earthly rather than divine love.

quiz.q: Who 'first he wroghte, and afterward he taughte'?
quiz.why: The good Parson practises what he preaches, an ideal contrast to corrupt clergy.

quiz.q: The Wife of Bath has had how many husbands?
quiz.why: The Prologue says she had five husbands at the church door.

scenes.text: In York, guilds roll pageant wagons through the streets, each acting a Bible scene.
Everyman is summoned by Death; only Good Deeds goes with him to the grave.

steps.title: Mystery and miracle plays
steps.body: Mystery plays: Bible stories from Creation to Doomsday, performed in cycles by guilds (York, Wakefield/Towneley, Chester, N-Town). The Wakefield Master's Second Shepherds' Play mixes farce (Mak the sheep-stealer) with the Nativity. Miracle plays: lives of saints.

steps.title: Morality plays and interludes
steps.body: Morality plays personify virtues and vices in a struggle for the soul: Everyman (c.1500), The Castle of Perseverance. Interludes: short secular plays (John Heywood). These led toward Elizabethan drama; the Vice figure influenced Iago and Richard III.

steps.title: Romance
steps.body: Medieval romance: chivalric adventure, courtly love and the marvellous. Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (late 14th c.) in alliterative stanzas with a 'bob and wheel'; Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur in prose.

steps.title: Courtly love
steps.body: A code of refined, often secret love in which the knight serves an idealised lady, from Provençal troubadours.

activity.prompt: Order the development toward Elizabethan drama.

quiz.why: Its characters are personified abstractions like Death, Fellowship and Good Deeds.
The Wakefield Master's play mirrors the Nativity with Mak's stolen lamb in a cradle.

quiz.q: The 'bob and wheel' is found in:
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
quiz.why: The Gawain-poet ends each alliterative stanza with a short 'bob' and rhyming 'wheel'.

The pilgrims are travelling to the shrine of:
The Canterbury Tales are mostly in:

The rooster hero of the Nun's Priest's Tale.
Sir Thomas Malory; printed by Caxton in 1485.

questions.q: The Wife of Bath's Tale answers: what do women most desire?
questions.why: The knight learns women desire mastery over husbands.

questions.q: The Host of the pilgrims is:
questions.why: Harry Bailly proposes the tale-telling contest.
Virtues and vices appear as characters.
Iago's witty, scheming manner recalls the morality Vice.

courses.title: Unit 2 · The Renaissance: Poetry and Pre-Shakespearean Drama
courses.summary: Renaissance humanism and Reformation, Wyatt, Surrey, Sidney and Spenser, the University Wits and Marlowe's Doctor Faustus.
outcomes: Explain humanism, Reformation and their literary effects
Describe the contributions of Wyatt, Surrey, Sidney and Spenser
Summarise The Faerie Queene Book I allegory
Analyse Doctor Faustus as Renaissance tragedy

scenes.text: Greek manuscripts reach Italy; scholars dream of reviving classical learning.
Thomas More imagines Utopia, an island of reason.

steps.title: Background
steps.body: Renaissance: revival of classical learning that began in Italy (14th–15th c.) and reached England c.1500. Humanism emphasised human dignity and Greek/Latin studies (Erasmus, More's Utopia, 1516). The Reformation (Henry VIII's break with Rome, 1534) and Tyndale's Bible shaped prose. Exploration and Copernicus widened horizons.

steps.title: Wyatt and Surrey
steps.body: Sir Thomas Wyatt introduced the Petrarchan sonnet into English ('Whoso list to hunt'). Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, devised the English (later Shakespearean) sonnet form and first used blank verse. Both appeared in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).

steps.title: Sidney
steps.body: Sir Philip Sidney: Astrophil and Stella (sonnet sequence), the Arcadia (prose romance), and An Apology for Poetry/Defence of Poesy, defending poetry as teaching and delighting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The 'Shakespearean' sonnet form predates Shakespeare: Surrey used it first.

activity.prompt: Match the work with its author.

quiz.why: Richard Tottel's 1557 anthology printed Wyatt and Surrey's poems.
More wrote it in Latin in 1516.
Astrophil (star-lover) and Stella (star) is Sidney's sequence.

scenes.text: A knight with a red cross rides beside Una to slay the dragon besieging her parents.
He fights Error, is deceived by Archimago and Duessa, and nearly despairs.

steps.title: Spenser (c.1552–1599)
steps.body: 'The Poets' Poet' (Lamb). Works: The Shepheardes Calender (1579, pastoral eclogues), Amoretti and Epithalamion (1595), The Faerie Queene (Books I–III 1590, IV–VI 1596).

steps.title: Design of The Faerie Queene
steps.body: Planned in twelve books, each with a knight embodying a virtue; six completed. Letter to Raleigh explains the aim 'to fashion a gentleman or noble person in vertuous and gentle discipline'. Gloriana = Elizabeth I. Written in the Spenserian stanza.

steps.title: Book I allegory
steps.body: Red Cross Knight = Holiness/St George/England; Una = true Church/Truth; Duessa = falsehood/Roman Church; Archimago = hypocrisy; Error = a monster vomiting books and papers; House of Holiness restores him; he slays the dragon (Satan).

steps.title: Multiple allegory
steps.body: Spenser's allegory works on moral, religious and political levels at once: answer with at least two levels.

activity.prompt: What does each figure represent in Book I?

quiz.q: How many books of The Faerie Queene did Spenser complete?
quiz.why: Six books were finished, plus the fragmentary Mutability Cantos.
The Faerie Queene Gloriana figures Queen Elizabeth I.
Spenser wrote the marriage ode for his wedding to Elizabeth Boyle in 1594.

scenes.text: Young Oxford and Cambridge graduates write for the new London playhouses.
Kyd's Hieronimo goes mad seeking revenge for his murdered son.

steps.title: Who they were
steps.body: Lyly (Euphues; prose style 'euphuism' with balance and alliteration), Peele, Greene (Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay; attacked Shakespeare as an 'upstart crow'), Nashe (The Unfortunate Traveller), Lodge, Kyd (The Spanish Tragedy) and Marlowe.

steps.title: The theatres
steps.body: The Theatre (1576, James Burbage), the Rose (1587), the Globe (1599). Companies: the Lord Chamberlain's Men (Shakespeare), the Admiral's Men (Alleyn acting Marlowe).

steps.title: Marlowe's achievement
steps.body: Christopher Marlowe (1564–1593): Tamburlaine, Doctor Faustus, The Jew of Malta, Edward II. Jonson praised 'Marlowe's mighty line': he made blank verse powerful on stage. His heroes are 'overreachers' (Harry Levin's term) driven by ambition for power, knowledge or wealth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Kyd is usually grouped with the Wits though he did not attend university; mention this nuance if asked.

activity.prompt: Match the play to its Wit.

quiz.why: In Greene's Groatsworth of Wit (1592) the 'upstart Crow' is generally taken to be Shakespeare.

quiz.q: Euphuism derives from a work by:
quiz.why: Lyly's Euphues (1578) gave its name to the ornate balanced style.
Harry Levin's study The Overreacher characterises Marlowe's aspiring heroes.

scenes.text: Faustus signs a deed in his blood: his soul to Lucifer for 24 years of Mephistopheles's service.
At the final hour he cries, 'See, see where Christ's blood streams in the firmament!'

steps.title: Plot
steps.body: Faustus, a Wittenberg scholar, rejects logic, medicine, law and divinity for magic. Good and Bad Angels compete. He conjures Mephistopheles, signs the pact, wastes his power on tricks (the Pope, the Emperor, the Duchess of Vanholt), summons Helen ('Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?'), and is carried off at midnight.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Chorus as prologue and epilogue, morality-play elements (Good/Bad Angel, Seven Deadly Sins, Old Man), comic subplot (Wagner, Robin). Two texts: A-text (1604) and B-text (1616).

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: Renaissance aspiration for knowledge versus medieval Christian moral framework. Is Faustus a tragic hero or a damned sinner? Critics see the play as both a celebration and a warning; his tragedy is his refusal to repent.

steps.title: Final soliloquy
steps.body: Time slows ('O lente, lente currite noctis equi'), then the clock strikes. Imagery of stars, blood and mountains; broken syntax shows terror. His last cry 'I'll burn my books!' rejects learning too late.

activity.prompt: Order the main events of Doctor Faustus.
items: Pageant of the Seven Deadly Sins

quiz.q: The pact gives Faustus how many years?
quiz.why: He bargains for 24 years of Mephistopheles's service.

quiz.q: 'Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?' refers to:
quiz.why: Faustus addresses the spirit of Helen of Troy.
The angels personify the conflict for his soul, like morality-play figures.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Shakespeare
courses.summary: Shakespeare's life and canon, the four periods, the great tragedies (Hamlet, Macbeth, Othello, King Lear), the comedies, and the sonnets.
outcomes: Divide the canon into periods and genres
Analyse Hamlet and Macbeth: plot, character, themes, imagery
Explain the features of Shakespearean romantic comedy
Discuss the Fair Youth and Dark Lady sonnets
Apply A.C. Bradley's view of Shakespearean tragedy

scenes.text: Born in Stratford-upon-Avon, 1564; by 1592 he is a known London playwright.
1623: Heminges and Condell publish the First Folio with 36 plays.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body: William Shakespeare (1564–1616), actor-shareholder of the Lord Chamberlain's Men (King's Men from 1603). Wrote about 37–38 plays, 154 sonnets, and narrative poems Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594).

steps.title: Four periods (Dowden)
steps.body: 1) Apprenticeship (to c.1594): Henry VI, Richard III, The Comedy of Errors, Titus Andronicus. 2) Development (c.1594–1600): A Midsummer Night's Dream, The Merchant of Venice, Henry IV, As You Like It, Twelfth Night. 3) Tragic period (c.1600–1608): Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, Antony and Cleopatra, problem plays. 4) Romances (c.1608–1613): Pericles, Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale, The Tempest.

steps.title: Stage conditions
steps.body: Thrust stage, no scenery, daylight performance, boy actors in female roles, verse and prose mixed (prose for low characters, letters, madness, comedy).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Exact dates of composition are uncertain; say 'c.' and give ranges.

activity.prompt: Assign plays to their genre.

quiz.why: Heminges and Condell published it seven years after Shakespeare's death.

quiz.q: Which belongs to the romance period?
quiz.why: Cymbeline (c.1610) is one of the late romances.
James I became their patron, renaming them the King's Men.

scenes.text: On the battlements of Elsinore the ghost of old Hamlet demands revenge.
In a graveyard, Hamlet holds Yorick's skull and thinks on mortality.

steps.title: Plot
steps.body: Claudius has murdered his brother, married Gertrude and taken the throne. Hamlet feigns madness, stages The Mousetrap, kills Polonius by mistake, is sent to England, returns; Ophelia drowns; Laertes duels Hamlet with a poisoned foil; Gertrude, Laertes, Claudius and Hamlet die; Fortinbras takes Denmark.

steps.title: Hamlet's delay
steps.body: Theories: Bradley's melancholy; Coleridge's excess of reflection; Freud/Jones's Oedipal reading; moral doubt about the ghost. Eliot called the play an 'artistic failure' lacking an objective correlative for Hamlet's emotion.

steps.title: Themes and imagery
steps.body: Revenge, mortality, appearance vs reality, corruption (images of disease, rot, poison: 'an unweeded garden'), action vs thought. Soliloquies: 'O that this too too solid flesh', 'O what a rogue and peasant slave', 'To be or not to be', 'How all occasions do inform against me'.

steps.title: Analyse a line
steps.body: 'To be, or not to be, that is the question': antithesis frames existence vs non-existence; the soliloquy moves from suicide to the fear of 'what dreams may come', concluding 'conscience does make cowards of us all'.

activity.prompt: Order these events in Hamlet.

quiz.q: Who called Hamlet 'most certainly an artistic failure'?
quiz.why: T.S. Eliot made the claim in 'Hamlet and His Problems' (1919).
Hamlet stabs through the curtain in Gertrude's closet, thinking it may be Claudius.

quiz.q: Who takes Denmark at the end?
quiz.why: The Norwegian prince Fortinbras arrives and claims the throne.

scenes.text: 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair': the witches greet Macbeth as future king.
Lear rages on the heath: 'Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks!'

steps.title: Macbeth
steps.body: Ambition prompted by prophecy and Lady Macbeth leads to Duncan's murder, tyranny, Banquo's murder, Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking and suicide, and Macbeth's death by Macduff. Imagery: blood, darkness, ill-fitting clothes, sleep. 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow' expresses nihilism.

steps.title: Othello
steps.body: Iago, passed over for Cassio, uses Desdemona's handkerchief to make Othello believe she is unfaithful; Othello smothers her and kills himself. Themes: jealousy ('the green-eyed monster'), race, reputation, honesty. Coleridge: Iago's 'motive-hunting of a motiveless malignity'.

steps.title: King Lear
steps.body: Lear divides his kingdom by flattery, banishes Cordelia, is cast out by Goneril and Regan; parallel subplot of Gloucester, Edgar and Edmund. Themes: sight/blindness, nature, justice, 'nothing'. Ends with Cordelia's death.

steps.title: Bradley's theory
steps.body: A.C. Bradley (Shakespearean Tragedy, 1904): the tragic hero is of high degree, has a fatal flaw, his fall causes waste of good, and character is destiny ('action issuing from character').

activity.prompt: Which tragedy?

quiz.why: Coleridge used the phrase about Iago's restless search for reasons for his hatred.
A.C. Bradley's lectures were published in 1904.
Gloucester, deceived by Edmund against Edgar, parallels Lear's misjudgement of his daughters.

scenes.text: Lovers flee Athens into a wood ruled by fairies, and wake changed.
The poet's mistress's eyes 'are nothing like the sun'.

steps.title: Romantic comedy
steps.body: Features: love as central theme, heroines in disguise (Rosalind, Viola, Portia), the 'green world' (Northrop Frye) of forest or magic, mistaken identity, music, fools (Touchstone, Feste), and endings in multiple marriages. Darker notes: Shylock in The Merchant of Venice, Malvolio in Twelfth Night.

steps.title: The Sonnets (1609)
steps.body: 154 sonnets: 1–126 to a Fair Youth (1–17 'procreation sonnets'), 127–152 to a Dark Lady, a Rival Poet appears; dedicated to 'Mr. W.H.'. Themes: time's destruction, poetry's immortality, love, beauty, betrayal.

steps.title: Sonnet 130
steps.body: 'My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun': an anti-Petrarchan parody of conventional comparisons; couplet 'And yet, by heaven, I think my love as rare / As any she belied with false compare'.

steps.title: Answer tip
steps.body: For comedy questions, discuss the heroine's role: Shakespeare's comic heroines usually lead the action and wit.

activity.prompt: Fair Youth or Dark Lady sonnet?

items.text: Sonnet 116 'Let me not to the marriage of true minds'
Sonnet 147 'My love is as a fever'

quiz.why: Frye used it in Anatomy of Criticism and essays on comedy.
It mocks the conventional exaggerated praise of the beloved.
Malvolio is Olivia's steward, tricked by Maria's forged letter in Twelfth Night.
