questions.q: 'Frailty, thy name is woman' is spoken by:
questions.why: In Hamlet's first soliloquy on Gertrude's remarriage.
Macduff, 'from his mother's womb untimely ripped'.
She is the youngest and most loving.

questions.q: 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow' follows news of:
questions.why: Macbeth hears the queen is dead.

questions.q: Venus and Adonis was published in:
Bradley's tragic hero's fall is chiefly due to:
questions.why: Bradley stresses character as the source of tragic action.
Boas grouped it with All's Well and Troilus and Cressida as problem plays.

questions.q: Prospero's island magic ends when he:
options: Breaks his staff and drowns his book
questions.why: He abjures 'this rough magic' in Act V.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Jacobean, Metaphysical and Milton
courses.summary: Ben Jonson and Jacobean drama, the Metaphysical poets (Donne, Herbert, Marvell), Cavalier poets, and Milton's Paradise Lost.
outcomes: Describe Jacobean tragedy (Webster) and Jonson's comedy
Define Metaphysical poetry and analyse Donne's conceits
Compare Herbert and Marvell
Analyse Paradise Lost Book I and the character of Satan

scenes.text: Volpone, 'the fox', pretends to be dying to fleece greedy legacy-hunters.
Webster's Duchess of Malfi faces death saying 'I am Duchess of Malfi still'.

steps.title: Ben Jonson (1572–1637)
steps.body: Classical, satirical dramatist: Every Man in His Humour, Volpone (1606), The Alchemist (1610), Bartholomew Fair; court masques with Inigo Jones; poems 'To Celia', 'On My First Son'. Followers called the 'Tribe of Ben'.

steps.title: Jacobean tragedy
steps.body: Darker, cynical, violent: Webster's The White Devil and The Duchess of Malfi, Middleton's The Changeling and Women Beware Women, Tourneur/Middleton's The Revenger's Tragedy, Ford's 'Tis Pity She's a Whore. Theatres closed by Parliament in 1642.

steps.title: Duchess of Malfi
steps.body: The widowed Duchess secretly marries her steward Antonio; her brothers Ferdinand and the Cardinal have her strangled by Bosola. Ferdinand's 'Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle: she died young' reveals guilt.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Jacobean = reign of James I (1603–1625); Caroline = Charles I. Do not call Webster Elizabethan.

activity.prompt: Jonson or Webster?

quiz.why: Parliament closed the theatres at the outbreak of the Civil War in 1642.

quiz.q: 'I am Duchess of Malfi still' shows:
quiz.why: Facing torture she asserts her identity and nobility.
Jonson set his satire on greed in Venice.

scenes.text: Donne scolds the sun for waking lovers: 'Busy old fool, unruly sun'.
Leaving his wife, he compares their souls to the legs of a compass.

steps.title: Origin of the term
steps.body: Dryden said Donne 'affects the metaphysics'; Dr Johnson (Life of Cowley, 1779) named them 'metaphysical poets' whose 'most heterogeneous ideas are yoked by violence together'. Eliot's 1921 essay revalued them for 'unified sensibility'.

steps.title: Features
steps.body: Conceits from science, law, geography, theology; colloquial dramatic openings; argument and wit; fusion of thought and passion; compression; irregular metre; love and religion as themes.

steps.title: 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning'
steps.body: 'If they be two, they are two so / As stiff twin compasses are two; / Thy soul, the fixed foot, makes no show / To move, but doth, if the other do.' The wife is the fixed foot, the poet the travelling foot; 'thy firmness makes my circle just'. The circle symbolises perfection and return.

steps.title: Donne's religious verse
steps.body: Holy Sonnets: 'Death, be not proud', 'Batter my heart, three-personed God'; Dean of St Paul's from 1621; sermons ('No man is an island', Devotions, Meditation XVII).

activity.prompt: Donne's love poem or religious poem?

quiz.q: Who said ideas are 'yoked by violence together'?
quiz.why: Johnson wrote it in his Life of Cowley, criticising metaphysical wit.

quiz.q: In the compass conceit, the fixed foot is:
quiz.why: The wife who stays at home is the fixed centre.

quiz.q: 'No man is an island' comes from Donne's:
quiz.why: It is from Meditation XVII of Devotions (1624).

scenes.text: George Herbert, country parson, shapes a poem like an altar.
Herrick urges virgins, 'Gather ye rosebuds while ye may'.

steps.title: George Herbert
steps.body: The Temple (1633): devotional poems of spiritual conflict and resolution: 'The Collar' (rebellion ended by 'Child!'/'My Lord'), 'Easter Wings' and 'The Altar' (shape poems), 'Love (III)', 'Virtue'.

steps.title: Andrew Marvell
steps.body: 'To His Coy Mistress' (carpe diem argument in three parts: If–But–Therefore), 'The Garden', 'An Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland'. Marvell assisted Milton as Latin secretary.

steps.title: Cavalier poets
steps.body: Royalist, elegant, lighter love lyrics, influenced by Jonson: Herrick ('To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time'), Lovelace ('To Althea, from Prison': 'Stone walls do not a prison make'), Suckling, Carew.

steps.title: Structure of 'To His Coy Mistress'
steps.body: 1) 'Had we but world enough, and time' — hypothetical slow courtship. 2) 'But at my back I always hear / Time's wingèd chariot' — mortality. 3) 'Now therefore' — let us seize the day. A logical syllogism.

activity.prompt: Order the argument of 'To His Coy Mistress'.
items: Had we but world enough and time
But Time's wingèd chariot hurries near
Now therefore let us sport us while we may

quiz.q: 'The Collar' ends with the speaker answering:
quiz.why: Rebellion collapses when God calls 'Child!' and he replies 'My Lord'.

quiz.q: 'Stone walls do not a prison make' is by:
quiz.why: Richard Lovelace wrote it in 'To Althea, from Prison'.
Its lines are arranged visually to resemble wings.

scenes.text: Satan wakes on a burning lake, rallies his fallen angels and builds Pandemonium.
In Eden, Eve tastes the fruit; 'Earth felt the wound'.

steps.title: Milton (1608–1674)
steps.body: Early: 'L'Allegro', 'Il Penseroso', Comus, 'Lycidas'. Prose: Areopagitica (1644, for freedom of the press). Latin Secretary under Cromwell; blind by 1652. Late: Paradise Lost (1667, 10 books; 1674, 12 books), Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes (1671).

steps.title: Book I
steps.body: Theme: 'Of Man's first disobedience', aim 'to justify the ways of God to men'. Satan and Beelzebub on the burning lake; Satan's speeches ('The mind is its own place', 'Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heav'n'); catalogue of devils; Pandemonium built.

steps.title: Is Satan the hero?
steps.body: Blake: Milton 'was of the Devil's party without knowing it'. Shelley admired Satan's defiance. C.S. Lewis (A Preface to Paradise Lost) argued Satan degenerates from archangel to serpent. Balanced view: Satan's grandeur in Books I–II is gradually exposed as self-deceiving.

steps.title: Grand style
steps.body: Latinate diction and syntax, long periodic sentences, epic similes, allusions, blank verse with enjambment.

activity.prompt: Early Milton or late Milton?

options: To justify the ways of God to men
quiz.why: Book I states this aim explicitly in the invocation.

quiz.q: 'Of the Devil's party without knowing it' was said by:
quiz.why: Blake wrote it in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell.
Milton argued against pre-publication licensing of books in 1644.

questions.q: Paradise Lost first edition had how many books?
Eliot's essay 'The Metaphysical Poets' appeared in:

questions.why: Capital of Hell built in Book I.

questions.q: 'The mind is its own place' is spoken by:
A Preface to Paradise Lost is by:

questions.why: Younger poets like Herrick 'sealed' to Ben.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Restoration and the 18th Century
courses.summary: Dryden, Restoration comedy, Pope and Swift, Dr Johnson, the 18th-century novel, and the transitional poets.
outcomes: Characterise Neoclassicism and the Augustan age
Analyse Dryden's and Pope's satire
Interpret Gulliver's Travels as satire
Trace the 18th-century novel from Defoe to Sterne
Identify pre-Romantic tendencies in Gray, Collins, Cowper

scenes.text: 1660: Charles II returns; theatres reopen with actresses on stage for the first time.
Dryden attacks Shaftesbury as Achitophel in a biblical allegory.

steps.title: Neoclassicism
steps.body: Reason, order, decorum, imitation of the ancients, 'general nature'; the heroic couplet; social and urban subjects; satire. Augustan age (c.1700–1745) named after Rome's Augustus: Pope, Swift, Addison.

steps.title: John Dryden (1631–1700)
steps.body: Poet Laureate (1668). Absalom and Achitophel (1681): political satire on the Exclusion Crisis (Absalom = Monmouth, Achitophel = Shaftesbury, David = Charles II). Mac Flecknoe (mock-heroic on Shadwell). An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668): dialogue comparing ancients, moderns, French and English drama. All for Love (1677) on Antony and Cleopatra.

steps.title: Restoration comedy
steps.body: Comedy of manners: Etherege (The Man of Mode), Wycherley (The Country Wife), Congreve (The Way of the World, 1700: Mirabell and Millamant's 'proviso scene'). Jeremy Collier attacked its immorality in 1698.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Absalom and Achitophel is political allegory, not religious poetry; the biblical story is a vehicle.

activity.prompt: Who is who in Absalom and Achitophel?

quiz.q: An Essay of Dramatic Poesy is in the form of:
quiz.why: Four speakers (Crites, Eugenius, Lisideius, Neander) debate drama; Neander represents Dryden.
Millamant and Mirabell set conditions for marriage in Act IV.
A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage criticised Restoration comedy.

scenes.text: Lord Petre snips a lock of Arabella Fermor's hair; Pope makes it an epic.
Gulliver wakes tied down by six-inch Lilliputians.

steps.title: Alexander Pope (1688–1744)
steps.body: An Essay on Criticism (1711: 'A little learning is a dang'rous thing', 'To err is human, to forgive divine'), The Rape of the Lock (1712/1714), The Dunciad (1728–43), An Essay on Man ('Whatever is, is right'), 'Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot' (portrait of Atticus = Addison). Master of the closed heroic couplet.

steps.title: Jonathan Swift (1667–1745)
steps.body: Dean of St Patrick's, Dublin. A Tale of a Tub, The Battle of the Books, Gulliver's Travels (1726), A Modest Proposal (1729). Gulliver: Book I Lilliput (pettiness of politics: Big-Endians vs Little-Endians, high and low heels), II Brobdingnag (giant king condemns Europeans as 'odious little vermin'), III Laputa (abstract science), IV Houyhnhnms (rational horses) and Yahoos (bestial humans).

steps.title: Reading Book IV
steps.body: Gulliver returns misanthropic, preferring horses to his family. 'Soft' readings see Swift satirising Gulliver's extremism; 'hard' readings see Swift's own pessimism about human nature.

steps.title: Scriblerus Club
steps.body: Pope, Swift, Gay (The Beggar's Opera, 1728), Arbuthnot and others satirised pedantry.

activity.prompt: Match the voyage to its satire.

quiz.q: 'A little learning is a dang'rous thing' is from:
quiz.why: It appears in Pope's 1711 Essay on Criticism.
Swift ironically proposes selling Irish babies as food to expose English exploitation.

quiz.q: Atticus in 'Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot' represents:
quiz.why: Pope's portrait of Atticus satirises Joseph Addison.

scenes.text: 1755: Johnson's Dictionary, nine years' labour, defines 'lexicographer' as 'a harmless drudge'.
Tom Jones, the foundling, tumbles from adventure to adventure toward Sophia.

steps.title: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784)
steps.body: A Dictionary of the English Language (1755), Rasselas (1759), The Rambler essays, 'The Vanity of Human Wishes', Preface to Shakespeare (1765: Shakespeare as 'poet of nature', defence against the unities), Lives of the Poets (1779–81). The 'Age of Johnson'; Boswell's Life (1791).

steps.title: Novelists
steps.body: Defoe: Robinson Crusoe (1719), Moll Flanders. Richardson: Pamela (1740), Clarissa. Fielding: Joseph Andrews (1742, parody of Pamela), Tom Jones (1749, 'comic epic poem in prose'). Smollett: Roderick Random, Humphry Clinker. Sterne: Tristram Shandy (1759–67), experimental, digressive.

steps.title: Transitional poets
steps.body: Thomson (The Seasons), Gray ('Elegy', 1751), Collins ('Ode to Evening'), Goldsmith ('The Deserted Village'), Cowper (The Task), Blake's early songs, Burns. Features: nature, melancholy, sympathy for humble life, early Romantic feeling.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Fielding called his novel a 'comic epic poem in prose' in the Preface to Joseph Andrews, not Tom Jones.

activity.prompt: Match the novel to its author.

quiz.why: After nine years of work it appeared in 1755.

quiz.q: Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare calls him:
quiz.why: Johnson praised Shakespeare for holding up a faithful mirror of manners and life.
Oliver Goldsmith's 1770 poem laments rural depopulation.

scenes.text: 1387 Canterbury Tales begun · 1590 Faerie Queene · 1600 Hamlet · 1667 Paradise Lost · 1726 Gulliver · 1755 Dictionary.
Practise linking text, period and context in every answer.

steps.title: Key dates sheet
steps.body: Chaucer c.1343–1400; Caxton 1476; Tottel 1557; Faerie Queene I–III 1590; Globe 1599; First Folio 1623; Theatres closed 1642; Restoration 1660; Paradise Lost 1667; Absalom and Achitophel 1681; Rape of the Lock 1714 (5-canto); Gulliver 1726; Pamela 1740; Tom Jones 1749; Gray's Elegy 1751; Dictionary 1755.

steps.title: Long answers (original)
steps.body: (1) 'Chaucer's General Prologue is a portrait gallery of 14th-century England.' Discuss. (2) Examine Faustus as a Renaissance overreacher. (3) Is Satan the hero of Paradise Lost? (4) Discuss Swift's satire in Gulliver's Travels Book IV. (5) Pope's use of mock-heroic in The Rape of the Lock.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.body: Euphuism; University Wits; Metaphysical conceit; Comedy of manners; Scriblerus Club; Graveyard poets.

steps.title: Structure for essays
steps.body: Introduction with thesis → context → 3–4 arguments each with quotation → counter-view → conclusion. Quote 2–3 short lines per argument.

activity.prompt: Arrange chronologically.

quiz.why: Hamlet (c.1600) predates Paradise Lost (1667), Gulliver (1726) and Tom Jones (1749).
Gray's meditation in a churchyard is linked to the graveyard school with Young and Blair.
John Gay's 1728 ballad opera satirised Walpole and Italian opera.

questions.why: Neoclassical ideals of reason and decorum.

uni-ba-eng-british-lit-2.title: British Literature: Romantic to Modern
uni-ba-eng-british-lit-2.description: Romantic poetry, the Victorian novel and poetry, Modernism in poetry, fiction and drama, and post-1945 writing. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. English programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Romantic Poetry
courses.summary: The Romantic revolt, Blake, Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads, and the second generation: Byron, Shelley and Keats.
outcomes: Explain the features and context of Romanticism
Analyse Blake's Songs of Innocence and of Experience
Discuss Wordsworth's theory of poetry from the 1800 Preface
Interpret Coleridge's supernatural poems
Compare Byron, Shelley and Keats

scenes.text: 1789: the Bastille falls; young Wordsworth feels 'Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive'.
Blake engraves his own poems with hand-coloured pictures: 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright'.

steps.title: Features of Romanticism
steps.body: Imagination over reason, emotion, nature as a living spiritual presence, the individual and the child, the supernatural and medieval, revolution and liberty, the common man, lyric self-expression, organic form. Period usually dated 1798 (Lyrical Ballads) to 1832 (Reform Act; Scott's death).

steps.title: William Blake (1757–1827)
steps.body: Poet-engraver and visionary. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794), 'Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul'. Paired poems: 'The Lamb'/'The Tyger', 'Holy Thursday', 'The Chimney Sweeper', 'Nurse's Song'. Prophetic books; The Marriage of Heaven and Hell.

steps.title: Lamb vs Tyger
steps.body: 'Little Lamb, who made thee?' — child's question answered with gentle Christ imagery. 'What immortal hand or eye / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?' — unanswered questions; forge imagery (hammer, chain, furnace, anvil) suggests a creator of terrible energy. 'Did he who made the Lamb make thee?'

steps.title: 'London'
steps.body: 'Mind-forg'd manacles', the chimney-sweeper's cry, the soldier's sigh, the harlot's curse: social critique of Church, state and industrial city.

activity.prompt: Innocence or Experience?

quiz.q: Songs of Experience was published in:
quiz.why: Blake issued Experience in 1794, combining it with Innocence.
In 'London' Blake suggests people are imprisoned by mental and institutional chains.
Blake leaves the riddle of the creator of terror and beauty open.

scenes.text: Five years later, Wordsworth returns to the Wye and feels 'a sense sublime / Of something far more deeply interfused'.
The 1800 Preface declares war on 'poetic diction'.

steps.title: Lyrical Ballads (1798)
steps.body: Joint volume by Wordsworth and Coleridge, opening with 'The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere' and closing with 'Tintern Abbey'. Division of labour (Biographia Literaria, ch. XIV): Coleridge on the supernatural made real; Wordsworth on ordinary life given 'the charm of novelty'.

steps.title: Preface (1800, revised 1802)
steps.body: Aim: 'incidents and situations from common life' in 'a selection of language really used by men'; humble rustic life chosen because passions are purer there. Poetry is 'the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity'. The poet is 'a man speaking to men'. Rejects artificial poetic diction (attacks Gray's sonnet).

steps.title: Tintern Abbey stages
steps.body: Wordsworth describes three stages: boyhood's 'glad animal movements', youth's passionate love of nature 'an appetite', and maturity hearing 'the still, sad music of humanity'. Nature becomes 'the anchor of my purest thoughts' and he blesses his sister Dorothy.

steps.title: Other works
steps.body: The Prelude (1805; published 1850), 'Intimations of Immortality' Ode, Lucy poems, 'Michael', 'Resolution and Independence', sonnets ('The world is too much with us', 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge').

activity.prompt: Order the stages of Wordsworth's relation to nature in Tintern Abbey.
items: Youth: nature as passion and appetite
Maturity: still, sad music of humanity
Sense of a presence deeply interfused

quiz.why: Wordsworth defines the origin of poetry in the Preface.

quiz.q: Wordsworth chose 'humble and rustic life' because:
options: Essential passions are purer and plainer there
quiz.why: He argued rural conditions let the essential passions of the heart grow and speak plainly.
Completed in 1805 and revised, it was published posthumously in 1850.

scenes.text: The Mariner shoots the albatross; the ship is becalmed under a 'bloody Sun'.
Coleridge wakes from an opium dream with Kubla Khan's pleasure-dome in his mind, until a person from Porlock interrupts.

steps.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
steps.body: Seven parts in ballad stanza. Crime (shooting the albatross), punishment (thirst, death of crew, Life-in-Death), redemption (blessing water-snakes 'unaware'; albatross falls from his neck), penance (telling his tale). Moral: 'He prayeth best, who loveth best / All things both great and small'.

steps.title: Kubla Khan and Christabel
steps.body: 'Kubla Khan' (1797, publ. 1816): 'In Xanadu did Kubla Khan / A stately pleasure-dome decree'; poem about creative imagination, unfinished. 'Christabel': unfinished Gothic poem. Conversation poems: 'Frost at Midnight', 'This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison'. 'Dejection: An Ode'.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Biographia Literaria (1817): primary imagination (living power of all perception), secondary imagination (echo of primary, 'dissolves, diffuses, dissipates, in order to recreate'), fancy (mechanical, aggregating). 'Willing suspension of disbelief'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not reduce the Mariner's moral to an animal-welfare message; it concerns sin, isolation and the unity of all life.

activity.prompt: Order the Mariner's journey.
items: Ship driven to the South Pole
Death and Life-in-Death dice for the crew
Return home and penance of telling

quiz.q: Imagination that 'dissolves, diffuses, dissipates, in order to recreate' is:
quiz.why: Coleridge assigns this recreative power to the secondary, poetic imagination.
Coleridge's preface says a visitor on business from Porlock broke his recollection of the dream.

quiz.q: The albatross falls from the Mariner's neck when he:
quiz.why: His spontaneous love for living creatures breaks the curse.

scenes.text: Shelley cries to the West Wind, 'Make me thy lyre'.
Keats hears a nightingale in a Hampstead garden and longs to 'fade far away'.

steps.title: Byron (1788–1824)
steps.body: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Don Juan (ottava rima, comic satire), 'She Walks in Beauty'. The 'Byronic hero': proud, moody, rebellious, guilt-haunted. Died at Missolonghi supporting Greek independence.

steps.title: Shelley (1792–1822)
steps.body: Radical idealist: 'Ode to the West Wind' (destroyer and preserver; 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?'), 'To a Skylark', 'Ozymandias' (sonnet on the ruin of tyranny), Prometheus Unbound, Adonais, A Defence of Poetry ('Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the World').

steps.title: Keats (1795–1821)
steps.body: Sensuous imagery; odes of 1819; 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer', 'La Belle Dame sans Merci', Endymion, 'The Eve of St. Agnes', Hyperion. Letters: negative capability, 'vale of Soul-making', 'chameleon poet'.

steps.title: Ode to a Nightingale
steps.body: Movement: numbness and heartache → wish for wine to escape → flight 'on the viewless wings of Poesy' → darkness and death-wish ('Now more than ever seems it rich to die') → bird as immortal → 'Forlorn!' returns him to self → 'Was it a vision, or a waking dream?'

activity.prompt: Which poet?

quiz.q: 'Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the World' — who?
quiz.why: It is the closing sentence of Shelley's A Defence of Poetry (written 1821).

quiz.q: Keats's great odes were written mainly in:
quiz.why: The Nightingale, Urn, Psyche, Melancholy, Indolence and Autumn odes date from 1819.
It is a 14-line sonnet with an unusual rhyme scheme.

questions.q: 'The world is too much with us' is a:
'He prayeth best, who loveth best' — source?
options: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

questions.why: Final lines of the Urn ode.
Coleridge's blank-verse conversation poem addressed to his sleeping son.
Blake wrote contrasting versions for both books.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Romantic Prose and the Victorian Novel
courses.summary: Jane Austen and Scott, Romantic essayists, and the Victorian novel: Dickens, the Brontës, George Eliot, Hardy.
outcomes: Analyse Austen's irony in Pride and Prejudice
Describe the Victorian context: industrialism, reform, faith and doubt
Discuss Dickens's social criticism
Compare Wuthering Heights and Jane Eyre
Explain Hardy's tragic vision and George Eliot's realism

scenes.text: At the Meryton assembly Darcy declares Elizabeth 'tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me'.
His letter after the failed proposal forces Elizabeth to see her own prejudice.

steps.title: Jane Austen (1775–1817)
steps.body: Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park, Emma (1815), Northanger Abbey and Persuasion (1817). Subject: courtship and marriage among the gentry; 'three or four families in a country village'; irony, free indirect discourse, moral growth through self-knowledge.

steps.title: The opening
steps.body: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.' Irony: the 'universal truth' is really the mothers' wish; in fact poor women need rich husbands, as the entail on Longbourn shows.

steps.title: Scott and the essayists
steps.body: Sir Walter Scott: Waverley (1814), Ivanhoe (1819); historical novel. Romantic essayists: Lamb (Essays of Elia), Hazlitt ('My First Acquaintance with Poets', The Spirit of the Age), De Quincey (Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, 1821).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Austen is not merely a romance writer; her novels are moral and economic comedies of manners.

activity.prompt: Austen novel or Scott novel?

quiz.q: Pride and Prejudice was published in:
quiz.why: It appeared in January 1813.

quiz.q: The Spirit of the Age is by:
quiz.why: Hazlitt's 1825 portraits of contemporaries.
Her narrator blends ironic commentary with characters' thoughts.

scenes.text: In Coketown the chimneys smoke and Gradgrind demands 'Facts' from children.
Oliver Twist asks, 'Please, sir, I want some more.'

steps.title: Context (1837–1901)
steps.body: Queen Victoria's reign: Industrial Revolution, Reform Acts (1832, 1867), railways, Empire, Utilitarianism, Chartism, Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859), crisis of faith, the 'Woman Question', serial publication of novels, circulating libraries.

steps.title: Charles Dickens (1812–1870)
steps.body: Pickwick Papers, Oliver Twist (workhouses), A Christmas Carol, David Copperfield (autobiographical Bildungsroman), Bleak House (Chancery), Hard Times (1854, Utilitarianism and industry), A Tale of Two Cities, Great Expectations (1861). Features: caricature, humour, pathos, social reform, serial cliffhangers.

steps.title: Hard Times
steps.body: Gradgrind's school fills children with facts; Sissy Jupe from the circus represents imagination; Louisa's loveless marriage to Bounderby and Tom's crime show the failure of the fact-system; Stephen Blackpool shows the worker's plight.

steps.title: Other novelists
steps.body: Thackeray (Vanity Fair, 'a novel without a hero'), Elizabeth Gaskell (Mary Barton, North and South: industrial novels), Trollope (Barsetshire novels), Disraeli (Sybil: 'two nations').

activity.prompt: Which Dickens novel targets which institution?

quiz.why: Thackeray subtitled it 'A Novel without a Hero'.

quiz.q: On the Origin of Species was published in:
quiz.why: Darwin published it in November 1859.

quiz.q: Sissy Jupe in Hard Times represents:
quiz.why: The circus girl embodies fancy and compassion against Gradgrind's facts.

scenes.text: Bertha Mason sets fire to Thornfield Hall.
On the moors, Catherine says, 'I am Heathcliff.'

steps.title: Charlotte Brontë
steps.body: Jane Eyre (1847), as 'Currer Bell': first-person Bildungsroman of an orphan governess; Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield, Moor House, Ferndean. Themes: independence, equality ('Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless?'), passion vs principle.

steps.title: Emily Brontë
steps.body: Wuthering Heights (1847), as 'Ellis Bell': nested narration by Lockwood and Nelly Dean; two houses (Heights = storm, Grange = calm); two generations; Heathcliff's revenge and final peace. Anne Brontë: Agnes Grey, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall.

steps.title: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans)
steps.body: Adam Bede, The Mill on the Floss (1860), Silas Marner, Middlemarch (1871–72): 'a study of provincial life'; psychological realism, moral seriousness, web of community, sympathy. Dorothea and Lydgate's failed ideals.

steps.title: Postcolonial rewriting
steps.body: Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) retells Bertha's story as Antoinette, a Creole woman: a key text linking this unit to postcolonial studies.

activity.prompt: Which novel?

quiz.why: Mary Ann (Marian) Evans adopted a male pseudonym to be taken seriously.
Jean Rhys imagines the life of Rochester's first wife.

quiz.q: Wuthering Heights is narrated mainly by:
quiz.why: Lockwood records Nelly Dean's account, creating a frame narrative.

scenes.text: Tess Durbeyfield works on a dairy farm in the Valley of the Great Dairies, in love with Angel Clare.
At Stonehenge she is arrested: 'Justice was done, and the President of the Immortals had ended his sport with Tess.'

steps.title: Wessex
steps.body: Hardy (1840–1928) set his 'novels of character and environment' in fictional Wessex (south-west England): Far from the Madding Crowd, The Return of the Native (Egdon Heath), The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891, 'A Pure Woman'), Jude the Obscure (1895). After Jude's hostile reception he wrote only poetry.

steps.title: Tragic vision
steps.body: Chance, coincidence, Immanent Will, indifferent universe, decline of rural life, conflict of individual desire with convention. Michael Henchard's sale of his wife at a fair begins the Mayor's tragedy: 'Character is Fate, said Novalis'.

steps.title: Hardy the poet
steps.body: 'The Darkling Thrush' (31 Dec 1900), 'Convergence of the Twain' (Titanic), Poems of 1912–13 on his wife Emma, The Dynasts (epic drama).

steps.title: Chance in Tess
steps.body: Tess's confession letter slides under the carpet and Angel never reads it: a coincidence that shapes tragedy and shows Hardy's ironic universe.

activity.prompt: Order Tess's story.
items: Tess goes to Trantridge; seduced by Alec
Tess kills Alec; arrest at Stonehenge

quiz.q: The Mayor of Casterbridge opens with Henchard:
quiz.why: Drunk at Weydon Priors fair, he auctions his wife and child to a sailor.
Hardy provocatively called Tess 'A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented'.

quiz.q: Hardy turned wholly to poetry after:
quiz.why: Hostile reviews of Jude (1895) made him abandon the novel.

questions.q: Confessions of an English Opium-Eater is by:

questions.why: The 'Bully of humility' in Hard Times.

questions.q: 'Two nations' — rich and poor — phrase from:
Egdon Heath is the setting of:
questions.why: Its brooding landscape dominates the novel.
Hardy's poem on the century's end.
Dickens drew on his own childhood.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Victorian Poetry and Prose
courses.summary: Tennyson, Browning, Arnold, the Pre-Raphaelites and Hopkins; Victorian sages Carlyle, Ruskin, Mill and Arnold's criticism.
outcomes: Analyse Tennyson's 'Ulysses' and In Memoriam
Discuss Browning's dramatic monologues
Interpret 'Dover Beach' and the crisis of faith
Describe Pre-Raphaelite and Hopkins's innovations
Summarise the Victorian sage writers

scenes.text: Old Ulysses, back in Ithaca, cannot rest: 'I will drink life to the lees'.
Mourning Hallam, Tennyson sees 'Nature, red in tooth and claw'.

steps.title: Alfred Lord Tennyson (1809–1892)
steps.body: Poet Laureate from 1850 after Wordsworth. Works: 'The Lady of Shalott', 'The Lotos-Eaters', 'Ulysses' (1842), 'Tithonus', In Memoriam A.H.H. (1850), 'The Charge of the Light Brigade', Maud, Idylls of the King, 'Crossing the Bar'.

steps.title: 'Ulysses'
steps.body: Dramatic monologue in blank verse. Ulysses rejects a dull life among 'a savage race'; hands rule to Telemachus; calls his mariners: 'Tho' much is taken, much abides'; closes 'To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.' Read as Victorian heroic will, and as a response to Hallam's death.

steps.title: In Memoriam
steps.body: 133 cantos in the 'In Memoriam stanza' (iambic tetrameter abba). Journey from grief and doubt (geology, evolution: 'red in tooth and claw') to faith (''Tis better to have loved and lost / Than never to have loved at all').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Tennyson succeeded Wordsworth, not Southey, as Laureate. 'In Memoriam stanza' rhymes abba, not abab.

activity.prompt: Match each line to its poem.

items.text: To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield
Nature, red in tooth and claw
I will drink life to the lees

quiz.why: Tennyson used enclosed tetrameter quatrains rhyming abba.
He succeeded Wordsworth in November 1850.
It is an unrhymed iambic pentameter monologue.

scenes.text: Fra Lippo Lippi, caught by the watch at night, defends painting real flesh.
At Dover, Arnold hears the 'melancholy, long, withdrawing roar' of the Sea of Faith.

steps.title: Robert Browning (1812–1889)
steps.body: Men and Women (1855), Dramatis Personae, The Ring and the Book (1868–69). Monologues: 'My Last Duchess', 'Porphyria's Lover', 'Fra Lippo Lippi', 'Andrea del Sarto' ('a man's reach should exceed his grasp'), 'The Bishop Orders His Tomb', 'Rabbi Ben Ezra' ('Grow old along with me!'). Obscurity, psychological insight, optimism. Married Elizabeth Barrett (Sonnets from the Portuguese).

steps.title: Matthew Arnold (1822–1888)
steps.body: Poems: 'Dover Beach' (c.1851, publ. 1867), 'The Scholar-Gipsy', 'Thyrsis', 'Sohrab and Rustum'. Prose: Culture and Anarchy (1869: 'sweetness and light', Barbarians/Philistines/Populace), 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time', 'The Study of Poetry' (touchstone method; poetry as 'criticism of life').

steps.title: 'Dover Beach'
steps.body: Calm sea at night → Sophocles heard 'the turbid ebb and flow / Of human misery' → 'The Sea of Faith' retreating → 'Ah, love, let us be true / To one another!' → world 'Where ignorant armies clash by night'. Personal love as refuge in a faithless world.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not call Arnold a Romantic; he is a Victorian poet-critic who also attacked Romantic self-absorption.

activity.prompt: Browning or Arnold?

options: Essays in Criticism First Series only
quiz.why: In 'The Study of Poetry' (1880) he proposes judging poetry by comparing it to great lines.

quiz.q: 'Ah, love, let us be true / To one another!' — poem?
quiz.why: It is the turning point of Arnold's 'Dover Beach'.

quiz.q: 'A man's reach should exceed his grasp' — poem?
quiz.why: The painter Andrea speaks these lines about ambition.

scenes.text: Young painters and poets form a Brotherhood in 1848 to return to art before Raphael.
Hopkins watches a falcon: 'I caught this morning morning's minion'.

steps.title: Pre-Raphaelites
steps.body: Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (1848): D.G. Rossetti, Holman Hunt, Millais. Poetry: detailed sensuous imagery, medievalism, symbolism. Christina Rossetti ('Goblin Market', 'Remember'), William Morris, Swinburne. Robert Buchanan attacked 'The Fleshly School of Poetry' (1871).

steps.title: Gerard Manley Hopkins (1844–1889)
steps.body: Jesuit priest; poems published posthumously by Robert Bridges in 1918. Sprung rhythm, inscape (individual essence), instress (its impact), compound words, alliteration. 'The Windhover', 'God's Grandeur', 'Pied Beauty', 'The Wreck of the Deutschland', 'terrible sonnets'.

steps.title: 'God's Grandeur'
steps.body: 'The world is charged with the grandeur of God. / It will flame out, like shining from shook foil'. Octave: humans 'have trod, have trod, have trod' and smeared nature; sestet: 'nature is never spent' because the Holy Ghost 'broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings'.

steps.title: Aestheticism
steps.body: Walter Pater's Studies in the History of the Renaissance (1873): 'To burn always with this hard, gem-like flame'. 'Art for art's sake'; Wilde; the 1890s Decadents.

activity.prompt: Hopkins term or Pre-Raphaelite/Aesthetic feature?

quiz.q: Hopkins's poems were first published in:
quiz.why: Robert Bridges edited the first collection in 1918.
Christina Rossetti published it in 1862.
Buchanan's 1871 article attacked Rossetti and Swinburne.

scenes.text: Carlyle lectures on heroes and hero-worship.
Wilde's Lady Bracknell gasps: 'A handbag?'

steps.title: Prose sages
steps.body: Carlyle: Sartor Resartus, On Heroes and Hero-Worship, Past and Present ('cash nexus'). Ruskin: Modern Painters, Unto This Last (political economy), Sesame and Lilies. J.S. Mill: On Liberty (1859), The Subjection of Women (1869). Newman: The Idea of a University. Pater (aestheticism).

steps.title: Late Victorian drama
steps.body: Oscar Wilde: Lady Windermere's Fan, An Ideal Husband, The Importance of Being Earnest (1895), comedy of manners with epigrams; The Picture of Dorian Gray (novel, 1890). G.B. Shaw's early plays (Arms and the Man, 1894; Mrs Warren's Profession) bring the Ibsenite problem play.

steps.title: Wildean epigram
steps.body: 'The truth is rarely pure and never simple.' Wilde inverts proverbs, exposing hypocrisy of Victorian earnestness; 'Bunburying' satirises double lives.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Victorian questions often ask about 'conflict between science and faith' — use In Memoriam, 'Dover Beach' and Hardy together.

activity.prompt: Match the prose work to its author.

quiz.why: Mill published On Liberty in 1859, the same year as Darwin's Origin.
Algernon invents an invalid friend Bunbury as an excuse to escape duties.

quiz.q: The 'cash nexus' phrase is associated with:
quiz.why: Carlyle criticised human relations reduced to cash payment in Past and Present and Chartism.

questions.why: Tennyson asked it to end every edition of his poems.

questions.q: Sonnets from the Portuguese is by:
Culture and Anarchy names the middle class:
questions.why: Arnold called the middle class Philistines.

options: 'Glory be to God for dappled things'

questions.q: The Ring and the Book is set in:
questions.why: Based on a 1698 Roman murder trial.
Arnold borrowed it from Swift for Culture and Anarchy.
In the Conclusion to The Renaissance (1873).

questions.q: The Importance of Being Earnest premiered in:

questions.why: He converted to Catholicism and became a Jesuit.
'This is my son, mine own Telemachus'.

questions.q: 'Dover Beach' ends with an image of:
questions.why: A darkling plain of confused struggle.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Modernism: Poetry, Fiction, Drama
courses.summary: Modernist context, Yeats, Eliot and the war poets; Conrad, Joyce, Woolf, Lawrence, Forster; Shaw and Irish drama.
outcomes: Describe Modernism's context and features
Analyse The Waste Land and Yeats's major poems
Discuss Owen and the war poets
Explain the techniques of Woolf and Joyce
Interpret Heart of Darkness and A Passage to India

lessons.title: Modernism, Yeats and the war poets

scenes.text: 1917: in a hospital at Craiglockhart, Wilfred Owen meets Siegfried Sassoon.
1919: Yeats writes, 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold'.

steps.title: Modernism (c.1910–1940)
steps.body: Response to World War I, urbanisation, Freud, Einstein, Nietzsche, Frazer's Golden Bough. Features: fragmentation, experiment, allusion, myth, stream of consciousness, free verse, subjectivity, difficulty. 'Make it new' (Pound). Imagism (Pound, H.D., 1912–17): direct treatment, economy, musical phrase.

steps.title: W.B. Yeats (1865–1939)
steps.body: Early Celtic Twilight ('The Lake Isle of Innisfree'); middle political ('Easter, 1916': 'A terrible beauty is born'); late symbolic ('The Second Coming' 1919/1920, 'Sailing to Byzantium', 'Among School Children', 'Byzantium'). A Vision: gyres, cycles of history. Nobel Prize 1923.

steps.title: War poets
steps.body: Rupert Brooke ('The Soldier', patriotic idealism) vs Wilfred Owen ('Dulce et Decorum Est', 'Anthem for Doomed Youth', 'Strange Meeting'; 'My subject is War, and the pity of War. The Poetry is in the pity.'), Sassoon, Isaac Rosenberg.

steps.title: 'Dulce et Decorum Est'
steps.body: Gas attack: 'GAS! Gas! Quick, boys!' — man drowning 'under a green sea'. Ending calls Horace's 'Dulce et decorum est / Pro patria mori' 'The old Lie'. Irony, graphic imagery, half-rhyme.

activity.prompt: Brooke-style idealism or Owen-style realism?

items.text: 'If I should die, think only this of me'
'What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?'
'Some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England'

quiz.q: 'A terrible beauty is born' is from:
quiz.why: Yeats's refrain responds to the executions after the Easter Rising.

quiz.q: Owen wrote 'The Poetry is in the':
quiz.why: In his draft preface he said his subject was the pity of war.
Ezra Pound launched Imagism with H.D. and Aldington around 1912.

scenes.text: Prufrock wanders yellow-fogged streets: 'I have measured out my life with coffee spoons'.
1922: The Waste Land, a heap of broken images, shocks readers.

steps.title: Eliot (1888–1965)
steps.body: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' (1915/1917), The Waste Land (1922), 'The Hollow Men' (1925), Ash-Wednesday (1930), Four Quartets (1943), Murder in the Cathedral (1935). Essays: 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1919). Nobel 1948.

steps.title: The Waste Land structure
steps.body: Five parts: I The Burial of the Dead, II A Game of Chess, III The Fire Sermon, IV Death by Water, V What the Thunder Said. Sources: Grail legend (Jessie Weston, From Ritual to Romance), Frazer. Tiresias as unifying consciousness. Ends with the Upanishadic 'Datta. Dayadhvam. Damyata. / Shantih shantih shantih'. Edited by Pound.

steps.title: Opening
steps.body: 'April is the cruellest month, breeding / Lilacs out of the dead land': inverts Chaucer's April renewal; spiritual death makes rebirth painful. Enjambed participles (breeding, mixing, stirring) enact reluctant stirring.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Datta, Dayadhvam, Damyata' means give, sympathise, control — from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, not the Gita.

activity.prompt: Order the five sections of The Waste Land.

quiz.why: The thunder's three commands come from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

quiz.q: Who edited The Waste Land drafts heavily?
quiz.why: Eliot dedicated it to Pound, 'il miglior fabbro', for his cuts.
Prufrock's measured, timid life is summed up by coffee spoons.

story.title: Mrs Dalloway said she would buy the flowers

scenes.text: Big Ben strikes; Clarissa's and Septimus's thoughts flow through one June day in 1923.
Kurtz whispers, 'The horror! The horror!'

steps.title: Conrad
steps.body: Joseph Conrad: Heart of Darkness (1899/1902): Marlow's journey up the Congo to Kurtz; frame narrative on the Thames; imperialism, darkness within. Chinua Achebe (1975) called Conrad 'a thoroughgoing racist'. Also Lord Jim, Nostromo.

steps.title: Joyce and Woolf
steps.body: Joyce: Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916), Ulysses (1922, one day 16 June 1904, Leopold Bloom, Homeric parallels, Molly's monologue), Finnegans Wake. Woolf: Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927; 'Time Passes'), A Room of One's Own (1929: 'a woman must have money and a room of her own'), essay 'Modern Fiction' ('an incessant shower of innumerable atoms').

steps.title: Lawrence and Forster
steps.body: D.H. Lawrence: Sons and Lovers (1913, Oedipal conflict, Paul Morel), The Rainbow, Women in Love. E.M. Forster: Howards End ('Only connect'), A Passage to India (1924: Marabar Caves, Aziz, Adela Quested, Fielding; 'Not yet, not there').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ulysses takes place on one day (Bloomsday, 16 June 1904), not over years.

activity.prompt: Match the novel to its author.

quiz.why: Ulysses unfolds on 16 June 1904 in Dublin.
His 1975 lecture 'An Image of Africa' attacked Conrad's portrayal of Africans.
Forster's Howards End (1910) uses it as its motto.

scenes.text: Professor Higgins bets he can pass off a flower girl as a duchess.
In Synge's Playboy, Christy is hailed a hero for 'killing' his father.

steps.title: George Bernard Shaw (1856–1950)
steps.body: Drama of ideas, Fabian socialism, wit, long prefaces: Arms and the Man, Candida, Man and Superman ('Life Force'), Major Barbara, Pygmalion (1913), Saint Joan (1923). Nobel 1925. Attacked 'Bardolatry'; championed Ibsen (The Quintessence of Ibsenism).

steps.title: Irish Literary Revival
steps.body: Abbey Theatre (1904) founded by Yeats and Lady Gregory. J.M. Synge: Riders to the Sea (1904), The Playboy of the Western World (1907, riots). Sean O'Casey: Juno and the Paycock, The Plough and the Stars.

steps.title: Arms and the Man
steps.body: Romantic Raina idealises Sergius's cavalry charge; the practical Swiss 'chocolate-cream soldier' Bluntschli exposes war's realities. Shaw satirises romantic notions of war and love.

steps.title: Linking
steps.body: Connect Shaw to Ibsen's problem play and contrast with Eliot's poetic drama and post-war absurd theatre (next unit).

activity.prompt: Shaw or Irish Revival dramatist?

quiz.why: Yeats and Lady Gregory opened it in Dublin in December 1904.
He carries chocolates instead of cartridges, deflating heroic ideals.

options: The Playboy of the Western World
quiz.why: Nationalist audiences rioted at the Abbey in 1907 over its portrayal of Irish peasants.

options: 'Turning and turning in the widening gyre'
'That is no country for old men'
'I have met them at close of day'

questions.why: Owen's dream encounter with a dead enemy.
'Poetry is not a turning loose of emotion, but an escape from emotion.'

questions.q: The Waste Land was published in:

questions.why: Burnt Norton, East Coker, The Dry Salvages, Little Gidding.

questions.q: A Room of One's Own is by:
Paul Morel is the hero of:
In A Passage to India, the crisis occurs at:

'Mistah Kurtz—he dead' is the manager's boy's line.
Especially in the Don Juan in Hell interlude.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Post-1945 Literature and Revision
courses.summary: Auden and 1930s poets, Orwell and Golding, post-war drama (Beckett, Osborne, Pinter), the Movement and Larkin, Hughes and Heaney; revision.
outcomes: Discuss Auden and the poetry of the 1930s
Analyse Orwell's and Golding's novels as political/moral fables
Explain Waiting for Godot and the Absurd
Contrast Larkin and Hughes
Revise the whole period with a timeline

scenes.text: Winston Smith writes 'DOWN WITH BIG BROTHER' in a forbidden diary.
On an island, boys with a conch try to govern themselves and fail.

steps.title: W.H. Auden (1907–1973)
steps.body: Leader of the 1930s 'Auden group' (Spender, MacNeice, Day-Lewis): political, left-leaning, colloquial. 'September 1, 1939' ('a low dishonest decade'), 'Musée des Beaux Arts' (suffering ignored, Bruegel's Icarus), 'In Memory of W.B. Yeats' ('poetry makes nothing happen'), 'The Unknown Citizen'.

steps.title: George Orwell
steps.body: Animal Farm (1945): allegory of the Russian Revolution ('All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others'); Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949): totalitarian surveillance, Newspeak, doublethink, Room 101. Essays: 'Shooting an Elephant', 'Politics and the English Language'.

steps.title: William Golding
steps.body: Lord of the Flies (1954): Ralph (order), Piggy (reason), Jack (savagery), Simon (spiritual insight), conch (democracy), the 'Beast' within. Nobel 1983.

steps.title: 'Musée des Beaux Arts'
steps.body: 'About suffering they were never wrong, / The Old Masters': in Bruegel, Icarus falls while the ploughman and ship carry on. Theme: human indifference to individual suffering; conversational free-flowing lines.

activity.prompt: Which work?

quiz.q: 'Poetry makes nothing happen' is from Auden's elegy for:
quiz.why: It is in 'In Memory of W.B. Yeats' (1939).

quiz.q: Golding won the Nobel Prize in:
quiz.why: He received it in 1983.
Orwell's 1949 novel coins doublethink, holding two contradictory beliefs.

scenes.text: 1953 Paris, 1955 London: Vladimir and Estragon wait for Godot.
Jimmy Porter rages in a Midlands attic flat.

steps.title: Samuel Beckett
steps.body: Waiting for Godot (French 1953, English 1955): two acts, almost identical; Vladimir and Estragon, Pozzo and Lucky, a boy messenger; 'Nothing to be done'; Vivian Mercier: 'a play in which nothing happens, twice'. Endgame, Krapp's Last Tape, Happy Days. Nobel 1969.

steps.title: Angry Young Men and after
steps.body: Osborne's Look Back in Anger (1956). Pinter: The Birthday Party, The Caretaker, The Homecoming — pauses, menace, power. Stoppard: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead (1966). Caryl Churchill: Top Girls (1982, feminism). Arnold Wesker: kitchen-sink realism.

steps.title: Ending of Godot
steps.body: Each act ends: 'Well, shall we go?' / 'Yes, let's go.' (They do not move.) The gap between word and action dramatises paralysis and absurd hope.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Beckett wrote Godot first in French (En attendant Godot); give both dates.

activity.prompt: Match play to dramatist.

quiz.q: 'A play in which nothing happens, twice' was said by:
quiz.why: Critic Vivian Mercier described Godot this way in 1956.

quiz.q: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead reworks:
quiz.why: Stoppard centres two minor courtiers from Hamlet.

quiz.q: Jimmy Porter is the hero of:
quiz.why: Osborne's angry young man in the 1956 play.

scenes.text: Larkin stops his bike and enters an empty church: 'Once I am sure there's nothing going on'.
Hughes's hawk declares, 'I sit in the top of the wood, my eyes closed.'

steps.title: The Movement and Larkin
steps.body: 1950s Movement (Larkin, Amis, Davie, Jennings, Enright): plain diction, irony, traditional forms, anti-Modernist. Larkin: The Less Deceived, The Whitsun Weddings (1964), High Windows. 'Church Going', 'Toads', 'This Be The Verse', 'An Arundel Tomb' ('What will survive of us is love').

steps.title: Ted Hughes
steps.body: The Hawk in the Rain (1957), Lupercal ('Hawk Roosting', 'Pike'), Crow; violent energy of nature, myth. Poet Laureate 1984. Married to Sylvia Plath (Ariel; confessional poetry); Birthday Letters (1998).

steps.title: Seamus Heaney
steps.body: Northern Irish; Death of a Naturalist (1966): 'Digging' ('Between my finger and my thumb / The squat pen rests. / I'll dig with it.'); bog poems in North (1975); translation of Beowulf (1999). Nobel 1995.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Larkin's 'Church Going' meditates ironically on a secular age's residual need for seriousness; Hughes's 'Hawk Roosting' gives a predator's ruthless monologue — restraint vs primal energy.

activity.prompt: Larkin, Hughes or Heaney?

quiz.q: 'What will survive of us is love' ends:
quiz.why: Larkin's tentative final line in 'An Arundel Tomb'.
He received it in 1995.
They reacted against Modernist difficulty and Dylan Thomas's rhetoric.

scenes.text: 1798 Lyrical Ballads → 1850 In Memoriam → 1922 Waste Land → 1955 Godot → 1966 Death of a Naturalist.
Practise comparisons across periods.

steps.title: Timeline
steps.body: 1789 Songs of Innocence · 1798 Lyrical Ballads · 1813 Pride and Prejudice · 1817 Biographia · 1819 Keats's odes · 1847 Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights · 1850 In Memoriam, The Prelude · 1859 Origin of Species · 1891 Tess · 1899 Heart of Darkness · 1922 Ulysses, The Waste Land · 1924 Passage to India · 1925 Mrs Dalloway · 1949 Nineteen Eighty-Four · 1954 Lord of the Flies · 1955 Godot (English) · 1956 Look Back in Anger.

steps.title: Long answers (original)
steps.body: (1) Wordsworth's view of nature in 'Tintern Abbey'. (2) The supernatural in Coleridge. (3) Keats as a poet of the senses. (4) Faith and doubt in Victorian poetry. (5) Hardy's fatalism. (6) The Waste Land as a poem of modern spiritual crisis. (7) Absurdity in Waiting for Godot.

steps.title: Reference-to-context practice
steps.body: Identify poem, poet, context and significance: (a) 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness' (b) 'Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!' (c) 'Turning and turning in the widening gyre' (d) 'I have measured out my life with coffee spoons'.

steps.title: RTC format
steps.body: Name the text and author → place in the work → paraphrase → explain significance and devices → link to theme.

quiz.q: 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness' opens:
quiz.why: It is the first line of Keats's 'To Autumn'.

quiz.q: 'Turning and turning in the widening gyre' is from:
quiz.why: It opens Yeats's 'The Second Coming'.
Pride and Prejudice (1813) precedes Jane Eyre (1847), Tess (1891) and Mrs Dalloway (1925).

questions.why: Orwell served in the Burma police.
Pozzo drives Lucky on a rope.

questions.why: He realises the beast is within.

uni-ba-eng-indian-writing.title: Indian Writing in English
uni-ba-eng-indian-writing.description: From Derozio and the Renaissance to Tagore, Aurobindo, the Big Three novelists, modern poets, drama, and contemporary and Dalit/women's writing. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. English programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Beginnings: 19th Century to Independence
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Indian Writing in English)
courses.summary: Macaulay's Minute and the colonial context, Derozio, Toru Dutt, Michael Madhusudan Dutt, Sarojini Naidu, Tagore, Aurobindo, and nationalist prose of Gandhi and Nehru.
outcomes: Explain the colonial context of English education in India
Discuss Derozio and Toru Dutt as early poets
Analyse Sarojini Naidu's and Tagore's poetry in English
Describe Aurobindo's Savitri and nationalist prose

scenes.text: Macaulay argues for a class 'Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste'.
At Hindu College, Calcutta, young teacher Henry Derozio inspires 'Young Bengal'.

steps.title: Context
steps.body: Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (1835) and the English Education Act; universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1857). Raja Rammohan Roy's English prose on social reform. Bengal Renaissance.

steps.title: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio (1809–1831)
steps.body: Often called the first Indian poet in English; teacher at Hindu College; 'To India — My Native Land', 'The Harp of India', The Fakeer of Jungheera. Romantic, patriotic tone.

steps.title: Toru Dutt (1856–1877)
steps.body: Educated in France and England; A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields (1876, translations); Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (1882, posthumous; Savitri, Lakshman); 'Our Casuarina Tree' — memory, childhood and mortality. Edmund Gosse praised her. Also Michael Madhusudan Dutt: The Captive Ladie (1849), before returning to Bengali.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Toru Dutt died at 21 and much was published posthumously; do not date Ancient Ballads to her lifetime.

activity.prompt: Match the work to its author.

items.text: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields

quiz.why: Macaulay presented the Minute on Indian Education in February 1835.
He inspired the 'Young Bengal' movement at Hindu College.
The tree recalls Toru's childhood and dead siblings, linking nature and remembrance.

scenes.text: Gokhale's ally Sarojini Naidu is hailed as 'the Nightingale of India'.
1913: Tagore's English Gitanjali wins the Nobel Prize.

steps.title: Sarojini Naidu (1879–1949)
steps.body: The Golden Threshold (1905), The Bird of Time (1912), The Broken Wing (1917). Lyrical, musical, colourful Indian scenes: 'In the Bazaars of Hyderabad', 'Palanquin Bearers', 'Indian Weavers' (birth, marriage, death through robe colours). Edmund Gosse urged her to write of India. President of the Indian National Congress (1925).

steps.title: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941)
steps.body: Gitanjali: Song Offerings (1912, English prose-poem translations; introduction by Yeats); Nobel 1913, first non-European laureate. Also The Gardener, Fruit-Gathering, plays (The Post Office, Chitra), essays (Nationalism, 1917). Founded Santiniketan (Visva-Bharati).

steps.title: Gitanjali 35
steps.body: 'Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; / Where knowledge is free': anaphora of 'Where', a prayer for a free and rational nation, ending 'into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake.'

steps.title: 'Indian Weavers'
steps.body: Three stanzas: 'Robes of a new-born child' (blue, morning), 'marriage-veils of a queen' (purple and green, evening), 'a dead man's funeral shroud' (white, night). Life cycle in colour and time of day.

activity.prompt: Order the stages in 'Indian Weavers'.
items: Break of day: robes of a new-born child
Fall of night: marriage veils of a queen
Moonlight chill: a dead man's funeral shroud

quiz.q: Tagore received the Nobel Prize in:
quiz.why: The Swedish Academy honoured Gitanjali in 1913.

quiz.q: Who wrote the introduction to the English Gitanjali?
quiz.why: W.B. Yeats introduced the 1912 India Society edition.
Sarojini Naidu's first collection appeared in 1905.

scenes.text: Arrested in the Alipore bomb case, Aurobindo has a spiritual experience in jail.
Gandhi writes Hind Swaraj on a ship from London to South Africa, 1909.

steps.title: Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950)
steps.body: Revolutionary turned yogi at Pondicherry. Savitri: A Legend and a Symbol — epic in blank verse (about 24,000 lines) on Savitri's victory over Death, symbolising the soul's transformation. The Life Divine; The Future Poetry (criticism).

steps.title: Gandhi
steps.body: Hind Swaraj (1909, critique of modern civilisation), An Autobiography or The Story of My Experiments with Truth (Gujarati 1925–29; English trans. Mahadev Desai), journals Young India and Harijan. Plain, direct English prose.

steps.title: Nehru and others
steps.body: Jawaharlal Nehru: Glimpses of World History (letters to Indira), An Autobiography (1936), The Discovery of India (1946, written in Ahmednagar Fort). Vivekananda's Chicago address (1893). Nirad C. Chaudhuri: The Autobiography of an Unknown Indian (1951).

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: For 'nationalism in Indian English writing', combine Tagore's Nationalism (critical of the nation-state), Gandhi's Hind Swaraj and Raja Rao's Kanthapura.

activity.prompt: Match the prose work.

quiz.q: The Discovery of India was written in:
quiz.why: Nehru wrote it during imprisonment in Ahmednagar Fort, 1942–46.
Aurobindo composed his epic in iambic pentameter blank verse.

quiz.q: Gandhi's autobiography was originally written in:
quiz.why: It was serialised in Gujarati and translated by Mahadev Desai.

scenes.text: Raja Rao writes in 1938: 'One has to convey in a language that is not one's own the spirit that is one's own.'
Critics argue: Indo-Anglian, Indo-English, or Indian Writing in English?

steps.title: Names
steps.body: 'Indo-Anglian' (used by the Writers Workshop and K.R. Srinivasa Iyengar's 1943 book), 'Indo-English', 'Indian Writing in English' (Iyengar's later title, 1962), 'Indian English Literature'. The last two are now standard.

steps.title: Foreword to Kanthapura (1938)
steps.body: Raja Rao: English is 'the language of our intellectual make-up — like Sanskrit or Persian was before — but not of our emotional make-up'; Indians should develop an Indian English rhythm, like the Irish or Americans.

steps.title: Positions
steps.body: Buddhadeva Bose called Indian English poetry a 'blind alley'; P. Lal's Writers Workshop (1958) defended it. Kamala Das: 'The language I speak / Becomes mine, its distortions, its queernesses / All mine' ('An Introduction'). Rushdie's controversial claim (1997) that Indian English prose outweighed vernacular writing was widely contested.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not present Indian English literature as a minor offshoot; give the bilingual context and the case both for and against.

activity.prompt: Defence of English or scepticism?

quiz.q: 'Not of our emotional make-up' describes English, according to:
quiz.why: Raja Rao's foreword to Kanthapura distinguishes intellectual from emotional make-up.
P. Lal founded it in Calcutta in 1958.

quiz.q: K.R. Srinivasa Iyengar's history is titled:
quiz.why: His standard survey Indian Writing in English appeared in 1962.

questions.q: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan appeared in:

questions.why: Tagore translated the songs into rhythmic prose.
He warned against the Western nation-state model.

questions.q: The Post Office is a play by:
Sarojini Naidu presided over Congress in:
The Autobiography of an Unknown Indian is by:
Madhusudan Dutt later wrote mainly in:
questions.why: His Bengali epic Meghnad Badh Kavya made his name.

questions.q: 'Where the mind is without fear' prays for:
questions.why: It imagines the ideal awakened country.

courses.title: Unit 2 · The Big Three: Anand, Narayan, Raja Rao
courses.summary: The founding novelists of the 1930s: Mulk Raj Anand's social realism, R.K. Narayan's Malgudi, and Raja Rao's Kanthapura; plus partition fiction.
outcomes: Analyse Untouchable as a social novel
Describe Narayan's Malgudi, irony and comedy using The Guide
Explain Kanthapura's Gandhian theme and sthala-purana form
Discuss partition fiction: Train to Pakistan

scenes.text: Bakha, a young sweeper, cleans latrines at dawn in a cantonment town.
At day's end he hears Gandhi speak, and a poet proposes the flush toilet as liberation.

steps.title: Anand (1905–2004)
steps.body: Social realist, humanist, influenced by Marxism and Gandhi. Untouchable (1935; preface by E.M. Forster), Coolie (1936), Two Leaves and a Bud (1937, tea plantation labour), The Village trilogy, The Private Life of an Indian Prince.

steps.title: Untouchable
steps.body: Covers a single day in Bakha's life. Key episode: Bakha accidentally touches a caste Hindu ('Keep to the side of the road!'); slapped; sister Sohini molested by the priest Kali Nath. Three solutions at the end: Christianity (Colonel Hutchinson of the Salvation Army), Gandhi's call to end untouchability, and the machine (the flush system, via the poet Iqbal Nath Sarshar).

steps.title: Technique
steps.body: Unity of time, compressed action, literal translations of Punjabi/Hindi expressions ('Posh, keep away'), abuse words, interior monologue in places.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The novel offers three possible solutions without definitively choosing one; avoid saying Anand endorses only the machine.

activity.prompt: Which solution to untouchability does each figure offer?

quiz.why: Forster wrote the preface for the 1935 edition.
Anand compresses the story into a single day in Bakha's life.

quiz.q: Two Leaves and a Bud depicts:
quiz.why: It exposes exploitation on an Assam tea estate.

scenes.text: Raju runs a shop at Malgudi station and becomes a tourist guide.
Mistaken for a holy man, he fasts for rain at the river.

steps.title: Narayan (1906–2001)
steps.body: Created the fictional South Indian town Malgudi. Swami and Friends (1935, published with Graham Greene's help), The Bachelor of Arts, The English Teacher, The Financial Expert, The Guide (1958; Sahitya Akademi award), The Man-Eater of Malgudi, Malgudi Days (stories).

steps.title: The Guide
steps.body: Two narrative strands alternate: present (Raju, out of jail, at a temple at Mangala, taken for a swami by Velan) and past (Raju's affair with Rosie, a dancer married to the archaeologist Marco; he manages her career, forges her signature and is jailed). Ending: Raju fasts; 'Velan, it's raining in the hills.'

steps.title: Style
steps.body: Simple, transparent English; gentle irony and comedy; ordinary middle-class lives; a cyclical sense of order restored; Indian sensibility without exotic decoration.

steps.title: Ambiguous ending
steps.body: Does it rain? Raju 'felt it was raining in the hills' as he sags down. Narayan leaves open whether this is a miracle, illusion or death — the ironic transformation of a con-man into a saint.

activity.prompt: Order Raju's life (chronological, not narrative order).
items: Taken for a swami at Mangala

quiz.q: Who helped publish Swami and Friends?
quiz.why: Graham Greene recommended it to a publisher in 1935.
Marco is an archaeologist absorbed in cave paintings.
Narayan won the Sahitya Akademi Award for English in 1960.

scenes.text: In a Karnataka village, an old widow, Achakka, narrates how Gandhi came to Kanthapura.
Moorthy leads the villagers in satyagraha; the village is destroyed.

steps.title: Raja Rao (1908–2006)
steps.body: Kanthapura (1938), The Serpent and the Rope (1960, Sahitya Akademi; metaphysical, Advaita Vedanta), The Cat and Shakespeare, Comrade Kirillov.

steps.title: Kanthapura
steps.body: Gandhian movement in a village: Moorthy (Gandhian hero), Bhatta (exploiter), Bade Khan (policeman), Skeffington Coffee Estate, Rangamma, Ratna; boycotts, toddy-picketing, police violence, exile. Gandhi as mythic figure; Rama-Ravana parallels (Gandhi = Rama, British = Ravana).

steps.title: Form
steps.body: Sthala-purana (legendary history of a place); breathless oral narrative with long sentences, Kannada rhythm and idioms; storytelling 'like the Puranas'. Foreword defends Indian English (see Unit 1).

steps.title: Answer tip
steps.body: Discuss Kanthapura's three layers: political (freedom struggle), social (caste reform), religious-mythic (Harikatha).

activity.prompt: Gandhian side or opposing side?

quiz.why: Old Achakka tells the story in the manner of village oral tradition.

options: A legendary history of a place
quiz.why: Raja Rao says every Indian village has a sthala-purana, a legendary history.

quiz.q: The Serpent and the Rope draws on:
quiz.why: The title echoes the Vedantic image of mistaking a rope for a serpent.

scenes.text: Summer 1947: a ghost train full of corpses arrives at a Punjab village.
Juggut Singh climbs the bridge to save his beloved's train.

steps.title: Train to Pakistan (1956)
steps.body: Khushwant Singh. Mano Majra, a Sikh–Muslim village on the Sutlej; trains mark time. Characters: Juggut Singh (Jugga, a badmash), Nooran, Hukum Chand (magistrate), Iqbal (Westernised activist), the Imam and Meet Singh. Climax: Jugga sacrifices himself to let the train to Pakistan pass.

steps.title: Other partition works
steps.body: Chaman Nahal's Azadi (1975), Manohar Malgonkar's A Bend in the Ganges, Bapsi Sidhwa's Ice-Candy-Man (1988; film Earth), Amitav Ghosh's The Shadow Lines (1988), Saadat Hasan Manto's Urdu stories in translation ('Toba Tek Singh').

steps.title: Themes
steps.body: Communal violence, failure of institutions and intellectuals, love across communities, moral redemption by the unlikely hero, the human cost of borders.

steps.title: Irony
steps.body: Iqbal, the educated reformer, theorises but does nothing; illiterate Jugga acts and dies. Khushwant Singh contrasts words and deeds.

activity.prompt: Which partition novel?

items.text: Lenny, a Parsi girl in Lahore

quiz.q: Train to Pakistan is set in:
quiz.why: Khushwant Singh's fictional border village is Mano Majra.
Lenny, a polio-afflicted Parsi child, narrates.

quiz.q: Iqbal in Train to Pakistan represents:
quiz.why: He talks of revolution but fails to act when it matters.

questions.q: The English Teacher is partly based on:
In Kanthapura, Gandhi is compared to:
questions.why: British rule is the demon Ravana.

options: A villager who believes Raju is holy
questions.why: He first treats Raju as a swami.
He wrote of the oppressed realistically.

questions.q: Raja Rao's narrative style in Kanthapura is:
questions.why: Long run-on sentences mimic village grandmothers' tales.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Modern Indian English Poetry
courses.summary: Post-1947 poetry: Nissim Ezekiel, A.K. Ramanujan, Kamala Das, Jayanta Mahapatra, R. Parthasarathy, Arun Kolatkar, Dom Moraes, Keki Daruwalla, and later voices.
outcomes: Analyse Ezekiel's irony and Indian English idiom
Discuss Ramanujan's memory, family and translation
Interpret Kamala Das's confessional feminism
Describe Mahapatra's Orissa landscapes and Kolatkar's Jejuri

scenes.text: Rain drives a scorpion under a sack of rice; it stings the poet's mother.
Peasants come 'like swarms of flies' chanting the name of God.

steps.title: Ezekiel (1924–2004)
steps.body: Bene Israel Jew from Bombay; 'father of modern Indian English poetry'. A Time to Change (1952), The Unfinished Man (1960), The Exact Name (1965), Hymns in Darkness (1976), Latter-Day Psalms (1982; Sahitya Akademi 1983). Urban Bombay, irony, self-scrutiny, craft.

steps.title: 'Night of the Scorpion'
steps.body: Narrative free verse: villagers' superstition ('May the sin of your previous birth be burned away'), father's rationalism and its collapse ('trying every curse and blessing, / powder, mixture, herb and hybrid'), holy man's incantation. Ending: 'My mother only said / Thank God the scorpion picked on me / And spared my children.' Maternal love beyond belief and reason.

steps.title: Indian English poems
steps.body: 'Goodbye Party for Miss Pushpa T.S.', 'The Patriot', 'The Professor': comic use of Indian English ('I am standing for peace and non-violence'; continuous tenses). Affectionate irony, not mockery.

steps.title: Other poems
steps.body: 'Background, Casually' ('I have made my commitments now... I cannot leave the island, / I was born here and belong'), 'Enterprise' (pilgrimage that dissolves: 'Home is where we have to gather grace'), 'Poet, Lover, Birdwatcher'.

activity.prompt: Order the movement of 'Night of the Scorpion'.
items: Rain drives the scorpion indoors; it stings the mother
Father tries curses, blessings and paraffin
Mother thanks God it spared her children

quiz.q: Latter-Day Psalms won the Sahitya Akademi Award in:
quiz.why: Ezekiel received the award in 1983 for Latter-Day Psalms.

quiz.q: 'Home is where we have to gather grace' ends:
quiz.why: The pilgrimage in 'Enterprise' teaches that grace is found at home.

quiz.q: 'Goodbye Party for Miss Pushpa T.S.' uses:
quiz.why: Ezekiel imitates the speaker's continuous tenses and formal clichés with affectionate irony.

scenes.text: In Madurai, poets sing of the river only when it floods.
The flood carries away a pregnant woman 'expecting identical twins'.

steps.title: Ramanujan (1929–1993)
steps.body: Poet, linguist, folklorist, translator (Tamil Sangam poetry: The Interior Landscape, 1967; Kannada vachanas: Speaking of Siva). Poetry: The Striders (1966), Relations (1971), Second Sight (1986). Taught at the University of Chicago.

steps.title: 'A River'
steps.body: Contrast: in summer the Vaikai is dry, showing 'the wet stones glistening like sleepy crocodiles'; old and new poets praise the flood but ignore the drowned poor ('a pregnant woman / expecting identical twins / with no more than a couple of houses'). Satire of poetic indifference to suffering.

steps.title: Memory and family
steps.body: 'Small-Scale Reflections on a Great House' (everything returns to the house), 'Obituary' (father left 'a changed mother and more / than one annual ceremony'), 'Self-Portrait', 'Of Mothers, Among Other Things'. Irony, precise images, Tamil akam/puram influence.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.body: Ramanujan's essay 'Is There an Indian Way of Thinking?' (context-sensitive thought) helps explain his poetics.

activity.prompt: Which Ramanujan text?

items.text: Is There an Indian Way of Thinking?

quiz.why: The poem describes the Vaikai river at Madurai.
It translates Virashaiva vachana poetry from Kannada.

quiz.q: The target of satire in 'A River' is:
quiz.why: Poets celebrate the flood's grandeur while ignoring the drowned woman and lost houses.

scenes.text: Told to 'fit in', she puts on a shirt and her brother's trousers.
'I am Indian, very brown, born in Malabar, I speak three languages.'

steps.title: Kamala Das (1934–2009)
steps.body: Also Madhavikutty in Malayalam. Summer in Calcutta (1965), The Descendants (1967), The Old Playhouse and Other Poems (1973). Autobiography My Story (1976). Confessional, frank about female desire and marriage.

steps.title: 'An Introduction'
steps.body: Assertion of identity against categorisers ('Don't write in English, they said'), language as her own; early marriage and lovelessness; defiance of gender roles ('Dress in sarees, be girl, / Be wife'); ending 'I too call myself I'. Free verse, conversational, bold.

steps.title: Other poems
steps.body: 'The Old Playhouse' (husband as captor; 'You called me wife, / I was taught to break saccharine into your tea'), 'My Grandmother's House' (lost love), 'The Sunshine Cat', 'A Hot Noon in Malabar'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not reduce her to 'erotic'; her poetry is about selfhood, freedom and the search for love.

activity.prompt: Theme in Kamala Das's poems.

quiz.why: She wrote Malayalam fiction as Madhavikutty.
Her first collection was published in 1965.

options: Home is where we gather grace
Thank God the scorpion picked on me
quiz.why: She asserts the universal self against those who would define her.

scenes.text: A state transport bus rattles toward the temple town of Jejuri.
Every stone, the priest says, is a god.

steps.title: Jayanta Mahapatra (1928–2023)
steps.body: Physicist-poet from Cuttack, Odisha. Relationship (1980; first Sahitya Akademi for English poetry, 1981), A Rain of Rites, 'Hunger' (a fisherman offers his daughter to the speaker: 'I heard him say: my daughter, she's just turned fifteen…'), 'Dawn at Puri'. Silence, guilt, landscape, ritual.

steps.title: Arun Kolatkar (1932–2004)
steps.body: Jejuri (1976; Commonwealth Poetry Prize): sequence of 31 poems on a pilgrimage town, sceptical, witty ('The Doorstep', 'A Low Temple', 'The Railway Station'); bilingual Marathi-English poet. Kala Ghoda Poems.

steps.title: Parthasarathy, Moraes, Daruwalla
steps.body: R. Parthasarathy: Rough Passage (1977): exile, return, language ('My tongue in English chains'). Dom Moraes: A Beginning (1957, Hawthornden Prize). Keki Daruwalla: Under Orion; landscape and violence. Later: Agha Shahid Ali (ghazals), Meena Kandasamy, Eunice de Souza ('Catholic Mother').

steps.title: 'A Low Temple'
steps.body: Inside the dark temple, 'A match struck right under her nose' shows gods; the speaker counts the arms of an eight-armed goddess and gets 'eighteen'; he steps out, lights a cigarette. Irony toward ritual, with curiosity.

activity.prompt: Match poem or book to poet.

quiz.q: The first Sahitya Akademi Award for English poetry went to:
quiz.why: Jayanta Mahapatra won it in 1981 for Relationship.
Kolatkar's sequence won the Commonwealth Poetry Prize in 1977.

quiz.q: 'My tongue in English chains' is by:
quiz.why: From Rough Passage, on the poet's alienation in English.

questions.q: My Story is the autobiography of:
