courses.title: Unit 4 · Indian Drama and Post-1980 Fiction
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Indian drama and fiction)
courses.summary: Indian drama in English and translation (Karnad, Tendulkar, Dattani), and post-Midnight's Children fiction: Rushdie, Desai, Ghosh, Roy, Seth, Mistry.
outcomes: Analyse Karnad's use of myth and folk forms in Hayavadana and Tughlaq
Discuss Tendulkar's Silence! The Court Is in Session and Dattani's themes
Explain Midnight's Children's magic realism and history
Interpret The God of Small Things and The Shadow Lines

scenes.text: A man with a horse's head seeks completion.
Devadatta and Kapila behead themselves; Padmini rejoins the heads to the wrong bodies.

steps.title: Karnad (1938–2019)
steps.body: Wrote in Kannada and translated many plays into English himself. Yayati (1961), Tughlaq (1964), Hayavadana (1971), Naga-Mandala (1988), Tale-Danda (1990), The Fire and the Rain (1995). Jnanpith 1998.

steps.title: Hayavadana
steps.body: Sources: Kathasaritsagara via Thomas Mann's The Transposed Heads. Main plot: Padmini, Devadatta (intellect) and Kapila (body); heads switched — question of which is the husband. Subplot: Hayavadana, half horse, becomes a complete horse. Folk form: Yakshagana conventions, Bhagavata narrator, masks, half-curtain, Ganesha invocation (himself 'incomplete'). Theme: incompleteness and identity.

steps.title: Tughlaq
steps.body: Muhammad bin Tughlaq, idealist sultan whose schemes (shifting the capital to Daulatabad, copper currency) fail; read as allegory of Nehruvian idealism and disillusionment in the 1960s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Hayavadana is not a Sanskrit original drama; it is a modern Kannada play adapting a Sanskrit tale through Mann.

activity.prompt: Hayavadana: what does each represent?

quiz.why: Karnad drew on Mann's novella The Transposed Heads, itself from the Kathasaritsagara.

quiz.q: Tughlaq is often read as an allegory of:
quiz.why: Critics link the failed visionary sultan with disillusionment after Nehru's idealism.
He won the Jnanpith Award in 1998.

scenes.text: Amateur actors stage a mock trial to pass time; it turns into a real assault on Leela Benare.
In Dattani's Tara, twins conjoined at birth discover who chose which leg.

steps.title: Vijay Tendulkar (1928–2008)
steps.body: Marathi dramatist widely studied in English translation: Silence! The Court Is in Session (Shantata! Court Chalu Ahe, 1967), Ghashiram Kotwal (1972), Sakharam Binder, Kanyadaan. Silence!: Benare, an unmarried pregnant teacher, is 'tried' by hypocritical colleagues; her final monologue indicts society.

steps.title: Mahesh Dattani (b.1958)
steps.body: First English-language playwright to win the Sahitya Akademi Award (1998, Final Solutions and Other Plays). Tara (gender discrimination; twins Tara and Chandan), Dance Like a Man, Final Solutions (communalism), Bravely Fought the Queen, On a Muggy Night in Mumbai (queer identities).

steps.title: Others
steps.body: Badal Sircar (Bengali: Evam Indrajit; Third Theatre), Mohan Rakesh (Hindi: Halfway House/Adhe Adhure), Asif Currimbhoy, Mahasweta Devi (Mother of 1084), Habib Tanvir (Charandas Chor).

steps.title: Tara's crisis
steps.body: Surgery to separate the twins gave the shared third leg to the boy Chandan though blood supply favoured Tara: the mother and grandfather's preference for a son. Gender bias inside a modern urban family.

activity.prompt: Match the play to the dramatist.

items.text: Silence! The Court Is in Session

quiz.why: Benare is the schoolteacher put on mock trial.

quiz.q: Dattani's Sahitya Akademi award (1998) was for:
quiz.why: The award honoured the collection Final Solutions and Other Plays.
The family favours the son over the daughter in the twins' separation.

scenes.text: At the stroke of midnight, 15 August 1947, Saleem Sinai is born.
He tells his story to Padma while pickling 'chutnification of history'.

steps.title: Salman Rushdie (b.1947)
steps.body: Midnight's Children (1981; Booker Prize; later 'Booker of Bookers' 1993 and 'Best of the Booker' 2008), Shame (1983), The Satanic Verses (1988; fatwa 1989), The Moor's Last Sigh. Essay 'Imaginary Homelands'.

steps.title: Midnight's Children
steps.body: Saleem's life mirrors the nation; 1,001 children born in the first hour of independence have magical powers; Saleem's telepathy; Shiva (his rival, switched at birth by Mary Pereira); events: Partition, 1965 war, Bangladesh 1971, Emergency (the 'Widow'). Narrated to Padma; 30 jars of pickles = 30 chapters.

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body: Magic realism, unreliable narration (Saleem's errors in dates), oral storytelling, hybrid 'chutnified' English, metafiction, historiographic metafiction (Linda Hutcheon's term).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saleem is not biologically his parents' child; he and Shiva were swapped at birth. That swap is central to the national allegory.

activity.prompt: Order the historical events in Midnight's Children.

quiz.q: Saleem was switched at birth with:
quiz.why: Mary Pereira swapped the babies Saleem and Shiva.

quiz.q: Midnight's Children won the Booker in:
quiz.why: It won in 1981, and later 'Booker of Bookers'.
Padma, a pickle-factory worker, interrupts and questions his narration.

scenes.text: In Ayemenem, Kerala, twins Estha and Rahel watch the Love Laws broken.
In The Shadow Lines, a boy learns that borders are lines drawn in the mind.

steps.title: Anita and Kiran Desai
steps.body: Anita Desai: Cry, the Peacock (1963), Clear Light of Day (1980), In Custody, Fire on the Mountain: psychological, women's inner lives. Kiran Desai: The Inheritance of Loss (Booker 2006).

steps.title: Amitav Ghosh
steps.body: The Circle of Reason, The Shadow Lines (1988; Sahitya Akademi 1989), The Glass Palace, The Hungry Tide (Sundarbans, ecology), Ibis trilogy (Sea of Poppies). Jnanpith 2018. Themes: borders, memory, history, migration.

steps.title: Arundhati Roy
steps.body: The God of Small Things (1997, Booker): non-linear narrative, child's perspective, wordplay; Ammu's love for Velutha, a Paravan (Dalit) carpenter, breaks the 'Love Laws' that 'lay down who should be loved, and how. And how much'; Sophie Mol's drowning. Caste, gender, history in Kerala.

steps.title: Seth and Mistry
steps.body: Vikram Seth: The Golden Gate (novel in verse, 1986, Onegin stanzas), A Suitable Boy (1993: Lata's choice of husband in 1950s India). Rohinton Mistry: Such a Long Journey, A Fine Balance (1995; Emergency). Also Aravind Adiga, The White Tiger (Booker 2008).

quiz.why: His caste makes his love for Ammu a transgression of the Love Laws.

quiz.why: Seth's novel uses 690 tetrameter sonnets modelled on Pushkin.

quiz.why: Ghosh's 2004 novel explores the tidal islands of the Sundarbans.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Women's, Dalit and Diasporic Writing; Revision
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Indian Writing in English)
courses.summary: Women's writing (Shashi Deshpande, Mahasweta Devi in translation), Dalit writing (Ambedkar, Bama, Omprakash Valmiki), diaspora (Lahiri, Mukherjee), and revision with exam practice.
outcomes: Discuss feminist concerns in Shashi Deshpande and Mahasweta Devi
Explain Dalit literature's aims through Ambedkar, Bama and Valmiki
Describe diasporic themes in Jhumpa Lahiri
Answer previous-year-style questions across the course

scenes.text: Jaya, a middle-class wife, breaks seventeen years of silence in a Bombay flat.
Dopdi Mejhen, a tribal rebel, stands naked and unbowed before the officer Senanayak.

steps.title: Shashi Deshpande (b.1938)
steps.body: The Dark Holds No Terrors (1980), Roots and Shadows, That Long Silence (1988; Sahitya Akademi 1990), Small Remedies. Middle-class women's selfhood, marriage, silence and voice.

steps.title: Mahasweta Devi (1926–2016)
steps.body: Bengali writer-activist for tribal people. 'Draupadi' (trans. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, 1981): Dopdi refuses to be clothed after custodial rape, confronting power; Mother of 1084 (Hajar Churashir Maa), Breast Stories, Imaginary Maps. Jnanpith 1996.

steps.title: Others
steps.body: Nayantara Sahgal (Rich Like Us), Githa Hariharan (The Thousand Faces of Night), Manju Kapur (Difficult Daughters), Ismat Chughtai ('Lihaaf', Urdu, in translation).

steps.title: 'Draupadi' as rewriting
steps.body: The Mahabharata's Draupadi is saved by Krishna's endless sari; Dopdi has no saviour and turns her nakedness into defiance: 'There isn't a man here that I should be ashamed.' Myth subverted to expose state violence.

activity.prompt: Match the work to its author.

steps.title: Ambedkar
steps.body: B.R. Ambedkar: Annihilation of Caste (1936; undelivered address to the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal of Lahore), 'Castes in India' (1916), Who Were the Shudras?. Argues caste is graded inequality sanctioned by scripture; calls for its destruction.

steps.title: Dalit literature
steps.body: Literature of testimony and resistance by Dalits about caste oppression; origins in Marathi Dalit Panthers (1972). Autobiographies central: Omprakash Valmiki's Joothan (Hindi 1997; trans. Arun Prabha Mukherjee), Bama's Karukku (Tamil 1992; trans. Lakshmi Holmström), Sharankumar Limbale's The Outcaste (Akkarmashi), Baby Kamble's The Prisons We Broke.

steps.title: Karukku
steps.body: Karukku = palmyra leaf with serrated edges, image of pain and also sharpness for resistance. Bama, a Dalit Christian woman, records caste discrimination within the Church and her leaving the convent. Testimonial, non-linear, Tamil dialect.

steps.title: Key concept
steps.body: Sharankumar Limbale's Towards an Aesthetic of Dalit Literature argues Dalit writing needs its own aesthetic based on lived experience, not upper-caste standards of 'beauty'.

Gogol, in America, renames himself Nikhil and drifts between worlds.

steps.title: Diaspora
steps.body: Writers of Indian origin abroad: themes of migration, memory, hybridity, generational conflict, nostalgia, 'imaginary homelands' (Rushdie). Old diaspora (indentured labour: V.S. Naipaul's A House for Mr Biswas) vs new diaspora (professional migration).

steps.title: Jhumpa Lahiri
steps.body: Interpreter of Maladies (2000 Pulitzer Prize; 'A Temporary Matter', 'Mrs. Sen's', 'The Third and Final Continent'), The Namesake (2003), Unaccustomed Earth, The Lowland.

steps.title: 'The Third and Final Continent'
steps.body: Narrator moves from India to London to Cambridge, Massachusetts; lodges with 103-year-old Mrs Croft ('A flag on the moon!'); the story celebrates ordinary immigrant achievement: 'I know that my achievement is quite ordinary.'

uni-ba-eng-literary-criticism.title: Literary Criticism & Theory
uni-ba-eng-literary-criticism.description: Classical and Indian poetics, English criticism from Sidney to Arnold, Eliot and New Criticism, structuralism and post-structuralism, and Marxist, feminist, psychoanalytic and historicist theory. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. English programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Classical and Indian Poetics
courses.summary: Plato's attack on poetry, Aristotle's Poetics, Horace's Ars Poetica, Longinus On the Sublime, and Indian poetics: rasa, dhvani, alamkara, vakrokti, auchitya.
outcomes: Explain Plato's theory of mimesis and objections to poets
Summarise Aristotle's response on mimesis, tragedy and catharsis
State Horace's and Longinus's key principles
Describe Bharata's rasa theory and Anandavardhana's dhvani

scenes.text: Plato: God makes the Idea of a bed, the carpenter a bed, the painter a picture of a bed.
Aristotle replies: imitation is natural to humans and a source of learning.

steps.title: Plato (Republic, Books II, III, X; Ion)
steps.body: Theory of Forms: reality = Ideas. Art imitates appearances, so it is 'thrice removed from truth' (the bed example). Objections: poets lie about gods (II–III), arouse emotions that should be controlled (X), and imitation corrupts character; poets compose by divine madness, not knowledge (Ion). Poets to be banished from the ideal state except hymns to gods and praises of good men.

steps.title: Aristotle (Poetics, c.335 BCE)
steps.body: Mimesis is natural and pleasurable; poetry imitates universals ('Poetry is more philosophical and higher than history; for poetry tends to express the universal, history the particular'); catharsis answers Plato's emotional objection; probability over fact; plot as soul of tragedy; tragedy superior to epic.

steps.title: Plato vs Aristotle grid
steps.body: Mimesis: copy of a copy (P) vs creative representation of universals (A). Emotion: feeds passions (P) vs purges/clarifies them (A). Truth: poets ignorant (P) vs poetry more philosophical than history (A).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Poetics is incomplete; the promised treatment of comedy is lost. Catharsis is mentioned only once in the definition of tragedy, hence its many interpretations (purgation, purification, clarification).

activity.prompt: Plato's view or Aristotle's view?

items.text: Art is thrice removed from truth
Poets should be banished from the ideal state

quiz.q: Plato's attack on poetry is chiefly in:
quiz.why: Books II, III and X of the Republic contain the main critique of poets.

quiz.q: Aristotle says poetry is more philosophical than history because it deals with:
quiz.why: History records what happened; poetry what may happen according to probability or necessity.

quiz.q: The Poetics' lost portion dealt with:
quiz.why: Aristotle promises a treatment of comedy that has not survived.

scenes.text: Horace writes a verse letter to the Pisos advising young poets.
Longinus says great writing strikes like a thunderbolt.

steps.title: Horace, Ars Poetica (c.19–10 BCE)
steps.body: Verse epistle to the Pisos. Principles: decorum (fitness of style to subject and character), unity and simplicity, utile et dulce — poetry should instruct and delight; in medias res; five acts; no violence on stage; no deus ex machina unless necessary; study Greek models 'by night and by day'; labour of revision (keep a work nine years).

steps.title: Longinus, On the Sublime (Peri Hupsous, 1st c. CE)
steps.body: Sublimity is 'the echo of a great soul'; it transports (ekstasis) rather than persuades. Five sources: (1) great thoughts, (2) strong, inspired emotion — both innate; (3) figures of speech, (4) noble diction, (5) dignified composition — arts. Example: Genesis 'Let there be light'; Sappho's ode.

steps.title: Decorum applied
steps.body: Horace: if a character is introduced as Achilles, make him 'impatient, wrathful, inexorable, fierce'; a new character must remain consistent to the end.

steps.title: Influence
steps.body: Horace shaped Renaissance and neoclassical criticism (Sidney, Jonson, Boileau, Pope); Longinus, via Boileau's 1674 translation, shaped Burke's and Romantic ideas of the sublime.

activity.prompt: Longinus's sources of the sublime: innate or acquired by art?

quiz.why: Horace says the poet who mixes the useful with the sweet wins every vote.

quiz.q: For Longinus, sublimity is 'the echo of':
quiz.why: He locates the sublime in the writer's greatness of mind.

quiz.q: How many sources of the sublime does Longinus give?
quiz.why: Two innate and three acquired sources make five.

scenes.text: As spices combine into flavour, says Bharata, factors combine to produce rasa.
A spectator watching Shakuntala's farewell tastes karuna rasa, the aesthetic of pathos.

steps.title: Bharata's Natyashastra
steps.body: Treatise on drama (dated variously, c.200 BCE–200 CE). Rasa sutra: 'vibhava-anubhava-vyabhichari-samyogad rasa-nishpattih' — rasa arises from the union of determinants (vibhava: causes such as characters and setting), consequents (anubhava: physical expressions) and transitory states (vyabhichari bhava, 33). Sthayi bhava: permanent emotion.

steps.title: Eight (nine) rasas
steps.body: Shringara (erotic/love; rati), Hasya (comic; hasa), Karuna (pathetic; shoka), Raudra (furious; krodha), Vira (heroic; utsaha), Bhayanaka (terrible; bhaya), Bibhatsa (odious; jugupsa), Adbhuta (marvellous; vismaya). Shanta (peace; nirveda/shama) added later, championed by Abhinavagupta.

steps.title: Commentators
steps.body: Bhatta Lollata (rasa in the character), Shankuka (inference/imitation), Bhatta Nayaka (generalisation — sadharanikarana), Abhinavagupta (rasa as universalised aesthetic relish in the sahridaya, the sensitive spectator).

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: Othello's murder of Desdemona: vibhava = Iago's plot and handkerchief; anubhava = trembling, weeping; vyabhichari = jealousy, despair; sthayi = shoka → karuna rasa (with raudra).

activity.prompt: Match the rasa to its sthayi bhava.

quiz.why: The Natyashastra lists eight; Shanta was added later as the ninth.
Bhatta Nayaka held that emotions are universalised for the spectator's enjoyment.

quiz.q: The ideal sensitive reader is called:
quiz.why: Sahridaya means 'of like heart', the competent reader who relishes rasa.

scenes.text: 'The village on the Ganga' — not literally on water, but suggesting coolness and sanctity.
Anandavardhana says the soul of poetry is what resonates beyond the words.

steps.title: Dhvani (Anandavardhana, Dhvanyaloka, 9th c.)
steps.body: Three powers of words: abhidha (denotation), lakshana (indication/secondary meaning), vyanjana (suggestion). Dhvani — suggested meaning — is the soul of poetry ('kavyasya atma dhvanih'). Types: vastu-dhvani (idea), alamkara-dhvani (figure), rasa-dhvani (emotion, the highest). Abhinavagupta's commentary Lochana.

steps.title: Other schools
steps.body: Alamkara (Bhamaha, Dandin): figures of speech as essence. Riti (Vamana): style is the soul of poetry ('ritir atma kavyasya'). Vakrokti (Kuntaka): oblique/striking expression. Auchitya (Kshemendra): propriety/appropriateness. Compare Horace's decorum.

steps.title: 'Gangayam ghoshah'
steps.body: 'A hamlet on the Ganga': literal meaning impossible (abhidha fails); lakshana gives 'on the bank'; vyanjana suggests coolness and holiness — dhvani.

steps.title: Comparative tip
steps.body: Rasa ≈ catharsis/emotional effect; dhvani ≈ Empson's ambiguity or Eliot's suggestion; auchitya ≈ decorum. Use such comparisons carefully, noting differences.

activity.prompt: Match the school to its founder/key figure.

quiz.q: The power of suggestion is called:
quiz.why: Vyanjana is the suggestive power through which dhvani operates.
Anandavardhana wrote it in 9th-century Kashmir.

quiz.q: Which school's Western parallel is decorum?
quiz.why: Kshemendra's auchitya, like Horace's decorum, stresses appropriateness.

options: Hymns to gods and praises of good men

questions.q: Horace advises keeping a work back for:
On the Sublime was popularised in France by:

questions.why: Style is the soul of poetry.

questions.q: Highest kind of dhvani for Anandavardhana:

courses.title: Unit 2 · English Criticism: Sidney to Arnold
courses.summary: Sidney's Apology, Dryden's Essay of Dramatic Poesy, Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare, Wordsworth and Coleridge, Shelley, and Matthew Arnold.
outcomes: Summarise Sidney's defence of poetry
Explain Dryden's comparative criticism and Johnson's judgements on Shakespeare
Compare Wordsworth's and Coleridge's theories of poetry
Apply Arnold's touchstone method and 'criticism of life'

scenes.text: 'Nature's world is brazen; the poets only deliver a golden,' writes Sidney.
Four friends in a barge on the Thames debate ancient vs modern drama while guns boom in the Dutch war.

steps.title: Sidney, An Apology for Poetry (c.1580, publ. 1595)
steps.body: Reply to Stephen Gosson's School of Abuse. Poetry is the oldest learning; the poet as maker (Greek poiein); superior to the philosopher (abstract precept) and historian (bare fact) because it unites precept and example. Answers four charges: poetry wastes time, is lies ('the poet nothing affirmeth, and therefore never lieth'), corrupts, and was banished by Plato. Criticises contemporary drama's breaking of unities and mixing of kings and clowns.

steps.title: Dryden, An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668)
steps.body: Dialogue: Crites (ancients), Eugenius (moderns), Lisideius (French), Neander (English; Dryden's voice). Neander defends English variety, tragicomedy and Shakespeare ('the largest and most comprehensive soul'), compares Jonson ('the more correct poet') and Shakespeare ('the greater wit'), and defends rhyme in serious plays. Dryden is called 'the father of English criticism' (Johnson).

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: If asked why poetry beats history for Sidney: the historian is tied to 'what is', so shows vice rewarded; the poet shows virtue rewarded and teaches by 'speaking picture'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sidney's essay has two titles (Apology for Poetry by Olney; Defence of Poesy by Ponsonby, both 1595); both are correct.

activity.prompt: Match the speaker to his position in Dryden's Essay.

quiz.why: Stephen Gosson's School of Abuse (1579) attacked poets and players.

quiz.q: 'The poet nothing affirmeth, and therefore never lieth' answers the charge that poetry:
quiz.why: Poets do not claim factual truth, so they cannot lie.

quiz.q: Who called Dryden 'the father of English criticism'?
quiz.why: Johnson wrote so in his Life of Dryden.

scenes.text: Johnson calls Shakespeare 'the poet of nature… that holds up to his readers a faithful mirrour of manners and of life'.
He also lists his faults with equal honesty.

steps.title: Merits
steps.body: Preface to Shakespeare (1765): characters are species, not individuals; 'just representations of general nature'; dialogue natural; mingling of tragic and comic justified as true to life; unities of time and place rejected — the audience 'always knows they are in a theatre'; only unity of action matters.

steps.title: Faults
steps.body: Sacrifices virtue to convenience (no clear moral purpose); loose plots; careless endings; gross jokes; bombast in tragic speeches; quibbles — 'A quibble was to him the fatal Cleopatra for which he lost the world, and was content to lose it.'

steps.title: Against the unities
steps.body: 'The spectators are always in their senses, and know, from the first act to the last, that the stage is only a stage.' If one can imagine Alexandria, one can imagine Rome.

steps.title: Exam structure
steps.body: Johnson's Preface: (1) test of time; (2) poet of nature; (3) tragicomedy defended; (4) faults; (5) unities rejected; (6) editorial principles.

activity.prompt: Johnson's praise or censure of Shakespeare?

items.text: Faithful mirror of manners and life

quiz.why: It prefaced his 1765 edition of Shakespeare's plays.
He argues spectators never believe the stage is real, so time and place may change.

quiz.q: For Johnson, the quibble was Shakespeare's:
quiz.why: He compares Shakespeare's love of puns to Antony's ruinous love for Cleopatra.

scenes.text: Wordsworth: poetry is 'the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings'.
Coleridge coins 'esemplastic' — the shaping power of imagination.

steps.title: Wordsworth, Preface (1800/1802)
steps.body: Subject: incidents of common life; language 'really used by men'; poet as 'a man speaking to men' with 'more lively sensibility'; poetry as 'the breath and finer spirit of all knowledge'; no essential difference between the language of prose and metrical composition; emotion recollected in tranquillity; metre adds pleasure.

steps.title: Coleridge, Biographia Literaria (1817)
steps.body: Ch. XIII: primary and secondary imagination vs fancy. Ch. XIV: Lyrical Ballads plan; definition of poem ('proposing for its immediate object pleasure, not truth') and poet ('brings the whole soul of man into activity'). Ch. XVII–XX: disagrees with Wordsworth on rustic language — 'a lingua communis' not peasant speech; metre is organic.

steps.title: Shelley and Keats
steps.body: Shelley's A Defence of Poetry (1821, publ. 1840) replies to Peacock's The Four Ages of Poetry: poetry as 'the expression of the imagination'; poets 'the unacknowledged legislators of the world'. Keats's letters: negative capability, the 'chameleon poet'.

steps.title: Wordsworth vs Coleridge
steps.body: W: language of rustics is best because of purer passions. C: rustic language, purified of provincialisms, is simply the general language of educated people; poetry differs from prose because of metre and passion.

activity.prompt: Wordsworth, Coleridge or Shelley?

quiz.why: Thomas Love Peacock's The Four Ages of Poetry (1820) mocked modern poetry.

quiz.q: Coleridge disagrees with Wordsworth chiefly about:
quiz.why: In chapters XVII–XX Coleridge rejects rustic speech as the ideal poetic language.
Coleridge coined it from Greek for 'to shape into one'.

scenes.text: Arnold keeps lines of Homer, Dante, Shakespeare and Milton in mind as touchstones.
He calls criticism 'a disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world'.

steps.title: 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time' (1864)
steps.body: Criticism creates the intellectual atmosphere for creative epochs; must be 'disinterested' (free from practical, political considerations); aim: 'to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world'; 'to see the object as in itself it really is'.

steps.title: 'The Study of Poetry' (1880)
steps.body: Poetry will replace religion; poetry is 'a criticism of life'; avoid historical and personal estimates, seek the real estimate; touchstone method (e.g., Dante's 'In la sua volontade è nostra pace'); 'high seriousness'; Chaucer lacks high seriousness; Dryden and Pope are 'classics of our prose'; Burns.

steps.title: Applying touchstones
steps.body: Compare an unknown passage with Hamlet's 'Absent thee from felicity awhile': if it lacks comparable high seriousness and truth, its value is lower — Arnold's method is comparative and evaluative, though critics call it subjective.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Sweetness and light' is from Culture and Anarchy; 'criticism of life' and touchstones from 'The Study of Poetry'.

activity.prompt: Which Arnold essay?

items.text: Best that is known and thought

quiz.why: He praises Chaucer's truth and style but finds no 'high seriousness'.
He judged their poetry conceived in the wits rather than the soul.

quiz.q: The 'historic' and 'personal' estimates are fallacies in:
options: Essays in Criticism, Second Series preface only
quiz.why: Arnold warns against both in 'The Study of Poetry'.

questions.q: 'Largest and most comprehensive soul' — of whom?
Johnson's Lives of the Poets was published:
Wordsworth's 1802 addition asks 'What is a Poet?' — answer:
Coleridge defines a poem's immediate object as:
'To see the object as in itself it really is' — Arnold's phrase in:

courses.title: Unit 3 · Eliot, Richards and New Criticism
courses.summary: T.S. Eliot's tradition and impersonality, I.A. Richards's practical criticism, Empson's ambiguity, and the American New Critics: close reading, intentional and affective fallacies, paradox and irony.
outcomes: Explain Eliot's tradition, impersonality and catalyst analogy
Describe Richards's Practical Criticism and four kinds of meaning
Define the intentional and affective fallacies
Perform a New Critical close reading

scenes.text: Oxygen and sulphur dioxide combine to form sulphurous acid in the presence of platinum, which stays unchanged.
'The mind of the poet is the shred of platinum,' writes Eliot.

steps.title: 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1919)
steps.body: Tradition must be obtained 'by great labour'; involves 'the historical sense' — 'not only of the pastness of the past, but of its presence'. Existing monuments form an ideal order modified by each new work. Impersonality: 'Poetry is not a turning loose of emotion, but an escape from emotion; it is not the expression of personality, but an escape from personality.' Catalyst analogy: poet's mind as platinum.

steps.title: Other key concepts
steps.body: Objective correlative ('Hamlet and His Problems', 1919): 'a set of objects, a situation, a chain of events which shall be the formula of that particular emotion'. Dissociation of sensibility ('The Metaphysical Poets', 1921). 'The Function of Criticism' (1923): 'the elucidation of works of art and the correction of taste'.

steps.title: Apply the objective correlative
steps.body: Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking — washing invisible blood, the taper — gives a sensory formula for guilt. Eliot argues Hamlet's disgust exceeds its object (Gertrude), so the play lacks an adequate correlative.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Eliot's impersonality does not mean poets have no emotions; 'only those who have personality and emotions know what it means to want to escape from these things'.

activity.prompt: Which Eliot essay?

quiz.q: In the catalyst analogy, the poet's mind is the:
quiz.why: Like platinum, the mind enables combination of feelings while remaining unchanged.

quiz.q: 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' was published in:
quiz.why: It appeared in The Egoist in 1919.

options: Elucidation of works of art and correction of taste
quiz.why: He says so in 'The Function of Criticism' (1923).

scenes.text: At Cambridge in the 1920s, Richards hands students poems without authors' names and collects their 'protocols'.
His student Empson finds seven types of ambiguity in a single line.

steps.title: I.A. Richards
steps.body: Principles of Literary Criticism (1924): value as balancing of impulses; emotive vs referential language; poetry as 'pseudo-statements'. Practical Criticism (1929): experiment showing readers' errors — stock responses, sentimentality, inhibition, doctrinal adhesions, mnemonic irrelevances. Four kinds of meaning: sense, feeling, tone, intention.

steps.title: William Empson
steps.body: Seven Types of Ambiguity (1930): ambiguity as 'any verbal nuance… which gives room for alternative reactions to the same piece of language'; richness, not defect. Some Versions of Pastoral.

steps.title: Empson's example
steps.body: Shakespeare's Sonnet 73: 'Bare ruined choirs, where late the sweet birds sang' — choirs suggest both trees and ruined monastery choirs (after the dissolution), carrying layers of loss.

steps.title: Link to Leavis
steps.body: F.R. Leavis (Scrutiny, The Great Tradition: Austen, George Eliot, James, Conrad) shared the Cambridge emphasis on close evaluative reading and moral seriousness.

activity.prompt: Richards's four kinds of meaning — match the description.

quiz.why: Richards reported his protocols experiment in 1929.

quiz.q: Seven Types of Ambiguity is by:
quiz.why: William Empson published it in 1930, aged 24.
They are emotive rather than scientifically verifiable.

scenes.text: Cleanth Brooks reads Donne's 'The Canonization' as a structure of paradox.
Wimsatt and Beardsley declare: the author's intention is neither available nor desirable as a standard.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body: Text as autonomous, organic unity; close reading of words, images, tension, irony, paradox, ambiguity; form and content inseparable; exclusion of biography, history, reader's emotions. Key figures: John Crowe Ransom (The New Criticism, 1941), Cleanth Brooks (The Well Wrought Urn, 1947), Robert Penn Warren (Understanding Poetry with Brooks, 1938), Allen Tate, W.K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley.

steps.title: Fallacies
steps.body: Intentional fallacy (1946): judging a poem by the author's intention. Affective fallacy (1949): confusing the poem with its results (the reader's emotions). Brooks's 'heresy of paraphrase': a poem's meaning cannot be reduced to a prose statement.

steps.title: Close reading in steps
steps.body: Keats's 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty': (1) note the chiasmus; (2) dramatic context — spoken by the urn; (3) tension between permanence of art and transience of life throughout the ode; (4) the line is ironic resolution within the poem's structure, not a philosophical claim to be judged true or false (Brooks).

steps.title: Critiques
steps.body: Accused of ignoring history, politics and readers; later theories (reader-response, New Historicism, Marxism) reacted against it.

activity.prompt: Order a New Critical close reading.
items: Read the poem closely, word by word
Show how the tensions are resolved into organic unity
State the meaning without appeal to biography

quiz.why: Wimsatt and Beardsley published it in 1946.
Cleanth Brooks argues in The Well Wrought Urn that paraphrase cannot capture a poem.

quiz.q: The affective fallacy confuses a poem with:
quiz.why: Judging by emotional results replaces the poem with psychology.

scenes.text: An unseen poem: 'Because I could not stop for Death'.
Apply Richards's and the New Critics' tools step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Read aloud twice. 2) Sense: paraphrase literal events. 3) Feeling and tone: attitude to death; to reader. 4) Diction: 'kindly', 'civility'. 5) Imagery and structure: carriage journey through life stages. 6) Tension/irony: courteous suitor = death. 7) Form: common metre, slant rhyme, dashes. 8) Unity: how parts make the whole.

steps.title: Worked answer outline
steps.body: Sense: speaker's ride with Death toward the grave. Tone: calm, ironic. Irony: Death as polite gentleman caller. Imagery: school (childhood), grain (maturity), setting sun (age), house as grave. Paradox: 'Centuries' feel 'shorter than the Day'. Form's dashes suspend time. Unity: life seen as a single carriage ride toward eternity.

steps.title: Common errors (Richards)
steps.body: Stock responses (assuming death poems must be gloomy), mnemonic irrelevances (personal memories), doctrinal adhesions (judging by religious belief), sentimentality.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body: Write a 300-word practical criticism of Blake's 'The Sick Rose' using the same eight steps.

activity.prompt: Which of Richards's reader errors?

items.text: 'All poems about roses are about love.'
'This reminds me of my grandmother's garden.'
'The poem is bad because it contradicts my faith.'

quiz.why: Richards found readers distracted by private associations.

quiz.q: In the sample poem, the house that is 'A Swelling of the Ground' is:
quiz.why: The low mound is the speaker's grave.

options: Close attention to the text itself
quiz.why: It trains attention on words, form and structure of the unseen text.

questions.q: Eliot's 'historical sense' involves perception of the past's:
Eliot says poetry is an escape from:
The objective correlative was coined in an essay on:
Principles of Literary Criticism appeared in:

options: Room for alternative reactions to language

questions.q: Dissociation of sensibility, per Eliot, set in during the:

courses.title: Unit 4 · Formalism, Structuralism and Post-structuralism
courses.summary: Russian Formalism, Saussure's linguistics, structuralist narratology, Barthes, Derrida's deconstruction, Foucault, and reader-response theory.
outcomes: Explain defamiliarisation and fabula/syuzhet
State Saussure's sign, langue/parole, and binary oppositions
Describe Barthes's 'Death of the Author' and Derrida's différance
Outline reader-response theory (Iser, Fish, Jauss)

scenes.text: Shklovsky: art exists 'to make the stone stony' — to restore sensation to perception.
Tolstoy describes property through the eyes of a horse, making the familiar strange.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body: Russian Formalists (Shklovsky, Eichenbaum, Jakobson, Tynyanov; OPOYAZ and Moscow Linguistic Circle, 1910s–20s). 'Literariness' (Jakobson) as object of study. Defamiliarisation/ostranenie (Shklovsky, 'Art as Technique', 1917). Device (priem). Fabula (chronological story) vs syuzhet (plot as arranged). Dominant. Literary evolution.

steps.title: Jakobson's communication model
steps.body: Six factors and functions: addresser (emotive), addressee (conative), context (referential), message (poetic), contact (phatic), code (metalingual). Poetic function 'projects the principle of equivalence from the axis of selection into the axis of combination'.

steps.title: Fabula vs syuzhet
steps.body: Wuthering Heights: fabula runs from the Earnshaws' childhood to Heathcliff's death; syuzhet begins in 1801 with Lockwood's visit and moves backward through Nelly's narration.

steps.title: Propp
steps.body: Vladimir Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (1928): 31 functions and 7 character types (villain, donor, helper, princess, dispatcher, hero, false hero) in Russian fairy tales — a bridge to structuralism.

activity.prompt: Jakobson's functions: match each to its factor.

quiz.why: Shklovsky's 1917 essay defines ostranenie, making the familiar strange.

options: The plot as arranged in the text
quiz.why: Syuzhet is the artistic ordering of the story's events.
Morphology of the Folktale lists 31 functions.

scenes.text: Saussure draws a tree and the word 'arbor': the link between them is arbitrary.
Barthes reads wine, wrestling and steak as myths of French culture.

steps.title: Saussure, Course in General Linguistics (1916)
steps.body: Sign = signifier (sound-image) + signified (concept); arbitrary relation; meaning is differential ('in language there are only differences without positive terms'); langue (system) vs parole (utterance); synchronic vs diachronic; syntagmatic vs paradigmatic relations.

steps.title: Structuralism
steps.body: Lévi-Strauss: myths structured by binary oppositions (raw/cooked, nature/culture); mythemes. Barthes, Mythologies (1957): second-order signification (myth naturalises ideology). Narratology: Todorov (equilibrium–disruption–new equilibrium; coined 'narratology'), Genette (order, duration, frequency, mood, voice; focalisation), Greimas (actants).

steps.title: Barthes's Paris Match cover
steps.body: A young Black soldier saluting the French flag: denotation = soldier saluting; myth = France is a great empire whose sons, without colour discrimination, serve it faithfully — imperialism naturalised.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saussure's Course was compiled posthumously by his students Bally and Sechehaye from lecture notes.

activity.prompt: Saussurean pairs: which side?

quiz.q: For Saussure the sign's link between signifier and signified is:
quiz.why: No natural link connects the sound 'tree' to the concept; it is conventional.
Roland Barthes's 1957 essays analyse modern myths.
Gérard Genette distinguished who sees (focalisation) from who speaks (voice).

scenes.text: 1967: Barthes declares 'the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author'.
1966: at Johns Hopkins, Derrida questions the very idea of a centre.

steps.title: Barthes (post-structuralist)
steps.body: 'The Death of the Author' (1967): a text is 'a tissue of quotations'; meaning lies in its destination, the reader. S/Z (1970): readerly (lisible) vs writerly (scriptible) texts; five codes. The Pleasure of the Text: plaisir and jouissance.

steps.title: Derrida and deconstruction
steps.body: 'Structure, Sign and Play' (1966); Of Grammatology (1967). Logocentrism; critique of binary oppositions (speech/writing, presence/absence) in which one term is privileged; différance (to differ and to defer); 'There is nothing outside the text' (il n'y a pas de hors-texte); trace, supplement, aporia. Deconstruction reverses and displaces hierarchies.

steps.title: Foucault
steps.body: Discourse, power/knowledge, episteme; 'What Is an Author?' (1969): the 'author-function'. Discipline and Punish (Panopticon). Influenced Said and New Historicism.

steps.title: Deconstructing a binary
steps.body: In The Tempest, civilised/savage privileges Prospero. A deconstructive reading shows Prospero's 'civilisation' depends on Caliban's labour and island knowledge — the privileged term relies on what it excludes.

activity.prompt: Match the concept to the thinker.

quiz.why: Derrida's coinage plays on French différer: to differ and to defer.
Foucault's 1969 lecture introduces the author-function.

options: Invites the reader to produce meaning
quiz.why: Writerly texts make the reader an active producer rather than a consumer.

story.title: Is there a text in this class?

scenes.text: A student asks Stanley Fish, 'Is there a text in this class?' — and the meaning depends on the community.
Wolfgang Iser shows readers filling gaps the text leaves open.

steps.title: Theorists
steps.body: Louise Rosenblatt (transactional theory; efferent vs aesthetic reading). Wolfgang Iser (The Implied Reader, The Act of Reading): gaps/blanks, implied reader, wandering viewpoint. Hans Robert Jauss: horizon of expectations (reception aesthetics, Konstanz School). Stanley Fish: affective stylistics; interpretive communities (Is There a Text in This Class?, 1980). Norman Holland: psychoanalytic reading. Jonathan Culler: literary competence.

steps.title: Gaps in practice
steps.body: In 'The Lady of Shalott' we never learn what the curse is; readers fill the gap with ideas about art, isolation or female confinement. Iser says this indeterminacy activates the reader.

steps.title: Against New Criticism
steps.body: Reader-response rejects the affective fallacy: the reader's experience is central to meaning.

steps.title: Answer tip
steps.body: Distinguish: Iser — individual reader and text's gaps; Fish — community conventions; Jauss — historical reception.

activity.prompt: Match the concept to the theorist.

options: Is There a Text in This Class?
quiz.why: Fish argues meanings are produced by communities sharing interpretive strategies.
Jauss's reception aesthetics studies how readers' expectations change historically.

quiz.q: Reader-response directly opposes the New Critical:
quiz.why: It restores the reader's response that the affective fallacy excluded.

questions.q: Course in General Linguistics was published in:
'There is nothing outside the text' — who?

courses.title: Unit 5 · Marxist, Feminist, Psychoanalytic and Historicist Theory; Revision
courses.summary: Marxist criticism (Lukács, Althusser, Williams, Eagleton), feminist criticism (Woolf, de Beauvoir, Showalter, Gilbert and Gubar, Cixous), psychoanalytic criticism (Freud, Lacan), New Historicism and Cultural Materialism, ecocriticism and queer theory; exam revision.
outcomes: Explain base/superstructure, ideology and interpellation
Describe the phases of feminist criticism and key texts
Apply Freudian and Lacanian concepts to literature
Distinguish New Historicism and Cultural Materialism
Answer theory questions applying a lens to a text

scenes.text: A policeman calls 'Hey, you there!' and the person who turns becomes a subject — Althusser's interpellation.
Raymond Williams studies how 'structures of feeling' shape a generation's art.

steps.title: Foundations
steps.body: Marx and Engels: economic base (forces and relations of production) shapes superstructure (law, politics, religion, art); ideology as false consciousness; class struggle. 'It is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but their social being that determines their consciousness' (1859 Preface).

steps.title: Key critics
steps.body: Georg Lukács: realism, typicality, totality (The Historical Novel). Gramsci: hegemony. Walter Benjamin: 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (aura). Althusser: Ideological State Apparatuses (school, church, media) vs Repressive State Apparatuses; interpellation. Raymond Williams: cultural materialism, 'structures of feeling', Keywords. Terry Eagleton: Literary Theory: An Introduction (1983). Fredric Jameson: The Political Unconscious ('Always historicize!').

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: Hard Times: Gradgrind's school as an Ideological State Apparatus interpellating children as utilitarian subjects for Coketown's factories; Stephen Blackpool shows working-class alienation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Marxist criticism is not only about 'poor characters'; it examines how a text's form and silences relate to ideology and history.

activity.prompt: Match the concept to the Marxist thinker.

quiz.why: Jameson opens The Political Unconscious (1981) with it.

quiz.q: Schools and churches are, for Althusser:
quiz.why: They reproduce ideology by consent rather than force.
He valued realist novels for representing social totality.

story.title: One is not born a woman

scenes.text: Woolf imagines Shakespeare's gifted sister Judith, denied education, dying unknown.
Gilbert and Gubar read Bertha Mason as Jane Eyre's angry double.

steps.title: Foundations
steps.body: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792). Virginia Woolf, A Room of One's Own (1929): money and a room; Judith Shakespeare; androgynous mind. Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex (1949): 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman'; woman as Other.

steps.title: Second-wave criticism
steps.body: Kate Millett, Sexual Politics (1970: patriarchy in Lawrence, Miller, Mailer). Elaine Showalter, A Literature of Their Own (1977): Feminine (imitation), Feminist (protest), Female (self-discovery) phases; gynocriticism. Gilbert and Gubar, The Madwoman in the Attic (1979): angel/monster, 'anxiety of authorship'.

steps.title: French feminism and beyond
steps.body: Hélène Cixous, 'The Laugh of the Medusa' (1975): écriture féminine. Julia Kristeva: semiotic vs symbolic. Luce Irigaray. Judith Butler, Gender Trouble (1990): gender as performativity (queer theory). bell hooks; Mohanty (postcolonial feminism). Alice Walker's womanism.

steps.title: Apply Showalter
steps.body: Early women novelists using male pseudonyms (Currer Bell, George Eliot) fall in the Feminine phase of imitation; later protest writing is Feminist; modern self-defined writing is Female.

activity.prompt: Order Showalter's three phases.

quiz.q: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' is from:
quiz.why: De Beauvoir argues femininity is socially constructed in The Second Sex (1949).
Elaine Showalter called for criticism of women's own writing tradition.
Cixous's 'The Laugh of the Medusa' urges women to write the body.

scenes.text: An infant sees itself in a mirror and greets a unified image it does not yet possess.
Freud reads Oedipus and Hamlet as dramas of repressed desire.

steps.title: Freud
steps.body: Unconscious, repression, id/ego/superego, Oedipus complex, dream-work (condensation, displacement, symbolisation), the uncanny (1919), 'Creative Writers and Day-Dreaming' (1908). Ernest Jones, Hamlet and Oedipus (1949): Hamlet's delay as Oedipal guilt.

steps.title: Lacan
steps.body: 'The unconscious is structured like a language'. Mirror stage; three orders: Imaginary, Symbolic (language, Name-of-the-Father), Real. Desire as lack; the objet petit a. 'Seminar on "The Purloined Letter"' (Poe).

steps.title: Others
steps.body: Carl Jung: collective unconscious, archetypes (influencing Northrop Frye's archetypal criticism, Anatomy of Criticism, 1957; Maud Bodkin). Harold Bloom: The Anxiety of Influence (1973). Kristeva: abjection.

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: Sons and Lovers: Paul Morel's attachment to his mother blocks his relationships with Miriam and Clara — a classic Oedipal reading; Lawrence himself knew Freud's ideas through Frieda.

activity.prompt: Freud, Lacan or Jung?

quiz.q: 'The unconscious is structured like a language' — who?
quiz.why: Lacan reread Freud through Saussurean linguistics.
Northrop Frye's archetypal theory of modes, symbols, myths and genres.

quiz.q: The Anxiety of Influence is by:
quiz.why: Bloom's 1973 theory of poets' Oedipal struggle with precursors.

scenes.text: Greenblatt opens with an anecdote about a Renaissance courtier and links it to Othello.
Ecocritics ask: what is the role of the land and its creatures in this poem?

steps.title: New Historicism
steps.body: Stephen Greenblatt (Renaissance Self-Fashioning, 1980; coined 'New Historicism' 1982). Louis Montrose: 'the historicity of texts and the textuality of history'. Parallel reading of literary and non-literary texts; anecdote; power, subversion and containment ('Invisible Bullets'); influenced by Foucault.

steps.title: Cultural Materialism
steps.body: British: Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield, Political Shakespeare (1985). Four features: historical context, theoretical method, political commitment, textual analysis. More optimistic about dissidence than New Historicism; inspired by Raymond Williams.

steps.title: Ecocriticism and queer theory
steps.body: Ecocriticism: Cheryll Glotfelty, The Ecocriticism Reader (1996): 'the study of the relationship between literature and the physical environment'; Lawrence Buell; Jonathan Bate, Romantic Ecology (1991). Queer theory: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick (Between Men; homosocial desire), Butler.

steps.title: Revision sheet
steps.body: Plato/Aristotle/Horace/Longinus · Bharata/Anandavardhana · Sidney/Dryden/Johnson · Wordsworth/Coleridge/Shelley/Arnold · Eliot/Richards/Empson/Leavis · New Critics · Formalists/Saussure/Barthes/Derrida/Foucault · Iser/Fish/Jauss · Marx/Althusser/Williams/Jameson · Woolf/de Beauvoir/Showalter/Gilbert & Gubar/Cixous/Butler · Freud/Lacan/Jung/Frye · Greenblatt/Dollimore & Sinfield · Glotfelty.

steps.title: Previous-year-style questions (original)
steps.body: (1) Compare Plato's and Aristotle's views of mimesis. (2) Discuss Eliot's concept of tradition. (3) Explain the intentional and affective fallacies. (4) What is deconstruction? Illustrate with a text. (5) Apply a feminist reading to Jane Eyre. (6) Explain rasa theory.

activity.prompt: New Historicism or Cultural Materialism?

quiz.q: 'The historicity of texts and the textuality of history' is from:
quiz.why: Louis Montrose's chiasmus defines the New Historicist position.
It launched British Cultural Materialism.

quiz.q: Glotfelty defines ecocriticism as the study of literature and:
quiz.why: Her introduction to The Ecocriticism Reader gives this definition.

questions.q: Literary Theory: An Introduction is by:
The Madwoman in the Attic appeared in:
Freud's essay on the uncanny appeared in:
Homosocial desire is Sedgwick's concept in:

uni-ba-eng-literary-forms.title: Literary Forms & Terms
uni-ba-eng-literary-forms.description: Poetry, drama, fiction and prose forms, prosody, figures of speech and critical terms. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. English programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Poetic Forms
courses.summary: The major kinds of poetry: lyric, sonnet, ode, elegy, epic, mock-epic, ballad and dramatic monologue, with defining features and canonical examples.
outcomes: Distinguish lyric, narrative and dramatic poetry
Identify Petrarchan, Shakespearean and Spenserian sonnets by rhyme scheme
Explain Pindaric, Horatian and irregular odes
Describe the conventions of the pastoral elegy and the epic
Recognise the dramatic monologue and the ballad

scenes.text: In 14th-century Italy, Petrarch writes sonnets to Laura: an octave posing a problem, a sestet answering it.
Wyatt and Surrey bring the form to England; Shakespeare's 154 sonnets make the three-quatrain-and-couplet pattern famous.

steps.title: The lyric
steps.body: A lyric is a short poem expressing the personal thoughts and feelings of a single speaker. The word comes from the Greek lyre. Lyric is the broad category that includes the sonnet, ode, elegy and song.

steps.title: The Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet
steps.body: Fourteen lines in iambic pentameter: an octave rhyming abbaabba and a sestet usually rhyming cdecde or cdcdcd. The turn (volta) comes at line 9. Milton's 'On His Blindness' is a classic English example.

steps.title: Shakespearean and Spenserian sonnets
steps.body: Shakespearean: abab cdcd efef gg — three quatrains and a closing couplet, the turn often at the couplet. Spenserian: abab bcbc cdcd ee — interlocking rhymes, used in Spenser's Amoretti.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Sonnet 18 ('Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?') rhymes day/temperate/May/date = abab. The couplet 'So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee' resolves the argument: poetry grants immortality. Form: Shakespearean.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not call every 14-line poem Petrarchan; check the rhyme scheme. Do not confuse the volta (a shift of thought) with a stanza break — Petrarchan sonnets are often printed as one block.

activity.prompt: Sort each rhyme feature by sonnet type.

items.text: Ends with couplet gg after independent quatrains
Volta at line 9 into a sestet

quiz.q: The volta in a Petrarchan sonnet usually occurs at:
quiz.why: The Petrarchan octave ends at line 8, so the shift in thought comes at the start of the sestet, line 9.
The Shakespearean sonnet uses three independent quatrains with fresh rhymes and a final couplet.

quiz.q: A lyric is best defined as:
options: A short poem expressing a single speaker's feelings
quiz.why: Lyric poetry centres on one speaker's personal emotion or thought, not on story or stage action.

scenes.text: Pindar's choral odes celebrate Olympic victors with strophe, antistrophe and epode.
Milton mourns Edward King in 'Lycidas'; Shelley mourns Keats in 'Adonais'.

steps.title: The ode
steps.body: An ode is a long, serious, elaborately structured lyric addressed to a person, object or idea. Pindaric odes have triadic structure (strophe, antistrophe, epode); Horatian odes use repeated regular stanzas and a calmer tone; the irregular (Cowleyan) ode varies line and stanza length freely, as in Wordsworth's 'Intimations' Ode.

steps.title: Keats's odes (1819)
steps.body: 'Ode to a Nightingale', 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', 'To Autumn' use ten- or eleven-line stanzas of Keats's own design. The Urn ode ends 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty'.

steps.title: The elegy and pastoral elegy
steps.body: An elegy is a formal poem of lament for the dead. The pastoral elegy (Theocritus, Virgil; in English 'Lycidas', 'Adonais', Arnold's 'Thyrsis') represents poet and mourned friend as shepherds, with an invocation of the muse, a procession of mourners, nature mourning, questioning of fate, and a final consolation.

steps.title: Other elegies
steps.body: Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' (1751) laments the anonymous rural dead; Tennyson's 'In Memoriam A.H.H.' (1850) mourns Arthur Hallam over 133 sections.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: An elegy needs a mourning occasion or meditative lament; a sad love poem is not automatically an elegy. 'Elegiac' describes tone; 'elegy' names the form.

activity.prompt: Order the typical conventions of a pastoral elegy as they unfold.

quiz.q: Strophe, antistrophe and epode belong to the:
quiz.why: Pindar's choral odes are built in triads of strophe, antistrophe and epode.

quiz.q: 'Adonais' is an elegy on the death of:
quiz.why: Shelley wrote 'Adonais' (1821) to mourn John Keats.

quiz.q: The pastoral elegy typically ends with:
quiz.why: After grief and questioning, the pastoral elegy turns to consolation, often that the dead lives on in heaven or nature.

scenes.text: Homer begins the Iliad mid-war, with the wrath of Achilles.
Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock' turns the theft of a lock of hair into a heroic battle.

steps.title: Epic
steps.body: An epic is a long narrative poem in elevated style about a heroic figure whose deeds matter to a nation or race. Primary (folk/oral) epics: Iliad, Odyssey, Beowulf, Mahabharata. Secondary (literary) epics: Virgil's Aeneid, Milton's Paradise Lost.

steps.title: Epic conventions
steps.body: Statement of theme, invocation to the muse, beginning in medias res, epic catalogues, epic similes, supernatural machinery, extended battle and journey to the underworld, and elevated diction.

steps.title: Paradise Lost, Book I
steps.body: Milton states the theme ('Of Man's first disobedience'), invokes the 'Heav'nly Muse', begins after Satan's fall (in medias res), lists the fallen angels (catalogue) and compares Satan's shield to the moon seen through Galileo's telescope (epic simile).

steps.title: Mock-epic
steps.body: Mock-epic (mock-heroic) applies epic conventions to a trivial subject for satire. Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock' has sylphs as machinery, a card game as battle and a toilette as arming of the hero; Dryden's 'Mac Flecknoe' crowns a dull poet.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mock-epic does not mock the epic form; it uses the form's grandeur to expose the triviality of its subject.

activity.prompt: Primary (oral/folk) or secondary (literary) epic?

options: In the voice of the muse
quiz.why: Epics often begin in the middle of the action and fill in earlier events later through flashback.

quiz.q: The card game of ombre in 'The Rape of the Lock' parodies:
quiz.why: Pope turns a game of cards into a mock battle to satirise the trivial concerns of fashionable society.
Paradise Lost was composed by a single literary author in writing, which makes it a secondary or literary epic.

scenes.text: Border villages sing of Sir Patrick Spens drowned at sea.
Browning's Duke points to a portrait of his 'last Duchess' and gives himself away.

steps.title: The ballad
steps.body: A ballad is a narrative song. The folk ballad is anonymous and oral, with quatrains (ballad stanza: alternating four- and three-stress lines rhyming abcb), refrains, incremental repetition, abrupt openings and dialogue. Literary ballads imitate it: Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner', Keats's 'La Belle Dame sans Merci'.

steps.title: Dramatic monologue
steps.body: A poem spoken by a single character (not the poet) to a silent listener at a dramatic moment, revealing the speaker's character unintentionally. Perfected by Robert Browning ('My Last Duchess', 1842) and Tennyson ('Ulysses').

steps.title: My Last Duchess
steps.body: The Duke of Ferrara speaks to an envoy arranging his next marriage. His line 'I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together' suggests he had his wife killed. Reader irony: we judge him more harshly than he realises.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Distinguish dramatic monologue from soliloquy (a character alone on stage speaking thoughts) and from lyric (poet's own voice).

activity.prompt: Ballad feature or dramatic monologue feature?

quiz.why: The common ballad quatrain rhymes only the second and fourth lines, abcb.

quiz.q: In 'My Last Duchess' the listener is:
quiz.why: The Duke addresses an envoy negotiating his marriage to a Count's daughter, who remains silent.

options: A deliberate imitation of the folk ballad by a known poet
quiz.why: Literary ballads like 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' are written by known authors who adopt folk ballad features.

questions.why: It uses the abbaabba octave and a sestet, the Petrarchan pattern.
Spenser linked his quatrains with shared rhymes.
Its stanzas vary in length and line pattern, the mark of the irregular ode.
Milton's pastoral elegy laments his Cambridge contemporary Edward King, drowned in 1637.
Arnold wrote 'Thyrsis' for his friend Arthur Hugh Clough.
Epic similes run over many lines, developing the comparison beyond the immediate point.
Dryden crowns Thomas Shadwell king of dullness in this mock-heroic poem.

questions.q: Supernatural machinery in 'The Rape of the Lock':
questions.why: Pope's sylphs, drawn from Rosicrucian lore, parody epic gods.

questions.q: 'La Belle Dame sans Merci' is a:
questions.why: Keats wrote it as a deliberate imitation of the ballad.
Robert Browning's monologues such as 'My Last Duchess' set the form's standard.
Tennyson's long elegy mourns Arthur Henry Hallam.
Gray meditates on the unremembered villagers buried in a country churchyard.
Beowulf derives from an oral Anglo-Saxon tradition, so it counts as a primary epic.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Prosody & Metre
courses.summary: Scansion of English verse: feet, metres, stanza forms, rhyme types, blank verse and free verse.
outcomes: Name and mark the five main metrical feet
Scan a line and name its metre
Identify couplet, terza rima, ottava rima, rhyme royal and Spenserian stanza
Distinguish blank verse from free verse
Recognise caesura, enjambment and kinds of rhyme

scenes.text: A heartbeat goes da-DUM, da-DUM: the iamb, the commonest foot in English.
Five iambs make a line of iambic pentameter: 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'

steps.title: The five main feet
steps.body: Iamb (x /): be-LOW. Trochee (/ x): TI-ger. Anapaest (x x /): in-ter-VENE. Dactyl (/ x x): MER-ri-ly. Spondee (/ /): HEART-BREAK. x = unstressed, / = stressed syllable.

steps.title: Line lengths
steps.body: Monometer 1 foot, dimeter 2, trimeter 3, tetrameter 4, pentameter 5, hexameter 6 (an iambic hexameter is an alexandrine), heptameter 7. Metre = foot type + number of feet.

steps.title: Scansion 1
steps.body: 'The CUR-few TOLLS the KNELL of PART-ing DAY' (Gray). Syllables: the-cur | few-tolls | the-knell | of-part | ing-day = 5 iambs → iambic pentameter.

steps.title: Scansion 2
steps.body: 'TY-ger TY-ger, BURN-ing BRIGHT' (Blake): TY-ger | TY-ger | BURN-ing | BRIGHT = three trochees and a stressed final syllable (catalectic) → trochaic tetrameter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Scan by natural speech stress, not by forcing a pattern. Count syllables first, mark stresses, then divide into feet. Occasional substitutions (e.g. a trochee at line start) do not change the dominant metre.

activity.prompt: Classify each word by its foot.

quiz.why: An alexandrine is a six-foot iambic line, used to close the Spenserian stanza.
A dactyl has one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed, as in MER-ri-ly.
The line has four stressed beats with trochaic falling rhythm and a dropped final syllable.

scenes.text: 'Stanza' is Italian for 'room': each stanza form is a room with its own shape.
Dante's terza rima links each tercet to the next like a chain of rooms.

steps.title: Couplets and tercets
steps.body: Heroic couplet: rhymed iambic pentameter pairs (Dryden, Pope). Terza rima: tercets rhyming aba bcb cdc (Dante; Shelley's 'Ode to the West Wind').

steps.title: Longer stanzas
steps.body: Rhyme royal: seven iambic pentameter lines ababbcc (Chaucer's 'Troilus and Criseyde'). Ottava rima: eight lines abababcc (Byron's 'Don Juan'). Spenserian stanza: nine lines ababbcbcc, eight pentameters and a final alexandrine (The Faerie Queene; Keats's 'Eve of St. Agnes').

steps.title: Worked identification
steps.body: A stanza has 8 pentameter lines rhyming abababcc with a comic twist in the couplet: ottava rima, as Byron uses for bathos in Don Juan.

steps.title: Memory aid
steps.body: Count lines: 7 = rhyme royal, 8 = ottava rima, 9 = Spenserian. Then confirm with the rhyme scheme.

activity.prompt: Match the rhyme scheme to the stanza form.

quiz.why: Its ninth line is an iambic hexameter, an alexandrine.
Shelley builds each section from terza rima tercets ending in a couplet.

quiz.q: The heroic couplet was the dominant form of:
quiz.why: Dryden and Pope used closed heroic couplets for satire and argument in the late 17th and 18th centuries.

scenes.text: 'To err is human; || to forgive, divine.' Pope's pause sits mid-line.
Wordsworth's sense flows over the line end, like a river past a bank.

steps.title: Kinds of rhyme
steps.body: Perfect/full rhyme: day/may. Masculine rhyme: final stressed syllable (de-LIGHT/to-NIGHT). Feminine rhyme: stressed then unstressed (NA-tion/STA-tion). Slant/half rhyme: near sound (soul/all). Internal rhyme: within a line. Eye rhyme: looks alike, sounds different (love/move).

steps.title: Caesura and enjambment
steps.body: Caesura: a strong pause within a line, often marked ||. End-stopped line: sense and syntax close at line end. Enjambment: sense runs on into the next line without pause.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: Keats, Endymion: 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever: / Its loveliness increases; it will never / Pass into nothingness'. Line 2 is enjambed into line 3; 'ever/never' is a feminine rhyme.

steps.title: Sound devices
steps.body: Alliteration: repeated initial consonants. Assonance: repeated vowel sounds. Consonance: repeated consonants within words. Onomatopoeia: words imitating sounds (buzz, hiss).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Alliteration depends on sound, not spelling: 'cat' and 'kite' alliterate; 'cent' and 'cat' do not.

activity.prompt: Name the device.

options: Sense running over the line end
quiz.why: An enjambed line carries its sentence directly into the next line without a pause.
The words look as though they rhyme but are pronounced differently.

quiz.q: A caesura is usually marked as:
quiz.why: Prosodists conventionally mark the mid-line pause with a double vertical bar.

scenes.text: Marlowe's 'mighty line' of unrhymed pentameter thunders across the Elizabethan stage.
Whitman's long lines in 'Leaves of Grass' follow breath, not metre.

steps.title: Blank verse
steps.body: Unrhymed iambic pentameter. Introduced into English by Surrey (translating the Aeneid), developed on stage by Marlowe and Shakespeare, and used for epic by Milton (Paradise Lost) and meditative verse by Wordsworth (The Prelude).

steps.title: Free verse (vers libre)
steps.body: Verse without regular metre or rhyme, organised by cadence, repetition, line breaks and imagery. Whitman, Eliot (partly), the Imagists, and many Indian English poets use it.

steps.title: Spot the difference
steps.body: 'To be, or not to be, that is the question' — ten/eleven syllables, iambic, unrhymed → blank verse (with a feminine ending). 'I celebrate myself, and sing myself' — no fixed metre across the poem → free verse.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Blank verse is NOT free verse: blank verse has strict metre but no rhyme; free verse has neither fixed metre nor fixed rhyme.

activity.prompt: Blank verse or free verse?

quiz.why: Blank verse keeps iambic pentameter but drops rhyme.

quiz.q: Who first used blank verse in English?
quiz.why: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, used it in his translation of books of the Aeneid.
Free verse shapes rhythm through natural cadence, repetition and placement of line breaks.

questions.why: Two unstressed syllables then a stressed one make an anapaest.
Chaucer used it in Troilus and Criseyde and some Canterbury Tales.
Eight lines with alternating rhymes and a final couplet.

questions.q: The Faerie Queene stanza has how many lines?
questions.why: The Spenserian stanza has nine lines.
Two consecutive stresses form a spondee.

questions.q: A rhyme on a final stressed syllable is:
questions.why: Masculine rhyme falls on the last, stressed syllable.
Assonance repeats vowel sounds in nearby words.

options: Completes its sense at the line end
questions.why: Syntax and sense pause at the end of an end-stopped line.
Pope perfected the closed heroic couplet.

questions.q: 'The curfew tolls the knell of parting day' is:
questions.why: It has ten syllables in five rising iambic feet.
Hopkins counted stresses per line regardless of unstressed syllables and called it sprung rhythm.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Dramatic Forms
courses.summary: Tragedy and Aristotle's terms, comedy and its kinds, tragicomedy, the history play, and modern forms: problem play, absurd drama, epic theatre; plus dramatic devices.
outcomes: Explain Aristotle's definition of tragedy and terms hamartia, catharsis, peripeteia, anagnorisis
Distinguish comedy of humours, comedy of manners and romantic comedy
Describe the problem play, Theatre of the Absurd and epic theatre
Identify dramatic devices: soliloquy, aside, chorus, dramatic irony, deus ex machina

scenes.text: In Athens, Oedipus searches for the killer of Laius and discovers it is himself.
Aristotle, watching such plays, writes the Poetics and defines tragedy.

steps.title: Aristotle's definition
steps.body: Tragedy is the imitation (mimesis) of an action that is serious, complete and of a certain magnitude, in embellished language, in dramatic not narrative form, through pity and fear effecting the catharsis of these emotions. Six parts: plot (mythos, the most important), character, thought, diction, song, spectacle.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body: Hamartia: the hero's error of judgement. Peripeteia: reversal of fortune. Anagnorisis: recognition, a change from ignorance to knowledge. Hubris: overweening pride (a common, but later, gloss). Catharsis: purgation or clarification of pity and fear.

steps.title: Oedipus Rex
steps.body: The messenger from Corinth comes to cheer Oedipus but reveals his birth: reversal and recognition coincide, which Aristotle praised as the finest plot.

steps.title: Elizabethan and revenge tragedy
steps.body: Elizabethan tragedy mixes Senecan elements (ghosts, revenge, violence, five acts). Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy founded the revenge tragedy; Hamlet transforms it. Shakespeare's tragic heroes fall partly through a flaw of character (Othello's jealousy, Macbeth's ambition).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Hamartia is not simply 'tragic flaw' as a moral vice; Aristotle meant a mistake or error. Also, the three unities: Aristotle insisted only on unity of action; unity of place was added by later Renaissance critics.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning.

quiz.q: For Aristotle the most important part of tragedy is:
quiz.why: Aristotle calls plot the soul of tragedy because tragedy imitates action, not persons.

quiz.q: The founder of English revenge tragedy:
quiz.why: Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy (c.1587) set the pattern of ghost, revenge and play-within-play.

quiz.q: Which unity did Aristotle actually insist on?
quiz.why: The Poetics demands unity of action; unity of place and strict time were codified later by Renaissance critics.

scenes.text: In the Forest of Arden, Rosalind disguised as Ganymede tutors Orlando in love.
In Restoration London, wits trade epigrams about marriage and money.

steps.title: Comedy
steps.body: A play of light tone ending happily, often in marriage, dealing with ordinary or social life. Old Comedy (Aristophanes) was satirical; New Comedy (Menander, Plautus, Terence) used stock plots of lovers and tricky servants.

steps.title: Kinds
steps.body: Romantic comedy: love, disguise, green world (Shakespeare's As You Like It, Twelfth Night). Comedy of humours: characters dominated by one 'humour' or obsession (Jonson's Every Man in His Humour, Volpone). Comedy of manners: witty satire of fashionable society (Congreve's The Way of the World; revived by Sheridan and Wilde). Sentimental comedy: 18th-century, virtue rewarded; Goldsmith and Sheridan reacted against it with 'laughing comedy'. Farce: improbable situations, physical humour.

steps.title: Tragicomedy
steps.body: Mixes serious danger with happy outcome: Beaumont and Fletcher; Shakespeare's late romances (The Winter's Tale, The Tempest). Guarini defended the form in Italy.

steps.title: Identify
steps.body: A play where Sir Fopling Flutter and rakish wits plot seductions in drawing-rooms, full of epigram: comedy of manners (Etherege, The Man of Mode, 1676).

activity.prompt: Classify each play.

quiz.q: The comedy of humours is associated with:
quiz.why: Jonson built comic characters around a single dominating humour or obsession.
Goldsmith championed 'laughing comedy' in opposition to the moralising sentimental comedy of his day.

quiz.q: The Tempest is usually classed as:
quiz.why: It moves through danger and loss to reconciliation, typical of Shakespeare's late romances.

scenes.text: Two tramps wait by a bare tree for someone called Godot. He does not come.
In Brecht's theatre a placard announces what will happen next, so that you think instead of weep.

steps.title: Problem play
steps.body: Drama of ideas debating a social question: Ibsen (A Doll's House, 1879, on marriage and women's autonomy), Shaw (Mrs Warren's Profession, on prostitution and economics). Also used for Shakespeare's dark comedies like Measure for Measure.

steps.title: Theatre of the Absurd
steps.body: Term coined by Martin Esslin (1961) for drama expressing the absurdity of human existence through illogical plots, circular structure and broken language: Beckett (Waiting for Godot), Ionesco (The Bald Soprano), Pinter (The Birthday Party, related 'comedy of menace').

steps.title: Epic theatre
steps.body: Bertolt Brecht's theatre aims at critical thought, using the alienation (Verfremdung) effect: songs, placards, direct address and episodic scenes (Mother Courage and Her Children).

steps.title: Other forms
steps.body: Kitchen-sink drama: working-class realism (Osborne's Look Back in Anger, 1956; 'Angry Young Men'). Poetic drama revival: Eliot's Murder in the Cathedral. Masque: courtly spectacle (Jonson).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Absurd drama is not merely 'nonsense'; it is a philosophical vision linked to Camus's idea of the absurd. Brecht's alienation is not emotional coldness but a technique to make the familiar strange.

activity.prompt: Assign each play to its movement.

quiz.why: Martin Esslin used the phrase as the title of his 1961 book.
Brecht distanced the audience from illusion so they would judge the social situation shown.
Critics applied the label to Pinter's early plays such as The Birthday Party.

scenes.text: Othello calls Iago 'honest' again and again while the audience squirms.
Alone on stage, Macbeth sees a dagger before him.

steps.title: Speech devices
steps.body: Soliloquy: a character alone speaks thoughts aloud (Hamlet's 'To be or not to be'). Aside: brief remark to the audience unheard by others. Monologue: long speech to other characters.

steps.title: Irony
steps.body: Dramatic irony: the audience knows what a character does not (Oedipus cursing the killer). Tragic irony is dramatic irony in tragedy. Verbal irony: saying the opposite of what is meant.

steps.title: Structural devices
steps.body: Chorus (Greek; Shakespeare's Henry V prologue), play-within-a-play (The Mousetrap in Hamlet), comic relief (Porter scene in Macbeth), deus ex machina (implausible rescue), denouement (unravelling). Freytag's pyramid: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, catastrophe/denouement.

steps.title: Identify
steps.body: Iago's lines to the audience 'I am not what I am' while others are on stage but cannot hear: an aside.

activity.prompt: Order Freytag's pyramid.

quiz.q: The Porter scene in Macbeth is an example of:
quiz.why: The drunken Porter's jokes briefly release tension right after Duncan's murder.

options: The audience knows more than a character
quiz.why: Dramatic irony depends on the gap between the audience's knowledge and the character's ignorance.
Hamlet stages a play reenacting his father's murder to test Claudius's guilt.

questions.q: Aristotle's Poetics names how many parts of tragedy?
questions.why: Plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle.
It is the change from ignorance to knowledge.
Senecan closet dramas supplied ghosts, bloodshed and five-act structure.

questions.q: Congreve's The Way of the World is a:
questions.why: It satirises fashionable Restoration society with wit.

questions.q: Every Man in His Humour is by:
questions.why: Ben Jonson's play launched the comedy of humours.

questions.q: A Doll's House was written by:
questions.why: Henrik Ibsen's 1879 play is a classic problem play.
Brecht named his anti-illusionist, episodic theatre 'epic'.

questions.q: Look Back in Anger premiered in:
questions.why: Osborne's play opened at the Royal Court in May 1956.

questions.q: A sudden improbable divine rescue is:
questions.why: Literally 'god from the machine', from the crane that lowered gods onto the Greek stage.

options: Spoken to the audience, unheard by others on stage
questions.why: Asides are brief, heard by the audience only.
It moves from tragic jealousy to restoration and reunion.

questions.q: Which is NOT a feature of absurd drama?
options: Logical cause-effect plot leading to resolution
questions.why: Absurd drama rejects neat causal plots and resolutions.

questions.q: Murder in the Cathedral is a:
questions.why: T.S. Eliot's 1935 verse play on Becket revived poetic drama.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Fiction & Prose Forms
courses.summary: The novel and its subgenres, the short story, narrative point of view, and non-fictional prose: essay, biography, autobiography.
outcomes: Trace the rise of the English novel
Distinguish picaresque, epistolary, Gothic, historical, Bildungsroman and stream-of-consciousness novels
Identify narrative point of view and unreliable narration
Describe the essay, biography and autobiography as forms

scenes.text: 1719: Robinson Crusoe is shipwrecked, and readers believe his journal could be real.
1740: Richardson's Pamela tells her trials in letters, written 'to the moment'.

steps.title: Definition and rise
steps.body: A novel is an extended prose fiction with realistic characters and plot. In England it rose in the 18th century with Defoe, Richardson, Fielding, Smollett and Sterne, helped by a growing middle-class readership and print culture (Ian Watt, The Rise of the Novel, 1957).

steps.title: Subgenres
steps.body: Picaresque: episodic adventures of a rogue (Lazarillo de Tormes; Fielding's Joseph Andrews shows influence). Epistolary: told in letters (Pamela, Clarissa). Gothic: terror, castles, the supernatural (Walpole's The Castle of Otranto, 1764; Radcliffe; Frankenstein). Historical: Scott's Waverley (1814). Bildungsroman: growth of a protagonist (David Copperfield, Great Expectations, A Portrait of the Artist). Stream of consciousness: flow of a mind (Joyce's Ulysses, Woolf's Mrs Dalloway).

steps.title: Identify
steps.body: A novel follows Pip from boyhood in the marshes through false expectations to moral maturity: Bildungsroman.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Stream of consciousness' (the technique/term from William James) is different from 'interior monologue', a specific method of presenting it in a character's direct thought.

activity.prompt: Classify the novels.

quiz.q: The first Gothic novel is usually said to be:
quiz.why: Horace Walpole's 1764 novel is traditionally credited as the first Gothic novel.
Scott's Waverley set the model for the historical novel.

quiz.q: The term 'stream of consciousness' was coined by:
quiz.why: The psychologist William James used the phrase in The Principles of Psychology (1890).

scenes.text: 'Call me Ishmael.' A first-person narrator steps forward.
George Eliot's narrator sees into every mind in Middlemarch.

steps.title: Persons and perspectives
steps.body: First-person: 'I' narrator, participant or witness. Third-person omniscient: knows all characters' thoughts and comments. Third-person limited: restricted to one character's consciousness. Second-person: 'you' (rare).

steps.title: Free indirect discourse
steps.body: Narration that blends a character's idiom with the narrator's voice without quotation marks: 'Emma was sure; Mr Elton was in love — what could be clearer?' Jane Austen used it pervasively.

steps.title: Unreliable narrator
steps.body: A narrator whose account the reader cannot fully trust because of ignorance, bias or deceit (Wayne Booth's term). Examples: Stevens in Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day; Nelly Dean partially in Wuthering Heights.

steps.title: Plot vs story
steps.body: E.M. Forster (Aspects of the Novel, 1927): story = events in time ('the king died and then the queen died'); plot = causality ('the queen died of grief'). He also divided characters into flat and round.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not identify the narrator with the author. Even a first-person narrator is a constructed voice.

activity.prompt: Identify the narrative mode.

items.text: Narrator comments on every character's motives
Character's thoughts in narrator's sentence, no quotation marks

quiz.q: Flat and round characters were defined by:
quiz.why: Forster introduced the distinction in Aspects of the Novel (1927).
Forster's example shows plot as events linked by causality.

quiz.q: An unreliable narrator is one who:
