quiz.why: Bias, limited knowledge or deceit make the narrator's account doubtful to the reader.

scenes.text: Poe argues a tale should be read at one sitting and aim at a single effect.
O. Henry's 'The Gift of the Magi' ends with a twist that turns sacrifice into irony.

steps.title: Features
steps.body: Brief prose fiction, readable in one sitting, focusing on a single incident, few characters and a unified effect. Poe's 1842 review of Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales gave the 'single effect' theory.

steps.title: Masters
steps.body: Poe and Hawthorne (USA), Maupassant (twist and realism), Chekhov (open endings, mood), Joyce's Dubliners (epiphany: a sudden revelation of truth), Katherine Mansfield; in India R.K. Narayan, Mulk Raj Anand, Ruskin Bond.

steps.title: Epiphany
steps.body: At the end of Joyce's 'Araby' the boy sees himself as 'a creature driven and derided by vanity': an epiphany, Joyce's term for a sudden spiritual manifestation.

steps.title: Answer pattern
steps.body: For a short-story question: setting, central incident, narrative voice, turning point, ending (twist/open/epiphany), and theme.

activity.prompt: Match the writer with the typical ending.

quiz.why: Poe argued in 1842 that every element of a tale should serve one preconceived effect.
Joyce borrowed 'epiphany' from theology for moments of sudden insight.
Guy de Maupassant's story ends with the revelation that the lost necklace was paste.

scenes.text: Montaigne, in his tower, tries out ('essaie') his thoughts on everything.
Boswell follows Dr Johnson with a notebook for twenty years.

steps.title: The essay
steps.body: A short prose composition on a subject, from the French essai (attempt). Montaigne's Essais (1580) were personal; Bacon's Essays (1597) were aphoristic and formal ('Of Studies'). Periodical essay: Addison and Steele (The Tatler, The Spectator). Familiar/personal essay: Charles Lamb (Essays of Elia), Hazlitt.

steps.title: Biography and autobiography
steps.body: Biography: a life written by another (Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson, 1791; Lytton Strachey's Eminent Victorians, 1918). Autobiography: one's own life (Gandhi's The Story of My Experiments with Truth; Nirad C. Chaudhuri's The Autobiography of an Unknown Indian). Memoir focuses on a part of life or public events.

steps.title: Formal vs personal
steps.body: 'Studies serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability' (Bacon) is aphoristic, impersonal: formal essay. Lamb's 'Dream Children' with its tender reverie is personal/familiar essay.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not call Bacon's essays 'personal': they are compressed, didactic and impersonal, unlike Lamb's.

activity.prompt: Classify the prose work.

items.text: The Story of My Experiments with Truth

quiz.why: Francis Bacon's 1597 Essays include 'Of Studies'.
Joseph Addison and Richard Steele produced The Spectator (1711–12).
Montaigne's French essai means a trial or attempt.

options: Growth and education of the protagonist

questions.q: The Rise of the Novel was written by:
questions.why: Ian Watt's 1957 study links the novel to realism and the middle class.

questions.q: Free indirect discourse is strongly associated with:
questions.why: Austen blended narrator and character voice pervasively.
Wayne Booth's 1961 book coined the term.
Charles Lamb wrote under the pen-name Elia.

options: A rogue hero in episodic adventures
Is restricted to one character's view
questions.why: It filters events through a single character.
Mary Shelley's novel combines Gothic horror with scientific speculation (it also uses letters as a frame).

courses.title: Unit 5 · Figures of Speech, Terms & Revision
courses.summary: Figures of speech, key literary terms (satire, allegory, conceit, pathetic fallacy), a technique for critical appreciation of an unseen poem, and exam revision.
outcomes: Identify metaphor, simile, metonymy, synecdoche, personification, oxymoron, hyperbole, apostrophe
Define satire, allegory, conceit, pathetic fallacy, objective correlative
Write a structured critical appreciation of an unseen poem
Answer short-note and identification questions under exam conditions

scenes.text: Jaques says the world IS a stage: metaphor, not simile.
'The Crown' announces a new policy: a part of royalty stands for the whole institution.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body: Simile: explicit comparison with 'like/as' ('My love is like a red, red rose'). Metaphor: implicit identification ('All the world's a stage'). Personification: human qualities to non-human things ('Death, be not proud' also uses apostrophe). Conceit: a striking, far-fetched extended comparison, esp. Metaphysical (Donne's compasses in 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning').

steps.title: Substitution
steps.body: Metonymy: a thing named by something associated ('the pen is mightier than the sword'). Synecdoche: part for whole or whole for part ('all hands on deck'). Transferred epithet: adjective moved to the wrong noun ('a sleepless night').

steps.title: Contrast and emphasis
steps.body: Oxymoron: contradictory terms together ('O loving hate'). Paradox: apparently self-contradictory statement with truth ('The child is father of the man'). Antithesis: balanced contrast ('To err is human, to forgive divine'). Hyperbole: exaggeration. Litotes: understatement by negation ('not bad'). Apostrophe: addressing an absent person or abstraction. Zeugma: one word governing two in different senses (Pope: 'stain her honour, or her new brocade').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Oxymoron is a two-word contradiction; paradox is a whole statement. Synecdoche uses a part of the thing; metonymy uses something merely associated.

activity.prompt: Name the figure of speech.

items.text: The pen is mightier than the sword
Or stain her honour, or her new brocade

quiz.q: 'The child is father of the man' is:
quiz.why: It is a seemingly contradictory statement that expresses a truth about growth, which is paradox.
The elaborate, intellectual comparison of lovers to a pair of compasses is the classic metaphysical conceit.
Sleeplessness belongs to the person, but the adjective is transferred to the night.

scenes.text: Ruskin complains when poets make the sea 'cruel': the pathetic fallacy.
Eliot wants an emotion expressed through a formula of objects: the objective correlative.

steps.title: Satire and allegory
steps.body: Satire: ridicule of vice or folly to correct it. Horatian satire is gentle and urbane; Juvenalian is bitter and indignant (Swift's 'A Modest Proposal'). Allegory: a narrative with a second, systematic meaning (Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress; Orwell's Animal Farm). Fable and parable are short allegories.

steps.title: Terms by coiners
steps.body: Pathetic fallacy: Ruskin (Modern Painters, 1856), attributing human feeling to nature. Objective correlative: Eliot ('Hamlet and His Problems', 1919). Negative capability: Keats (letter, 1817), being in uncertainties without irritable reaching after fact. Willing suspension of disbelief: Coleridge (Biographia Literaria, 1817). Dissociation of sensibility: Eliot ('The Metaphysical Poets', 1921).

steps.title: More terms
steps.body: Imagery, symbol (object standing for more than itself), motif, theme, tone, persona, irony, bathos (ludicrous descent from the elevated), pathos, carpe diem ('seize the day': Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress'), ubi sunt, in medias res.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not attribute 'negative capability' to Coleridge or 'objective correlative' to Arnold: these coiner questions are frequent in exams.

activity.prompt: Who coined the term?

quiz.q: 'A Modest Proposal' is an example of:
quiz.why: Swift's savage, indignant irony about eating children is Juvenalian in spirit.
Its farm story systematically represents the Russian Revolution and Stalinism.

options: Anticlimactic descent from lofty to trivial
quiz.why: Pope popularised the term for a ludicrous drop from the sublime to the ridiculous.

lessons.title: Lab: Critical appreciation of an unseen poem

scenes.text: The exam paper prints a poem you have never read. Panic? No: there is a method.
Read twice, annotate, then write in a set order.

steps.title: The method
steps.body: 1) Read twice; identify speaker, situation, subject. 2) Paraphrase briefly. 3) Theme. 4) Form: kind of poem, stanza, rhyme, metre. 5) Language: diction, imagery, figures of speech. 6) Sound: alliteration, rhythm. 7) Tone and shift. 8) Personal evaluation with evidence.

steps.title: Worked sample
steps.body: Lines: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o'er vales and hills'. Speaker: solitary walker. Simile 'lonely as a cloud' sets isolation. Metre: iambic tetrameter (I WAN | dered LONE | ly AS | a CLOUD). Stanza: six lines ababcc. Theme: memory of nature restoring the mind ('the bliss of solitude'). Tone: from loneliness to joy.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Always quote briefly and comment on effect: 'The alliteration in "fluttering and dancing" mimics movement' is better than listing devices.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Pure paraphrase earns few marks; device-spotting without effect earns few marks. Combine both with interpretation.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of a critical appreciation answer.
items: Read twice and identify speaker and situation
Analyse imagery and figures of speech

quiz.q: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' opens with a:
quiz.why: The comparison uses 'as', so it is a simile.

quiz.q: The best way to discuss a device is to:
options: Quote it and explain its effect
quiz.why: Examiners reward linking a quoted device to its effect on meaning or tone.

quiz.q: A six-line stanza rhyming ababcc in tetrameter, as in 'Daffodils', ends with a:
quiz.why: The final cc lines rhyme together, forming a couplet.

scenes.text: One sheet: forms, metres, stanzas, terms with coiners.
Practise five short notes in 30 minutes.

steps.title: Quick sheet
steps.body: Sonnets: Petrarchan abbaabba cdecde; Shakespearean abab cdcd efef gg; Spenserian abab bcbc cdcd ee. Stanzas: rhyme royal 7, ottava rima 8, Spenserian 9 + alexandrine. Feet: iamb x/, trochee /x, anapaest xx/, dactyl /xx, spondee //. Tragedy terms: hamartia, peripeteia, anagnorisis, catharsis.

steps.title: Short-note practice (original)
steps.body: Write 150 words each: (a) Dramatic monologue with reference to Browning. (b) Mock-epic. (c) Comedy of manners. (d) Bildungsroman. (e) Objective correlative.

steps.title: Long-answer practice
steps.body: (1) Discuss the conventions of the pastoral elegy with examples. (2) Trace the development of the English sonnet from Wyatt to Milton. (3) Explain Aristotle's concept of tragedy and apply it to one play.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Short note: definition → origin/coiner → 2 features → 2 examples → one line of significance.

activity.prompt: Final drill: which category?

quiz.q: A villanelle has how many lines?
quiz.why: A villanelle has 19 lines: five tercets and a quatrain with two refrains (e.g. Dylan Thomas's 'Do not go gentle').
The essay is a short non-fictional prose composition.
Aristotle says tragedy arouses and purges pity and fear.

questions.why: Two contradictory words joined together form an oxymoron.

questions.q: 'Death, be not proud' addresses death; this is:
questions.why: Directly addressing an abstraction is apostrophe.
Understatement by negating the opposite is litotes.

questions.q: Objective correlative was coined in an essay on:
Negative capability appears in a letter by:
questions.why: Keats wrote to his brothers in December 1817.
Marvell urges seizing the day before time destroys love.
It follows the angry tone of the Roman poet Juvenal.
Bunyan's Christian journeys through allegorical places like Vanity Fair.

questions.q: 'Dissociation of sensibility' describes a split between:
questions.why: Eliot claimed post-Metaphysical poets ceased to fuse thought with feeling.

questions.q: 'The cruel, crawling foam' (Kingsley) was Ruskin's example of:
questions.why: Ruskin cited it to show false human emotion attributed to nature.
Antithesis places opposites in parallel structure.

questions.q: In critical appreciation, the final step is usually:
questions.why: An evaluative conclusion supported by evidence closes the answer.

uni-ba-eng-postcolonial-lit.title: Postcolonial Literature
uni-ba-eng-postcolonial-lit.description: Theory and texts of postcolonial writing: Africa, the Caribbean, South Asia, Australia/Canada, with Fanon, Said, Bhabha and Spivak. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. English programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Postcolonial Concepts and Theory
courses.summary: Colonialism and postcolonialism; Fanon, Said's Orientalism, Bhabha's hybridity and mimicry, Spivak's subaltern, Ngũgĩ's language debate, The Empire Writes Back.
outcomes: Define colonialism, imperialism, decolonisation and postcolonialism
Explain Said's Orientalism
Apply Bhabha's hybridity, mimicry and ambivalence
Discuss Spivak's 'Can the Subaltern Speak?'
Compare Achebe's and Ngũgĩ's positions on language

scenes.text: On a train in Lyon a child points: 'Look, a Negro!' Fanon feels himself fixed by the gaze.
In Algeria, Fanon works as a psychiatrist and joins the liberation struggle.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: Colonialism: settlement and control of territory. Imperialism: ideology and system of domination. Decolonisation: political and cultural undoing of colonial rule. 'Post-colonial' (hyphenated) often means after independence; 'postcolonial' names a critical approach to the effects of colonisation from contact onward. Also: settler colony, metropolis/centre vs periphery, diaspora, neo-colonialism, 'writing back'.

steps.title: Frantz Fanon (1925–1961)
steps.body: Martinican psychiatrist. Black Skin, White Masks (1952): psychology of colonised identity, internalised inferiority, language ('To speak a language is to take on a world, a culture'). The Wretched of the Earth (1961; preface by Sartre): violence of decolonisation, critique of the national bourgeoisie, three phases of the native intellectual (assimilation, remembering the past, fighting/revolutionary literature).

steps.title: Apply Fanon
steps.body: A colonised student who speaks only the coloniser's language at home and despises local speech displays Fanon's first phase: assimilation. A writer who turns to folk legend shows the second; one who writes to mobilise people shows the third.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Postcolonial' is not just a period label; it includes resistance during colonial rule.

activity.prompt: Order Fanon's three phases of the native intellectual.
items: Return to and remembering of native past
Fighting phase: literature that awakens the people

quiz.q: Black Skin, White Masks appeared in:
quiz.why: Fanon published it in French as Peau noire, masques blancs in 1952.

quiz.q: Who wrote the preface to The Wretched of the Earth?
quiz.why: Jean-Paul Sartre wrote the famous preface in 1961.
Kwame Nkrumah used the term for indirect domination after formal independence.

scenes.text: European paintings show the 'East' as harems, deserts and timeless despots.
1978: Edward Said argues these images are a discourse of power.

steps.title: Edward Said (1935–2003)
steps.body: Palestinian-American critic at Columbia. Orientalism (1978), Culture and Imperialism (1993), The World, the Text, and the Critic.

steps.title: Orientalism
steps.body: Three senses: academic field; a style of thought based on a binary of Orient vs Occident; a Western 'corporate institution for dealing with the Orient… for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over' it. Draws on Foucault's discourse and Gramsci's hegemony. The Orient is represented as irrational, sensual, static, feminine; the West as rational, progressive, masculine.

steps.title: Contrapuntal reading
steps.body: In Culture and Imperialism Said reads canonical novels alongside empire: e.g. Mansfield Park's wealth depends on Antigua plantations.

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: A novel describing an Indian bazaar as 'teeming, chaotic and unchanging since antiquity' constructs the Orient as static: a classic Orientalist trope.

activity.prompt: Orientalist binary: which side is the 'Orient' assigned?

quiz.q: Said drew on which thinker's idea of discourse?
quiz.why: Said used Foucault's notion of discourse as knowledge linked to power.
Said develops it in Culture and Imperialism (1993).
He argues it is a Western style of dominating and having authority over the Orient.

story.title: Almost the same, but not quite

scenes.text: The colonial 'babu' copies English manners; the copy unsettles the original.
A young woman, Bhubaneswari Bhaduri, hangs herself in 1926 — and her message goes unread.

steps.title: Homi K. Bhabha
steps.body: The Location of Culture (1994). Hybridity: colonial encounter produces mixed cultural forms that challenge purity. Mimicry: the colonised imitates the coloniser — 'almost the same, but not quite' — producing menace and mockery. Ambivalence: colonial discourse is split between attraction and repulsion. Third Space of enunciation.

steps.title: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
steps.body: 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988). Subaltern (from Gramsci; Subaltern Studies group, Ranajit Guha): groups outside hegemonic power. Spivak argues the subaltern woman is doubly silenced — by colonial discourse ('white men saving brown women from brown men') and native patriarchy (sati debate). Her answer: 'The subaltern cannot speak' (later qualified). Strategic essentialism.

steps.title: Macaulay and mimicry
steps.body: Macaulay's 'class of persons Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste' is Bhabha's key example: the mimic man both serves and subverts colonial authority.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Subaltern' does not mean simply 'poor'; it means those without access to hegemonic discourse and representation.

activity.prompt: Bhabha or Spivak concept?

quiz.q: 'Almost the same, but not quite' defines:
quiz.why: Bhabha uses this phrase in 'Of Mimicry and Man'.

quiz.q: Spivak's example of doubly silenced women involves:
quiz.why: She analyses the colonial and Hindu debates over sati, where women's voices are absent.

quiz.q: The Location of Culture was published in:
quiz.why: Bhabha's essay collection appeared in 1994.

scenes.text: In a Kenyan school, a child caught speaking Gikuyu wears a sign: 'I AM STUPID'.
Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o announces he will write in Gikuyu.

steps.title: Ngũgĩ
steps.body: Decolonising the Mind (1986): language carries culture; colonial education's 'cultural bomb'; bids farewell to English for Gikuyu (Devil on the Cross, written on toilet paper in prison). Earlier English novels: Weep Not, Child, A Grain of Wheat.

steps.title: Achebe
steps.body: 'The African Writer and the English Language' (1965): English can be made 'to carry the weight of my African experience' — 'a new English, still in full communion with its ancestral home but altered to suit its new African surroundings'.

steps.title: The Empire Writes Back (1989)
steps.body: Ashcroft, Griffiths and Tiffin. 'English' (standard, imperial) vs 'english' (variants). Strategies: abrogation (rejecting standard norms) and appropriation (reshaping the language), untranslated words, glossing, code-switching. Canonical counter-discourse: rewriting classics (Wide Sargasso Sea from Jane Eyre; Coetzee's Foe from Robinson Crusoe; Césaire's Une Tempête).

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: Achebe inserts Igbo proverbs ('Proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten') into English prose: appropriation.

activity.prompt: Canonical text and its postcolonial rewriting.

quiz.why: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o published it in 1986.
The Empire Writes Back defines abrogation as refusing the privileged centre's language norms.
Coetzee retells Defoe's story through Susan Barton and the mute Friday.

questions.q: Gramsci's term borrowed by Subaltern Studies:
'White men saving brown women from brown men' is Spivak's phrase about:
The Empire Writes Back's authors include:
Achebe's essay on language argues English can be:
Devil on the Cross was written in:
Third Space is Bhabha's term for:
options: Space of cultural negotiation and hybridity

courses.title: Unit 2 · African Literature
courses.summary: Negritude, Achebe's Things Fall Apart, Ngũgĩ, Soyinka's drama and poetry, Coetzee and Gordimer, and contemporary African women writers.
outcomes: Explain Negritude and its critics
Analyse Things Fall Apart: Okonkwo, Igbo society, colonial arrival
Discuss Soyinka's Death and the King's Horseman and 'Telephone Conversation'
Describe apartheid-era South African fiction and Adichie

scenes.text: In 1930s Paris, Senghor and Césaire celebrate Black identity: Negritude.
Soyinka quips: 'A tiger does not proclaim his tigritude; he pounces.'

steps.title: Negritude
steps.body: Francophone movement (1930s) by Aimé Césaire (Martinique; Notebook of a Return to the Native Land, 1939; Discourse on Colonialism), Léopold Sédar Senghor (Senegal; later president) and Léon-Gontran Damas. Affirmed African culture, rhythm, emotion and Black dignity against colonial assimilation.

steps.title: Critiques
steps.body: Soyinka's tigritude remark; Fanon and others saw it as reverse essentialism. Senghor's 'emotion is Negro as reason is Hellenic' was criticised.

steps.title: Anglophone poets
steps.body: Gabriel Okara ('Once Upon a Time': 'I have learned to wear many faces / like dresses'), David Diop ('Africa'), Christopher Okigbo (Labyrinths), Kofi Awoonor, Dennis Brutus, Wole Soyinka ('Telephone Conversation'), Niyi Osundare.

steps.title: 'Once Upon a Time'
steps.body: A father tells his son that people once 'laughed with their hearts' but now smile with teeth and 'ice-block-cold eyes'; he wants to 'unlearn' false manners. Theme: lost authenticity under Westernised urban life.

activity.prompt: Negritude founder or Anglophone poet?

quiz.q: Notebook of a Return to the Native Land is by:
quiz.why: Aimé Césaire's long poem (1939) coined and enacted Negritude.
Soyinka argued identity should be lived, not loudly asserted.
Gabriel Okara's poem contrasts sincere past with masked present.

scenes.text: Okonkwo throws Amalinze the Cat and becomes famous through the nine villages.
At the end, the District Commissioner plans a book: The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger.

steps.title: Chinua Achebe (1930–2013)
steps.body: Things Fall Apart (1958; title from Yeats's 'The Second Coming'), No Longer at Ease, Arrow of God, A Man of the People, Anthills of the Savannah. Essay 'An Image of Africa' (1975) on Conrad. Wanted to show that African peoples 'did not hear of culture for the first time from Europeans'.

steps.title: Part One: Igbo society
steps.body: Okonkwo's fear of being like his father Unoka; Ikemefuna's death (Okonkwo strikes the blow); Ezinma and Ekwefi; egwugwu court, harvest, proverbs, chi; Okonkwo accidentally kills a clansman and is exiled to Mbanta for seven years.

steps.title: Parts Two and Three: colonial arrival
steps.body: Missionaries (Mr Brown, conciliatory; Rev. Smith, zealous); Nwoye converts; Enoch unmasks an egwugwu; church burned; leaders humiliated; Okonkwo beheads the messenger and hangs himself. Ironic ending: his story becomes 'a reasonable paragraph' in the Commissioner's book.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Achebe does not idealise Igbo society: twins abandoned, osu outcasts and Okonkwo's violence are shown critically. Its 'falling apart' is from both internal tensions and colonial force.

activity.prompt: Order the events of Things Fall Apart.
items: Ikemefuna comes to live with Okonkwo
Accidental killing and exile to Mbanta
Okonkwo kills the messenger and hangs himself

quiz.q: The novel's title is taken from:
quiz.why: It quotes 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold' from Yeats's 'The Second Coming'.
He must leave for seven years after accidentally killing Ezeudu's son.

quiz.q: The District Commissioner's planned book shows:
quiz.why: Okonkwo's tragedy becomes a paragraph in a book titled The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes.

scenes.text: In Oyo, 1946, Elesin must follow the dead king into the other world by ritual death.
A man phones a London landlady: 'Madam, I warned, I hate a wasted journey — I am African.'

steps.title: Wole Soyinka (b.1934)
steps.body: Nigerian; Nobel 1986 (first African laureate). Plays: The Lion and the Jewel, A Dance of the Forests, The Road, Kongi's Harvest, Death and the King's Horseman (1975). Prison memoir The Man Died. Yoruba myth (Ogun).

steps.title: Death and the King's Horseman
steps.body: Based on a 1946 event. Elesin Oba delays his ritual suicide for a new bride; British District Officer Pilkings intervenes; Elesin's son Olunde, returned from medical studies in England, dies in his place; Elesin strangles himself. Soyinka's note rejects a simple 'clash of cultures' reading: the main conflict is metaphysical.

steps.title: 'Telephone Conversation'
steps.body: Landlady asks 'HOW DARK?'; the speaker ironically describes himself as 'West African sepia', palms and soles 'peroxide blonde'; satire of racism through wit and capital letters.

steps.title: Ngũgĩ's novels
steps.body: Weep Not, Child (1964), The River Between, A Grain of Wheat (1967; Mau Mau, Uhuru, betrayal by Mugo), Petals of Blood, Wizard of the Crow.

activity.prompt: Soyinka or Ngũgĩ?

quiz.why: He became the first African Nobel laureate in Literature in 1986.
His son Olunde performs the ritual death that Elesin failed to complete.

quiz.q: A Grain of Wheat is set around:
quiz.why: It unfolds in the days before Kenya's independence in 1963.

scenes.text: Professor Lurie, disgraced, helps at an animal clinic in the Eastern Cape.
In Enugu, Kambili's world cracks open under a hibiscus-filled garden.

steps.title: South African writing
steps.body: Alan Paton (Cry, the Beloved Country, 1948). Nadine Gordimer (Nobel 1991; July's People, Burger's Daughter). J.M. Coetzee (Nobel 2003; Waiting for the Barbarians, Life & Times of Michael K, Disgrace 1999 — both Booker). Athol Fugard (drama: 'Master Harold'... and the Boys). Bessie Head (Botswana; Maru).

steps.title: Contemporary
steps.body: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie: Purple Hibiscus (2003), Half of a Yellow Sun (2006; Biafra), Americanah, talk 'The Danger of a Single Story' (2009). Ben Okri: The Famished Road (Booker 1991; abiku spirit child). Buchi Emecheta: The Joys of Motherhood. Tsitsi Dangarembga: Nervous Conditions.

steps.title: 'The Danger of a Single Story'
steps.body: Adichie argues that one stereotyped narrative about a place or people creates stereotypes that are 'incomplete', robbing people of dignity; links directly to Said's critique of representation.

steps.title: Answer tip
steps.body: For a question on African women writers, combine Emecheta, Dangarembga and Adichie: double colonisation by empire and patriarchy.

activity.prompt: Match the novel to its author.

quiz.why: He won the Nobel Prize in 2003.

quiz.q: Half of a Yellow Sun is set during:
quiz.why: The yellow sun was on the Biafran flag (1967–70).
In Yoruba belief, a child repeatedly born and dying; Azaro in The Famished Road is one.

questions.q: Things Fall Apart was published in:

questions.why: He narrates Okonkwo's end to the Commissioner.

questions.q: Cry, the Beloved Country is by:
Nervous Conditions takes its title from:
questions.why: 'The status of native is a nervous condition'.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Caribbean Literature
courses.summary: Derek Walcott, Kamau Brathwaite and nation language, V.S. Naipaul, Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea, Jamaica Kincaid and others.
outcomes: Analyse Walcott's 'A Far Cry from Africa' and Omeros
Explain Brathwaite's 'nation language'
Discuss Naipaul's mimic men and A House for Mr Biswas
Interpret Wide Sargasso Sea as counter-discourse

scenes.text: News of the Mau Mau uprising reaches St Lucia; Walcott, of African and European descent, is torn.
In Omeros, fishermen Achille and Hector echo Homer's heroes.

steps.title: Walcott (1930–2017)
steps.body: St Lucian poet-dramatist; Nobel 1992. In a Green Night (1962), The Castaway, Another Life, The Star-Apple Kingdom ('The Schooner Flight': 'either I'm nobody, or I'm a nation'), Omeros (1990, Caribbean epic in terza-rima-like tercets). Plays: Dream on Monkey Mountain.

steps.title: 'A Far Cry from Africa'
steps.body: Responds to the Mau Mau rebellion and colonial violence: 'I who am poisoned with the blood of both, / Where shall I turn, divided to the vein? / I who have cursed / The drunken officer of British rule, how choose / Between this Africa and the English tongue I love?' Hybrid identity and moral conflict.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body: Hybridity, history ('The Sea Is History'), language, the Adamic poet naming a new world (essay 'The Muse of History'), rejection of both nostalgia for Africa and servility to Europe.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Walcott does not resolve the dilemma in 'A Far Cry from Africa'; the poem ends with questions.

activity.prompt: Walcott work: poem/epic or play?

quiz.why: He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992.

quiz.q: 'A Far Cry from Africa' responds to:
quiz.why: The poem addresses colonial violence in Kenya during the Mau Mau rebellion.
Its title is the Greek for Homer and it rewrites Homeric figures as St Lucian fishermen.

story.title: The hurricane does not roar in pentameter

scenes.text: Brathwaite argues that iambic pentameter cannot capture a Caribbean hurricane.
Reggae, calypso and dub poetry carry the rhythm of the people.

steps.title: Kamau Brathwaite (1930–2020)
steps.body: Barbadian poet-historian. The Arrivants trilogy (Rights of Passage, Masks, Islands). History of the Voice (1984): 'nation language' — the submerged African-influenced English of the Caribbean, distinct from 'dialect' (a pejorative). 'The hurricane does not roar in pentameters.'

steps.title: Performance poetry
steps.body: Louise Bennett ('Colonization in Reverse', Jamaican Creole), dub poets Linton Kwesi Johnson and Mutabaruka, Grace Nichols ('Epilogue': 'I have crossed an ocean / I have lost my tongue / from the root of the old one / a new one has sprung'), John Agard ('Half-Caste', 'Listen Mr Oxford Don').

steps.title: 'Colonization in Reverse'
steps.body: Bennett comically describes Jamaicans migrating to England — 'Wat a joyful news, Miss Mattie' — 'colonizin / Englan in reverse': ironic inversion of empire in Creole.

steps.title: Linking
steps.body: Nation language is an example of 'abrogation and appropriation' from The Empire Writes Back.

activity.prompt: Match the poem to the poet.

items.text: I Is a Long Memoried Woman

quiz.why: He defines it in History of the Voice (1984).
Dialect implies a broken, inferior form; nation language asserts legitimacy.
Johnson pioneered reggae-backed dub poetry in Britain.

scenes.text: Mohun Biswas, born with six fingers and unlucky, marries into the domineering Tulsi family.
He dies owning a house in Port of Spain — mortgaged, but his.

steps.title: Naipaul (1932–2018)
steps.body: Trinidadian of Indian descent, lived in England; Nobel 2001. The Mystic Masseur, A House for Mr Biswas (1961), The Mimic Men (1967), In a Free State (Booker 1971), A Bend in the River (1979). Travel books on India: An Area of Darkness, India: A Wounded Civilization, A Million Mutinies Now.

steps.title: A House for Mr Biswas
steps.body: Based on his father's life. Biswas's struggle for independence from the Tulsis at Hanuman House; work as sign-painter and journalist; repeated failed houses; final house as symbol of identity and dignity in a rootless colonial society.

steps.title: Mimicry and criticism
steps.body: The Mimic Men: colonial politician Ralph Singh in exile; 'We pretended to be real… we mimic men of the New World'. Critics (Said, Walcott, Achebe) accused Naipaul of a contemptuous view of the 'Third World'.

steps.title: Compare with Bhabha
steps.body: Naipaul presents mimicry as emptiness; Bhabha sees mimicry as potentially subversive. Good exam contrast.

activity.prompt: Naipaul fiction or travel/non-fiction?

quiz.why: He received the Nobel Prize in 2001.

quiz.q: In a Free State won the:
quiz.why: It won the Booker Prize in 1971.
The Tulsi family dominates Biswas at Hanuman House.

lessons.title: Jean Rhys and Caribbean women writers

scenes.text: Antoinette Cosway's family home at Coulibri is burned by former slaves.
In an English attic, renamed 'Bertha', she dreams of fire and holds a candle.

steps.title: Wide Sargasso Sea (1966)
steps.body: Jean Rhys (Dominica-born). Prequel to Jane Eyre. Part I: Antoinette narrates childhood in post-emancipation Jamaica (Emancipation Act 1833); Christophine, her Martinican nurse; Tia ('a white nigger'). Part II: Rochester (unnamed) narrates the marriage in Dominica, renames her Bertha; obeah. Part III: Thornfield attic; dream of burning the house.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: Counter-discourse to Brontë; Creole identity between Black Jamaicans and English whites; patriarchy and property (marriage law before Married Women's Property Act); naming as power. Spivak's 'Three Women's Texts and a Critique of Imperialism' (1985).

steps.title: Other women writers
steps.body: Jamaica Kincaid (Antigua): A Small Place (1988, polemic on tourism), Annie John, 'Girl'. Merle Collins, Olive Senior, Erna Brodber, Edwidge Danticat (Haiti).

steps.title: 'Girl'
steps.body: One breathless sentence of a mother's instructions ('this is how to sew on a button… on Sundays try to walk like a lady and not like the slut you are so bent on becoming'): gender, colonial respectability, mother-daughter conflict.

activity.prompt: Order the three parts of Wide Sargasso Sea.
items: Rochester narrates the honeymoon in Dominica
Antoinette as 'Bertha' in the Thornfield attic

quiz.q: Wide Sargasso Sea's heroine's real name:
quiz.why: Rochester renames Antoinette 'Bertha', stripping her identity.

quiz.q: Spivak's essay on Jane Eyre and Wide Sargasso Sea is:
options: Three Women's Texts and a Critique of Imperialism
quiz.why: Her 1985 essay reads Jane Eyre, Wide Sargasso Sea and Frankenstein.

options: Tourism and colonial legacy in Antigua
quiz.why: Kincaid addresses the tourist directly to expose colonial and postcolonial corruption.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Settler Colonies, South Asia and the Diaspora
courses.summary: Australian, Canadian and New Zealand writing including Indigenous voices; Sri Lankan and Pakistani writing; postcolonial readings of empire texts like Kim and A Passage to India; revision.
outcomes: Describe settler-colony literature and Indigenous resistance writing
Discuss Margaret Atwood's 'survival' thesis and Oodgeroo Noonuccal
Analyse Ondaatje and Sidhwa as South Asian postcolonial writers
Apply postcolonial theory to colonial texts and answer exam questions

scenes.text: In 1964 Oodgeroo Noonuccal (Kath Walker) publishes We Are Going, the first book by an Aboriginal woman poet.
Atwood argues the central Canadian symbol is survival.

steps.title: Settler colonies
steps.body: Australia, Canada, New Zealand: settlers were colonised by Britain yet also colonisers of Indigenous peoples — a double position. Themes: landscape, exile, national identity, the 'cultural cringe' (A.A. Phillips, 1950).

steps.title: Australia
steps.body: Patrick White (Voss; Nobel 1973), Judith Wright ('Bora Ring'), Les Murray, Peter Carey (Oscar and Lucinda; True History of the Kelly Gang — both Booker). Indigenous: Oodgeroo Noonuccal ('We Are Going', 'No More Boomerang'), Sally Morgan (My Place, 1987), Kim Scott, Alexis Wright (Carpentaria). Stolen Generations.

steps.title: Canada and New Zealand
steps.body: Canada: Margaret Atwood (Survival, 1972; The Handmaid's Tale; Surfacing), Alice Munro (Nobel 2013), Michael Ondaatje, Thomas King (Indigenous). New Zealand: Katherine Mansfield, Janet Frame, Keri Hulme (The Bone People, Booker 1985), Witi Ihimaera (The Whale Rider; Māori).

steps.title: 'We Are Going'
steps.body: The last of a tribe visit a former bora ground now a town dump: 'We are the corroboree and the bora ground, / We are the old sacred ceremonies'; ends 'The bora ring is gone. / The corroboree is gone. / And we are going.' Dispossession and cultural loss.

activity.prompt: Which country?

quiz.why: A.A. Phillips used it in a 1950 essay for Australians' sense of cultural inferiority.

quiz.q: Atwood's Survival (1972) is a study of:
quiz.why: She argues survival and victimhood are central themes of Canadian writing.

quiz.q: Patrick White won the Nobel in:
quiz.why: He was the first Australian Nobel laureate in Literature, 1973.

scenes.text: In a ruined Italian villa, a burned man, a nurse, a thief and a Sikh sapper wait out the war.
Kip hears of Hiroshima and leaves: they would never drop such a bomb on a white nation.

steps.title: Sri Lanka
steps.body: Michael Ondaatje (Sri Lanka-born Canadian): The English Patient (1992, Booker), Running in the Family (memoir), Anil's Ghost (civil war). Shyam Selvadurai (Funny Boy, 1994, Tamil–Sinhala conflict and queer identity). Romesh Gunesekera (Reef).

steps.title: Pakistan and Bangladesh
steps.body: Bapsi Sidhwa (Ice-Candy-Man, The Crow Eaters), Mohsin Hamid (The Reluctant Fundamentalist, 2007: dramatic monologue to an American in Lahore after 9/11; Exit West), Kamila Shamsie (Burnt Shadows; Home Fire, rewriting Antigone), Tahmima Anam (A Golden Age, 1971 war).

steps.title: Kip in The English Patient
steps.body: The Sikh sapper Kirpal Singh serves the British Army; news of the atomic bombs makes him reject the West's claims to civilisation — a postcolonial turn inside a European war novel.

steps.title: Linking
steps.body: Hamid's The Reluctant Fundamentalist uses the dramatic monologue (cf. Browning) to reverse the Orientalist gaze: the Pakistani speaks, the American listens.

activity.prompt: Match the novel to its author.

quiz.q: The English Patient won the Booker in:
quiz.why: It shared the 1992 Booker Prize with Sacred Hunger.

quiz.q: The Reluctant Fundamentalist is narrated by:
quiz.why: Changez tells his story to an American stranger in a Lahore café.
Shamsie transposes Sophocles' Antigone to British Muslim families.

scenes.text: Kim, an Irish orphan in Lahore, plays spy in the Great Game.
Prospero claims Caliban's island; Caliban answers: 'This island's mine.'

steps.title: Kipling's Kim (1901)
steps.body: Kim, Irish orphan, travels with a Tibetan lama while trained as a spy for British intelligence. Said's introduction: Kim shows a rich India but within an unquestioned imperial order. Kipling's 'The White Man's Burden' (1899) as imperial ideology.

steps.title: The Tempest
steps.body: Caliban as colonised native ('You taught me language, and my profit on't / Is I know how to curse'); Prospero as coloniser; readings by Octave Mannoni, George Lamming (The Pleasures of Exile), Césaire's Une Tempête, Roberto Fernández Retamar ('Caliban').

steps.title: Others
steps.body: Heart of Darkness (Achebe's critique), A Passage to India (liberal humanism limited by empire; 'No, not yet… No, not there'), Robinson Crusoe (Friday; Coetzee's Foe), Jane Eyre (Bertha; Rhys, Spivak), Mansfield Park (Said).

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: In A Passage to India, the friendship of Aziz and Fielding fails: 'not yet' — the landscape itself says friendship is impossible while the colonial relationship exists. A postcolonial reading notes both Forster's critique of the Raj and his Orientalist images of 'muddle'.

activity.prompt: Empire text and postcolonial response.

quiz.q: 'You taught me language, and my profit on't / Is I know how to curse' is spoken by:
quiz.why: Caliban turns the coloniser's language against him.
Kipling's 1899 poem urged the US to colonise the Philippines.
Kimball O'Hara is the orphaned son of an Irish soldier.

scenes.text: Africa · Caribbean · South Asia · settler colonies — one shared history of empire, many answers.
Apply a concept to a text in every answer.

steps.title: Concept–text pairs
steps.body: Orientalism → Kim, A Passage to India. Mimicry → Naipaul's The Mimic Men, Macaulay. Hybridity → Walcott, Rushdie. Subaltern → Mahasweta Devi's 'Draupadi', Wide Sargasso Sea. Language → Achebe vs Ngũgĩ; Brathwaite's nation language. Counter-discourse → Wide Sargasso Sea, Foe, Une Tempête. Fanon's phases → Things Fall Apart, A Grain of Wheat.

steps.title: Long answers (original)
steps.body: (1) Things Fall Apart as a response to colonial representations of Africa. (2) Hybridity in Walcott's poetry. (3) Wide Sargasso Sea as a 'writing back' to Jane Eyre. (4) Language debate in postcolonial literature. (5) Apply Said's Orientalism to one colonial novel.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.body: Negritude; Nation language; Cultural cringe; Mimicry; Abrogation; Contrapuntal reading; Stolen Generations.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Define the concept with its theorist → identify it in two textual moments with quotation → note complexity (e.g., Achebe critiques Igbo society too) → conclude.

activity.prompt: Final drill: theorist for each concept.

quiz.why: Rhys retells the story of Rochester's first wife from her side.
Phillips coined it for Australia's cultural inferiority complex.

quiz.why: Achebe argued for an English altered to carry African experience.

steps.title: Double colonisation

scenes.text: No drill has gone deeper than about 12 km, yet we know the core is liquid on the outside.
Seismic waves bend and vanish in patterns that reveal every layer below our feet.

steps.title: Layers and discontinuities
steps.body:
- **Crust**: continental (granitic, ~35 km average, up to ~70 km under mountains) and oceanic (basaltic, 5–10 km).
- **Mohorovičić (Moho) discontinuity** separates crust from mantle.
- **Mantle** to ~2,900 km; the **asthenosphere** (roughly 100–250 km) is weak and partially molten, letting the rigid **lithosphere** (crust + upper mantle) move.
- **Gutenberg discontinuity** (~2,900 km) separates mantle and core.
- **Outer core** liquid (iron–nickel); **inner core** solid, from ~5,150 km to the centre (~6,371 km). The Lehmann discontinuity separates them.

steps.title: Seismic evidence
steps.body: P-waves (compressional) travel through solids and liquids; S-waves (shear) travel only through solids. S-waves do not pass through the outer core, giving an **S-wave shadow zone** beyond about 103° from the epicentre; P-waves are refracted, giving a **P-wave shadow zone** between about 103° and 142°. This proves a liquid outer core.

steps.title: From continental drift to plate tectonics
steps.body:
**Wegener (1912)** proposed continental drift from Pangaea, citing jigsaw fit, matching fossils (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris), tillite deposits and rock belts. He lacked a driving force. **Sea-floor spreading** (Hess, 1960s) supplied it: new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges, shown by symmetric magnetic stripes and young ocean-floor ages near ridges. **Plate tectonics** unites these: about seven major and many minor plates move a few cm/year.
- **Divergent**: ridges, rift valleys (Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift).
- **Convergent**: ocean–continent → trench + volcanic arc (Andes); ocean–ocean → island arcs (Japan); continent–continent → fold mountains (Himalaya, India–Eurasia).
- **Transform**: plates slide past (San Andreas Fault).

steps.title: India's journey
steps.body: The Indian plate separated from Gondwana and moved north; its collision with Eurasia began roughly 50 million years ago, building the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau, which are still rising. This is why the Himalayan belt is in the highest seismic zone of India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Lithosphere ≠ crust: the lithosphere includes the uppermost mantle.
- Wegener's theory is continental drift; plate tectonics is the later, broader theory.
- Fold mountains form at continent–continent convergence, not at divergent boundaries.

activity.prompt: Classify each feature by plate-boundary type.

quiz.q: Which discontinuity separates the mantle from the core?
quiz.why: The Gutenberg discontinuity at about 2,900 km depth marks the mantle–core boundary.

quiz.q: The S-wave shadow zone proves that
quiz.why: S-waves cannot travel through liquids, so their absence beyond about 103° shows the outer core is liquid.
The Indian and Eurasian continental plates collided, crumpling sediments into fold mountains.

quiz.q: Which was NOT evidence used by Wegener?
options: Symmetric magnetic stripes on the sea floor
quiz.why: Magnetic striping was discovered in the 1950s–60s and supports sea-floor spreading, after Wegener.

lessons.title: Weathering, mass wasting and the cycle of erosion

story.title: Why do mountains not last forever?

scenes.text: Frost splits rocks on a Ladakh slope while monsoon rain rots granite in Karnataka.
Davis imagined every landscape ageing from youth to old age; Penck disagreed.

steps.title: Weathering
steps.body:
**Weathering** is in-situ breakdown of rock, without transport.
- **Physical (mechanical)**: frost wedging, exfoliation (onion-peel weathering from heating–cooling and unloading), salt crystallisation, block disintegration. Dominant in dry and cold climates.
- **Chemical**: solution (limestone by carbonic acid), oxidation (iron → rust colours), hydration, hydrolysis (feldspar → clay), carbonation. Dominant in hot, humid climates; produces laterite in India.
- **Biological**: roots, burrowing animals, lichens.
**Mass wasting** is downslope movement under gravity: slow (soil creep, solifluction) and rapid (landslides, rockfall, mudflow, debris avalanche).

steps.title: Davis vs Penck
steps.body: **W.M. Davis (1899), Geographical Cycle**: landscape = f(structure, process, stage). After rapid uplift, the land passes through **youth** (V-shaped valleys, waterfalls), **maturity** (maximum relief, meanders begin) and **old age** (broad floodplains) ending as a **peneplain** with monadnocks. **Walther Penck**: uplift and erosion act together; slope form depends on the rate of uplift (waxing, uniform, waning development), and slopes retreat parallel to themselves. **L.C. King** stressed pediplanation by parallel slope retreat in semi-arid lands, ending in a **pediplain**.

steps.title: Applying the models
steps.body: A broad, gently rolling surface with isolated residual hills in peninsular India: Davis would call it a peneplain with monadnocks (old stage); King would call the hills inselbergs on a pediplain formed by scarp retreat. The same landscape gets different explanations from different models.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Weathering is not erosion: erosion involves transport by an agent.
- Davis assumed rapid uplift followed by a long still-stand; Penck did not.
- Exfoliation is physical weathering even though it is often aided by chemical change.

quiz.why: Soil creep is the very slow downslope movement of soil under gravity.

By Bengal the Ganga spreads into meanders, ox-bow lakes and the world's largest delta.

steps.title: Landforms by stage
steps.body:
- **Upper course (erosion)**: V-shaped valleys, gorges and canyons, waterfalls, potholes, interlocking spurs.
- **Middle course**: meanders, alluvial fans at the mountain foot, river terraces.
- **Lower course (deposition)**: floodplains, natural levees, ox-bow lakes (cut-off meanders), braided channels, deltas (arcuate like the Nile and Ganga, bird's-foot like the Mississippi, estuaries where tides sweep sediment away, e.g. Narmada and Tapi).
**Drainage patterns**: dendritic (uniform rock), trellis (folded rock), radial (dome or volcano, e.g. Amarkantak rivers), rectangular (jointed rock), centripetal (basin).

steps.title: Morphometry formulas
steps.body:
Using Strahler stream ordering (two 1st-order streams join to form a 2nd order, etc.):
- **Bifurcation ratio Rb = Nu / N(u+1)** (number of streams of one order ÷ next higher order). Typical 3–5.
- **Drainage density Dd = ΣL / A** (total stream length ÷ basin area, km/km²).
- **Stream frequency Fs = ΣN / A** (number of streams per km²).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A basin has 24 first-order, 6 second-order, 2 third-order and 1 fourth-order stream. Rb(1/2) = 24/6 = **4.0**; Rb(2/3) = 6/2 = **3.0**; Rb(3/4) = 2/1 = **2.0**. Mean Rb = (4 + 3 + 2)/3 = **3.0**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: The same basin: total stream length 180 km, area 60 km². Dd = 180/60 = **3.0 km/km²**. Number of streams = 24 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 33, so Fs = 33/60 = **0.55 per km²**. High Dd suggests impermeable rock, sparse vegetation or heavy rainfall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Two streams of different order joining do not raise the order (a 1st joining a 2nd stays 2nd).
- Drainage density uses length, stream frequency uses count.
- Estuaries, not deltas, form at the mouths of the Narmada and Tapi.

lessons.title: Glacial, aeolian, karst and coastal landforms

scenes.text: Ice carves cirques in Kashmir, wind builds barchans in Jaisalmer.
Groundwater dissolves caves in Meghalaya; waves cut cliffs at Varkala.

steps.title: Glacial
steps.body: Erosional: **cirque** (armchair hollow, often holding a tarn), **arête**, **horn** (Matterhorn), **U-shaped valley**, **hanging valley**, **roches moutonnées**. Depositional: **moraines** (terminal, lateral, medial, ground), **drumlins** (egg-shaped hills), **eskers** (sinuous ridges from meltwater streams), **outwash plains**.

steps.title: Aeolian and karst
steps.body: **Wind**: deflation hollows, **mushroom rocks** (abrasion near the ground), yardangs, zeugen, inselbergs; depositional **barchans** (crescent dunes with horns pointing downwind), seif (longitudinal) dunes, **loess** (fine wind-blown silt, e.g. China's Loess Plateau). **Karst** (limestone dissolved by carbonic acid): sinkholes, swallow holes, uvalas, poljes, caves with **stalactites** (hang from roof) and **stalagmites** (rise from floor). Examples: Borra Caves (Andhra Pradesh), Mawsmai (Meghalaya).

steps.title: Coastal
steps.body: Erosional: cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves → arches → stacks → stumps. Depositional: beaches, spits, bars, tombolos, lagoons (Chilika and Pulicat lie behind sand bars). **Emergent coasts** (land uplifted or sea fell) show raised beaches; **submergent coasts** show rias and fjords.

steps.title: Memory aid
steps.body: Stalactite has a **c** for ceiling; stalagmite has a **g** for ground. Barchan horns point the way the wind goes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Eskers are made by meltwater, drumlins by moving ice.
- Loess is wind-deposited, not river-deposited.
- A spit is attached to land at one end; a bar may close a bay completely.

courses.summary: Atmosphere composition and structure, insolation and heat budget, lapse rates, pressure belts and planetary winds, humidity and precipitation, air masses and cyclones, Köppen classification, ocean relief, temperature, salinity, currents and tides.

story.title: Why is Shimla cooler than Chandigarh?

scenes.text: A two-hour drive up 1,900 metres and the air is noticeably cooler.
The air is heated from below by the ground, not directly by the Sun.

steps.title: Composition and layers
steps.body:
Dry air by volume: nitrogen ~78%, oxygen ~21%, argon ~0.93%, carbon dioxide ~0.04%, plus water vapour (0–4%), dust and ozone.
- **Troposphere** (about 8 km at poles to 18 km at equator): weather, temperature falls with height. Top = tropopause.
- **Stratosphere** (to ~50 km): ozone layer absorbs UV, temperature rises with height.
- **Mesosphere** (to ~80 km): coldest layer, meteors burn.
- **Thermosphere** (includes the ionosphere): reflects radio waves, aurorae.
- **Exosphere**: outermost.

steps.title: Insolation and heat budget
steps.body: Of 100 units of incoming solar radiation, about 35 are reflected back (the Earth's **albedo**), about 14 absorbed by the atmosphere and about 51 absorbed by the surface. The surface re-radiates long-wave (terrestrial) radiation that greenhouse gases absorb, so the atmosphere is heated mainly from below. Heat transfer: conduction, convection, advection, radiation. Insolation varies with latitude (angle of rays), season, day length, cloud cover and distance from the Sun.

steps.title: Lapse rates
steps.body:
- **Normal (environmental) lapse rate** ≈ **6.5 °C per 1,000 m**.
- **Dry adiabatic lapse rate** ≈ **9.8 °C per 1,000 m** (rising unsaturated air).
- **Wet (saturated) adiabatic rate** ≈ 4–7 °C per 1,000 m (latent heat released).
- **Temperature inversion**: temperature increases with height, e.g. on calm winter nights in valleys, causing fog and smog in Delhi winters.
Formula: **T_h = T_0 − (lapse rate × h)**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. Sea-level temperature 30 °C. At 3,000 m with the normal lapse rate: 30 − 6.5 × 3 = 30 − 19.5 = **10.5 °C**.
2. An unsaturated parcel at 25 °C rises 2,000 m: 25 − 9.8 × 2 = **5.4 °C**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ozone is in the stratosphere, not the troposphere.
- Do not use the dry adiabatic rate for still surrounding air; that uses the environmental lapse rate.
- Convert metres to kilometres before multiplying by a per-km rate.

activity.prompt: Foothill town at 300 m records 32 °C. Using 6.5 °C per km, temperature at a hill station at 2,300 m?

quiz.q: The ozone layer lies mainly in the
quiz.why: Most ozone is concentrated in the stratosphere, where it absorbs ultraviolet radiation.
The average environmental fall of temperature with height is about 6.5 °C per kilometre.
About 35 of every 100 units of insolation are reflected back to space.
In an inversion, colder air lies below warmer air, the reverse of normal.

scenes.text: Around 1 June the south-west monsoon bursts over Kerala.
Pressure differences, the Coriolis force and the shifting ITCZ all play a part.

steps.title: Pressure belts and planetary winds
steps.body:
- **Equatorial low** (doldrums, ITCZ) ~0–5°.
- **Subtropical highs** (horse latitudes) ~30° N/S.
- **Subpolar lows** ~60° N/S.
- **Polar highs**.
Winds blow from high to low pressure and are deflected by the **Coriolis force** (right in the north, left in the south — **Ferrel's law**): **trade winds** (30°→equator, north-east and south-east trades), **westerlies** (30°→60°, the Roaring Forties in the south), **polar easterlies**. Three-cell model: Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells. **Jet streams** are fast upper-air westerlies; the subtropical westerly jet and the tropical easterly jet influence the Indian monsoon.

steps.title: Humidity and precipitation
steps.body:
- **Absolute humidity**: grams of water vapour per m³ of air.
- **Relative humidity (RH) = actual vapour ÷ maximum the air can hold at that temperature × 100**.
- **Dew point**: temperature at which air becomes saturated.
Precipitation types: **convectional** (equatorial afternoon storms), **orographic** (windward side of mountains, e.g. Western Ghats; leeward rain-shadow, e.g. the Deccan interior), **cyclonic/frontal**.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Air at 30 °C can hold 30 g/m³; it actually holds 18 g/m³. RH = 18/30 × 100 = **60%**. If it cools so that its capacity falls to 18 g/m³, RH becomes **100%**: that temperature is the dew point.

steps.title: Mawsynram and Leh
steps.body: Moist Bay of Bengal winds funnel into the Khasi Hills, giving Mawsynram and Cherrapunji some of the world's highest rainfall (orographic). Leh, behind the Himalaya, is a cold desert in the rain shadow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Winds are named after the direction they blow FROM.
- The Coriolis force is zero at the equator.
- RH can rise without adding water, simply by cooling the air.

activity.prompt: Air holds 12 g/m³ of vapour; at its temperature it could hold 20 g/m³. Relative humidity in %?

quiz.q: In the Northern Hemisphere winds are deflected to the
quiz.why: Ferrel's law: the Coriolis force deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

quiz.q: Rainfall on the windward Western Ghats is
quiz.why: Moist winds forced up the Ghats cool and condense, producing orographic rain.

quiz.q: Dew point is the temperature at which
quiz.why: At the dew point relative humidity reaches 100% and condensation begins.

lessons.title: Air masses, cyclones and climate classification

scenes.text: Cyclone Fani hit Odisha in 2019 with winds over 170 km/h.
Western disturbances bring winter rain to Punjab and snow to Kashmir.

steps.title: Air masses and fronts
steps.body: An **air mass** is a large body of air with uniform temperature and humidity, named by source: mT (maritime tropical), cT (continental tropical), mP, cP, and arctic. Where two meet a **front** forms: cold, warm, stationary and occluded fronts.

steps.title: Tropical vs temperate cyclones
steps.body:
**Tropical cyclones**: form over warm seas (above about 26–27 °C) between roughly 5° and 30° latitude, need Coriolis force, have a calm **eye**, very strong winds, move east to west, weaken over land. Called hurricanes (Atlantic), typhoons (West Pacific), cyclones (Indian Ocean).
**Temperate (extra-tropical) cyclones**: form along polar fronts in mid-latitudes, are larger, have fronts but no eye, move west to east with the westerlies; western disturbances reaching India are related systems.

steps.title: Köppen scheme
steps.body: Based on temperature and precipitation: **A** tropical humid (Af rainforest, Am monsoon, Aw savanna), **B** dry (BWh hot desert, BSh steppe), **C** warm temperate (Cwa monsoon with dry winter, Cs Mediterranean), **D** cold snow-forest, **E** polar (ET tundra), and H highland. In India: Amw on the Konkan–Malabar coast, Aw over much of the peninsula, BWhw in western Rajasthan, Cwg over the Ganga plain, Dfc in Arunachal, E in high Himalaya (as given in NCERT-level descriptions).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Tropical cyclones do not form on the equator (no Coriolis force).
- 's' in Köppen means a dry summer; 'w' means a dry winter.
- Temperate cyclones have fronts; tropical cyclones generally do not.

lessons.title: Oceanography: relief, salinity, currents and tides

scenes.text: A bottle dropped off Florida can wash up in Norway.
The Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Drift carry it, and keep north-west Europe mild.

steps.title: Ocean-floor relief
steps.body: **Continental shelf** (gentle, to about 200 m depth; rich fisheries and oil, e.g. Bombay High), **continental slope**, **continental rise**, **abyssal plain** (3–6 km deep), **mid-ocean ridges**, **seamounts and guyots**, **trenches** (deepest: Mariana Trench, ~11 km).

steps.title: Temperature and salinity
steps.body: Surface temperature falls from the equator to the poles; with depth there is a sharp **thermocline**. **Salinity** = grams of dissolved salt per 1,000 g of seawater (‰ or PSU); average about **35‰**. Higher where evaporation is high and fresh water inflow low (Red Sea ~40‰, Dead Sea and Lake Van far higher); lower near river mouths and melting ice (Baltic Sea). Highest open-ocean salinity is in the subtropics, not at the equator, because equatorial rainfall dilutes it.

steps.title: Currents and tides
steps.body:
Currents are driven by planetary winds, temperature and salinity differences, Coriolis force and coastline shape. Warm: Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil, Agulhas. Cold: Labrador, Oyashio, California, Humboldt (Peru), Benguela, Canaries. Cold currents on western coasts of continents in the tropics help form deserts (Atacama, Namib). The North Indian Ocean currents **reverse with the monsoon**.
**Tides** are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity (and the Sun's): **spring tides** at new and full moon (Sun, Moon, Earth aligned), **neap tides** at first and last quarter. There are usually two high tides in about 24 h 50 min.

steps.title: Solved example: salinity
steps.body: A 2 kg sample of seawater leaves 74 g of salts when evaporated. Salinity = 74/2,000 × 1,000 = **37‰**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Salinity is per thousand (‰), not per cent.
- Spring tides have nothing to do with the season spring.
- The Humboldt is a cold current; the Gulf Stream is warm.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Human and economic geography
courses.summary: Nature and schools of human geography, population distribution, growth and the demographic transition, migration, rural and urban settlements with Christaller's central place theory, and economic location theories of von Thünen and Weber.
outcomes: Contrast determinism, possibilism and neo-determinism
Compute density, sex ratio, growth rate and doubling time
Explain the demographic transition model and migration theories
Classify settlements and explain central place theory
Apply von Thünen and Weber location theories

story.title: Does nature decide, or do people?

scenes.text: In Rajasthan, people built stepwells and johads to store scarce rain.
Was their life dictated by the desert, or a choice among possibilities?

steps.title: Schools of thought
steps.body:
- **Environmental determinism**: nature controls human life (Ratzel, Ellen Churchill Semple, Ellsworth Huntington).
- **Possibilism**: nature offers possibilities, humans choose (Vidal de la Blache, Lucien Febvre, who coined the term).
- **Neo-determinism / stop-and-go determinism** (Griffith Taylor): humans can modify nature but within limits, like traffic obeying signals.
Later approaches: **quantitative revolution** (1950s–60s, models and statistics), **behavioural**, **welfare/radical** (inequality, poverty), **humanistic** (lived experience, sense of place), **postmodern**.

steps.title: Classifying an example
steps.body: Flood-plain zoning that restricts building in a river's high-risk zone accepts nature's limits but still uses the land wisely — this fits **neo-determinism**. Terrace farming in the Himalaya shows humans adapting slopes, a **possibilist** view.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: In a long answer, define each school, name its proponents, give one Indian example and end with a critique: determinism ignores technology; possibilism can overstate human freedom.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Vidal de la Blache is the father of possibilism, not determinism.
- Griffith Taylor's view is 'stop-and-go determinism', not pure possibilism.

activity.prompt: Match the thinker to the school.

quiz.why: Lucien Febvre named the idea developed by Vidal de la Blache.
Griffith Taylor compared human use of nature to traffic obeying signals.
In the 1950s–60s geographers adopted statistical methods and spatial models.

options: human experience and sense of place
quiz.why: It centres the perceptions, values and lived experience of people.

scenes.text: UN estimates in 2023 put India as the world's most populous country.
Density, sex ratio and growth rate turn such headlines into measurable indicators.

steps.title: Key measures
steps.body:
- **Arithmetic density** = population ÷ area (persons/km²). India (Census 2011): **382/km²**; Bihar highest among states (1,106).
- **Sex ratio (India definition)** = females per 1,000 males. India 2011: **943**; Kerala 1,084.
- **Growth rate** = (P₂ − P₁)/P₁ × 100. India 2001–2011 decadal growth: **17.7%**.
- **Crude birth/death rate** per 1,000 people; natural increase = CBR − CDR.
- **Doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ annual growth rate (%)** (rule of 70).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A district has 5,40,000 males and 5,13,000 females. Sex ratio = 5,13,000/5,40,000 × 1,000 = **950**. If its area is 2,600 km², density = 10,53,000/2,600 = **405 persons/km²**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Population grew from 80 lakh to 92 lakh in ten years. Decadal growth = 12/80 × 100 = **15%**. With CBR 20 and CDR 7 per 1,000, natural increase = 13 per 1,000 = 1.3% per year, so doubling time ≈ 70/1.3 ≈ **54 years**.

steps.title: Demographic transition model
steps.body: Stage 1 high birth and death rates, slow growth; Stage 2 death rate falls (health, food), population explodes; Stage 3 birth rate falls (urbanisation, education, contraception), growth slows; Stage 4 both low, stable; Stage 5 (some versions) birth below death, decline (Japan). India is broadly in late Stage 3. **Malthus** (1798) argued population grows geometrically and food arithmetically, leading to positive and preventive checks.

steps.title: Migration
steps.body: Push factors (unemployment, floods, conflict) and pull factors (jobs, services). **Ravenstein's laws** (1885): most migrants move short distances, by steps, long-distance migrants go to big cities, women dominate short-distance moves, each stream produces a counter-stream. **Lee's model** (1966) adds origin, destination, intervening obstacles and personal factors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- India's sex ratio is females per 1,000 males; many international sources use males per 100 females.
- Divide by the earlier population, not the later, for growth rate.
- Natural increase per 1,000 must be divided by 10 to get per cent.

quiz.why: Census 2011 recorded 943 females per 1,000 males.

quiz.why: Rule of 70: 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years.

options: death rate falls while birth rate stays high
quiz.why: Better health lowers mortality before fertility falls, causing rapid growth.

quiz.why: This is one of Ravenstein's laws of migration.

story.title: Why are there many villages but few metros?

scenes.text: You buy bread in your locality but travel to a big city for a heart surgeon.
Walter Christaller turned this everyday fact into hexagons.

steps.title: Rural settlements
steps.body: Types: **clustered/compact** (fertile plains, e.g. Ganga plain), **semi-clustered**, **hamleted** (fragmented, e.g. middle Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh), **dispersed** (hills, forests, e.g. Meghalaya, Himachal). Patterns: linear (along roads, rivers), rectangular, circular, star-like, T-shaped, double. Site factors: water supply, defence, high ground, fertile land.

steps.title: Urban settlements
steps.body: Census of India definition of a town: statutory town, or **census town** with population ≥ 5,000, density ≥ 400 per km², and ≥ 75% of male main workers in non-agricultural work. Urban models: **Burgess concentric zone** (1925), **Hoyt sector** (1939), **Harris and Ullman multiple nuclei** (1945). **Primate city** (Jefferson) far larger than the next; **rank–size rule** (Zipf): P_n = P₁/n.

steps.title: Christaller's central place theory (1933)
steps.body: Assumptions: an isotropic plain, evenly spread population, rational consumers going to the nearest centre. Concepts: **threshold** (minimum population needed to support a good) and **range** (maximum distance people will travel). Market areas become **hexagons** to avoid overlaps and gaps. Principles: **marketing (K = 3)**, **transport or traffic (K = 4)**, **administrative (K = 7)**. Higher-order centres are fewer and farther apart. August Lösch (1940s) later modified the theory.

steps.title: Solved example: rank–size
steps.body: If the largest city has 1,20,00,000 people, the rank–size rule predicts the 4th city to have 1,20,00,000/4 = **30,00,000** and the 6th city 20,00,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- K = 3 marketing, K = 4 transport (traffic), K = 7 administrative.
- Threshold is a population; range is a distance.
- Burgess is concentric; Hoyt is sectoral.

activity.prompt: Match each principle to its K-value.

quiz.why: Hexagons fill space without gaps or overlaps while staying close to circles.

quiz.q: The minimum population needed to support a service is its
quiz.why: Threshold is the minimum demand that makes a good or service viable.

quiz.q: The multiple-nuclei model was proposed by
quiz.why: Harris and Ullman (1945) proposed that cities grow around several nuclei.

quiz.q: By rank–size rule, if the top city has 90 lakh, the 3rd city has
quiz.why: P₃ = 90/3 = 30 lakh.

lessons.title: Economic location theories: von Thünen and Weber

story.title: Milk near the city, wheat far away

scenes.text: Dairy farms crowd around big cities; wheat comes from far-off fields.
Steel plants sit near iron and coal in Jharkhand and Odisha. Two classic theories explain both.

steps.title: Von Thünen (1826)
steps.body:
An isolated state with one city on a flat, uniform plain. Farmers maximise **location rent**:
**LR = Y(p − c) − Y·f·d**, where Y = yield per unit area, p = market price per unit, c = production cost per unit, f = freight rate per unit per km, d = distance. Land use forms **concentric rings**: (1) market gardening and dairy, (2) forest (fuel wood, heavy), (3) intensive arable, (4) arable with fallow, (5) three-field system, (6) ranching; then wilderness.

steps.title: Weber (1909): least-cost industrial location
steps.body: Industry locates where total transport cost is lowest, then adjusts for labour and agglomeration. **Material index (MI) = weight of localised raw materials ÷ weight of product**. MI > 1 (weight-losing, e.g. iron and steel, sugar) → locate near raw materials; MI < 1 or ubiquitous materials (weight-gaining, e.g. soft drinks, bakeries) → near market. **Locational triangle** with two material sources and one market; **isodapanes** join points of equal extra transport cost.

steps.title: Solved example: material index
steps.body: To make 1 tonne of sugar a mill uses about 10 tonnes of sugarcane: MI = 10/1 = **10** → strongly weight-losing, so mills are near cane fields (as in UP and Maharashtra).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Von Thünen's second ring is forest, not grain — wood was heavy and needed close to the city.
- In Weber, ubiquities (water, air) available everywhere do not pull industry.
- Location rent ≠ land rent paid to a landlord; it is the economic surplus from position.

activity.prompt: Y = 1,000 kg/ha, p = ₹30/kg, c = ₹18/kg, f = ₹0.20 per kg per km, d = 25 km. Location rent in ₹/ha?

quiz.why: Perishable, high-value produce is grown nearest the market.

quiz.q: Material index greater than 1 means the industry should locate near
quiz.why: Weight-losing processes save transport by locating near the raw material.
Weber used isodapanes to show points of equal extra transport cost away from the least-cost point.

quiz.q: With Y(p − c) = 12,000 and Y·f = 150 per km, the margin of cultivation is
quiz.why: 12,000/150 = 80 km, where location rent falls to zero.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Geography of India
courses.summary: India's location and physiographic divisions, Himalayan and peninsular drainage, the monsoon mechanism and rainfall distribution, soils and natural vegetation, and agriculture, minerals, energy and industrial regions.
outcomes: Describe the six physiographic divisions of India
Contrast Himalayan and peninsular rivers
Explain the onset, advance and retreat of the monsoon
Classify Indian soils and forest types
Locate major crops, minerals and industrial regions
Compute cropping intensity and other agricultural indices

scenes.text: India spans about 3,214 km north–south and 2,933 km east–west.
In that space sit the youngest mountains and some of the oldest rocks on Earth.

steps.title: Location facts
steps.body: Mainland India extends between about **8°4′ N and 37°6′ N** and **68°7′ E and 97°25′ E**. Area about **3.28 million km²** (2.4% of world land). The **Tropic of Cancer** (23.5° N) passes through eight states (Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram). **Indian Standard Time** is based on **82°30′ E** (near Mirzapur/Prayagraj), 5 h 30 min ahead of GMT. Southernmost point: Indira Point (Great Nicobar).

steps.title: Physiographic divisions
steps.body:
1. **Northern mountains**: Trans-Himalaya; Himalaya in three parallel ranges — **Himadri** (Greater, avg ~6,000 m, Everest, Kanchenjunga), **Himachal** (Lesser; Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar; hill stations), **Shiwaliks** (outer, with **duns** like Dehradun); and the Purvanchal hills.
2. **Northern plains** (Indus–Ganga–Brahmaputra): **bhabar** (pebbles, streams vanish), **terai** (marshy), **bhangar** (older alluvium, kankar), **khadar** (new alluvium).
3. **Peninsular plateau**: Central Highlands (Malwa, Bundelkhand, Chotanagpur) and Deccan Plateau, bounded by Western and Eastern Ghats. Anaimudi (2,695 m) is the highest peak of peninsular India.
4. **Indian desert** (Thar). 5. **Coastal plains** (western: Kachchh, Konkan, Kanara, Malabar; eastern: Utkal, Andhra, Coromandel). 6. **Islands**: Andaman & Nicobar (volcanic/tectonic) and Lakshadweep (coral).

steps.title: Solved example: time difference
steps.body: Every 1° of longitude = 4 minutes of time. Longitudinal extent ≈ 97°25′ − 68°7′ = 29°18′ ≈ 29.3°. Time difference ≈ 29.3 × 4 = **117 min ≈ 2 hours** between Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat — this is why the Sun rises about two hours earlier in the east.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Bhabar comes before terai going south from the hills.
- Khadar is new alluvium; bhangar is old.
- Lakshadweep islands are coral, not volcanic; Barren Island (Andamans) is India's only active volcano.

activity.prompt: Two places differ by 15° of longitude. Local time difference in minutes?

quiz.q: IST is based on the meridian
quiz.why: Indian Standard Time is the local time of 82°30′ E.
The Shiwaliks are the outermost and lowest range, made of unconsolidated sediments.

quiz.why: Khadar is fresh alluvium deposited yearly on floodplains.

story.title: Rivers that never dry, rivers that wait for rain

scenes.text: The Ganga flows even in May, fed by Himalayan snow.
Many peninsular rivers shrink to trickles before the monsoon.

steps.title: Himalayan vs peninsular rivers
steps.body:
| Himalayan | Peninsular |
|---|---|
| Perennial (snow + rain) | Seasonal, rain-fed |
| Antecedent, deep gorges | Old, graded, shallow valleys |
| Meanders, shifting courses | Fixed courses |
| Large deltas | Deltas (east) / estuaries (west) |

**Indus system**: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej (Indus Waters Treaty 1960 gives eastern rivers Ravi, Beas, Sutlej to India). **Ganga system**: Bhagirathi and Alaknanda meet at **Devprayag**; tributaries Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi ('sorrow of Bihar'), Son, Chambal. **Brahmaputra**: Tsangpo in Tibet, Dihang in Arunachal, Jamuna in Bangladesh.

steps.title: Peninsular rivers
steps.body: East-flowing to the Bay of Bengal: **Mahanadi, Godavari (largest peninsular river, 'Dakshin Ganga'), Krishna, Kaveri** — form deltas. West-flowing to the Arabian Sea: **Narmada and Tapi** flow through rift valleys and form estuaries; also short swift rivers of the Western Ghats (Sharavati with Jog Falls).

steps.title: Map practice
steps.body: On an outline map, trace the Narmada between the Vindhyas (north) and Satpuras (south); the Tapi just south of the Satpuras. Mark Devprayag, the Kosi and the Godavari delta — these are frequent map questions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Godavari is the longest peninsular river, not the Krishna.
- The Narmada flows west, not east.
- Devprayag (not Rudraprayag) is where the name Ganga begins.

activity.prompt: Classify each river.

quiz.why: At Devprayag the two head-streams join to form the Ganga.
The Kosi shifts course and floods north Bihar frequently.
The Tapi flows west through a rift valley and enters the sea as an estuary.

options: snow and glaciers as well as rain
quiz.why: Snow and glacier melt sustain flow in the dry season.

scenes.text: About three-quarters of India's annual rainfall falls between June and September.
Rain decides soils, forests and the fate of kharif crops.

steps.title: Monsoon mechanism
steps.body:
- Summer heating creates a low over north-west India; the **ITCZ** shifts north (to about 20–25° N).
- South-east trades cross the equator, are deflected by the Coriolis force and become the **south-west monsoon**.
- The **subtropical westerly jet** shifts north of the Himalaya; the **tropical easterly jet** sets up over the peninsula.
- **El Niño** (warm eastern Pacific) is often linked with weaker Indian monsoons; the **Indian Ocean Dipole** also matters.
Two branches: **Arabian Sea branch** (Western Ghats, onset in Kerala around 1 June) and **Bay of Bengal branch** (north-east India, then up the Ganga plain). **Retreating monsoon** (Oct–Nov) brings rain to Tamil Nadu coast with the north-east monsoon. Seasons: cold weather, hot weather (mango showers, kalbaisakhi, loo), south-west monsoon, retreating monsoon.

steps.title: Soils (ICAR classification, simplified)
steps.body:
- **Alluvial**: most widespread, Indo-Gangetic plain; rich in potash, poor in nitrogen.
- **Black (regur)**: Deccan lava; clayey, retains moisture, self-ploughing cracks; ideal for **cotton**.
- **Red and yellow**: crystalline rocks, red from iron oxide; Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Chhattisgarh.
- **Laterite**: high rainfall, leaching; Western Ghats, Meghalaya; cashew, tea, coffee.
- **Arid**, **saline**, **peaty/marshy**, **forest/mountain** soils.

steps.title: Natural vegetation
steps.body: Tropical evergreen (rainfall > 200 cm; Western Ghats, NE), tropical deciduous (100–200 cm moist, 70–100 cm dry; the most widespread; teak, sal), tropical thorn (< 70 cm; Rajasthan), montane forests (oak, deodar, then alpine meadows), and **mangroves** (Sundarbans, sundari trees). India State of Forest Report 2021 put forest cover at about **21.7%** of geographical area.

steps.title: Solved example: share of monsoon rain
steps.body: A station receives 1,180 mm in a year, of which 885 mm falls in June–September. Share = 885/1,180 × 100 = **75%**, typical of monsoon India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Tamil Nadu gets most of its rain in Oct–Dec, not June–Sept.
- Black soil is ideal for cotton; laterite is poor unless manured.
- Deciduous (monsoon) forests, not evergreen, are India's most widespread type.

story.title: From Punjab's wheat to Odisha's iron

scenes.text: The Green Revolution transformed Punjab and Haryana in the 1960s.
The Chotanagpur plateau holds coal and iron that feed India's steel belt.

steps.title: Agriculture
steps.body:
Crop seasons: **kharif** (sown with the monsoon, June–July: rice, maize, cotton, soybean, groundnut), **rabi** (sown Oct–Dec, harvested March–April: wheat, gram, mustard), **zaid** (summer: watermelon, cucumber, fodder). Leading states (broadly): rice — West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab; wheat — Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab; cotton — Gujarat, Maharashtra; tea — Assam; coffee — Karnataka; sugarcane — Uttar Pradesh.
**Cropping intensity = gross cropped area ÷ net sown area × 100**.

steps.title: Solved example: cropping intensity
steps.body: A district has net sown area 2,40,000 ha and gross cropped area 3,36,000 ha. Cropping intensity = 3,36,000/2,40,000 × 100 = **140%**: on average 40% of the land is cropped twice in a year.

steps.title: Minerals and energy
steps.body:
- **Coal**: Gondwana coalfields of Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro (Damodar valley), Korba, Talcher, Singrauli; tertiary coal in the north-east.
- **Iron ore**: Odisha–Jharkhand belt (Mayurbhanj, Noamundi), Bailadila (Chhattisgarh), Karnataka, Goa.
- **Petroleum**: Digboi (Assam, oldest refinery area), Bombay High, Ankleshwar, KG basin.
- **Bauxite**: Odisha (Koraput), Jharkhand. **Mica**: Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan.
Non-conventional energy: solar (Rajasthan, Gujarat), wind (Tamil Nadu, Gujarat).

steps.title: Industrial regions
steps.body: Major regions: Mumbai–Pune, Hugli, Bengaluru–Chennai, Gujarat (Ahmedabad–Vadodara), **Chotanagpur** (steel: Jamshedpur, Bokaro, Durgapur, Rourkela, Bhilai), Vishakhapatnam–Guntur, Gurugram–Delhi–Meerut, Kollam–Thiruvananthapuram.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wheat is a rabi crop; rice is mainly kharif.
- Cropping intensity can exceed 100%; it cannot be below 100%.
- Jharia is a coalfield, not an iron mine.
